Business structure affects how a company is organized and managed. The guide introduces important considerations involved in selecting a business entity, including administrative responsibilities and organizational planning.

Safety is an essential part of construction operations. Contractors must understand the importance of workplace hazard awareness, safety responsibilities, and organized jobsite practices.

Customer Relations

Professional customer relationships depend on clear communication, accurate expectations, and organized documentation. Strong customer service practices support effective project coordination and business reputation.

Financial Management

Financial management helps contractors understand business expenses, cash flow, project costs, and the financial position of their companies. These concepts are important for informed business decisions.

Construction Accounting

Accounting provides information about business transactions and financial performance. Reviewing basic accounting principles helps contractors understand the importance of accurate records and organized reporting.

Determine whether you are pursuing the Louisiana Master Plumber license or the Master Natural Gas Fitter license. Each classification involves different technical responsibilities and examination requirements.

Step 2: Review Eligibility Requirements

After passing the required examination, follow the Board's instructions for completing the applicable licensing paperwork and satisfying the remaining requirements.

State Requirements

The State Plumbing Board of Louisiana establishes licensing requirements for professionals performing regulated plumbing and natural gas work.

A Louisiana Master Plumber is qualified to perform plumbing installation, repair, and maintenance and may employ licensed journeyman plumbers and registered apprentices within the applicable regulatory framework.

A Louisiana Master Natural Gas Fitter is qualified to install, repair, and alter natural gas systems and employ licensed natural gas fitters and registered apprentices.

Master-level professionals must understand more than technical installation procedures. Business responsibilities, financial management, customer relationships, contracts, safety, and applicable laws are also important parts of operating professionally.

The NASCLA guide addresses these business-related subjects and supports candidates preparing for the designated examination components.

Louisiana license holders must also satisfy applicable continuing education and licensing renewal responsibilities established by the State Plumbing Board.

Prepare for the NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors with a complete collection of nine approved exam references. The NASCLA Master Unlimited Electrical Contractor Exam Book Package brings together the electrical code, federal safety regulations, project management resources, energy standard, business and law guide, workplace electrical safety standard, field reference, and electrical theory book used for this open-book examination.

This package is designed for electrical contractors, master electricians, unlimited electricians, and qualifying individuals preparing for a contractor-level examination. The exam extends beyond installation rules and electrical calculations. Candidates are also expected to understand project design and management, workplace safety, business operations, code compliance, energy requirements, wiring methods, electrical equipment, special installations, and communication systems.

Having the correct reference books is an essential part of open-book preparation. Candidates must bring their own approved materials to the testing center because the references are not supplied onsite. This package helps eliminate the need to search for each publication separately and gives candidates a coordinated set of books for study and examination-day use.

The National Electrical Code serves as the primary installation reference, while the OSHA publications address construction and general-industry safety. The Project Management Body of Knowledge and NASCLA Contractors Guide support project planning, business operations, contracts, risk management, and contractor responsibilities. ANSI/ASHRAE/IES Standard 90.1 addresses energy-efficiency requirements for applicable buildings and sites. NFPA 70E focuses on electrical safety-related work practices, Ugly’s Electrical References provides practical formulas and tables, and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications reinforces the principles used in electrical calculations and code applications.

Owning the books is only the beginning of effective preparation. Candidates should learn how each reference is organized, identify which publication applies to a particular subject, and practice locating information under timed conditions. A well-planned study routine combines electrical knowledge, code interpretation, calculation practice, project-management review, safety preparation, and repeated book navigation.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors is intended for master electricians and unlimited electricians who conduct business involving the installation, maintenance, and repair of electrical work in accordance with applicable standards and codes.

The examination contains 100 scored questions. Candidates must answer at least 75 questions correctly to meet the minimum passing score. The examination allows 270 minutes, providing four hours and thirty minutes to complete the scored questions and any additional experimental items.

Ten non-scored experimental questions are administered in addition to the scored examination. These questions are used in the development of future licensing examinations and do not count toward the candidate’s final result.

The scored examination is divided among the following subject areas:

  • Project Design and Management: 8 questions
  • Safety: 9 questions
  • Electrical Theory and Principles: 11 questions
  • General Code Requirements: 17 questions
  • Wiring and Protection: 17 questions
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: 16 questions
  • Equipment for General Use: 13 questions
  • Special Occupancies, Special Equipment, and Special Conditions: 8 questions
  • Communication Systems: 1 question

General code requirements, wiring and protection, and wiring methods and materials account for a substantial portion of the examination. Candidates should devote significant study time to NEC organization, conductor requirements, branch circuits, feeders, services, overcurrent protection, grounding, bonding, raceways, cables, boxes, fittings, and installation rules.

Contractor-level preparation should also address project design and management. Candidates may need to apply concepts involving project planning, scheduling, communication, procurement, contracts, quality, cost, risk, and coordination. The included project-management and business-law references support these areas.

A physical diagram or blueprint packet is provided at the testing center. Candidates should be prepared to interpret plans, specifications, schedules, symbols, equipment information, and project requirements. A silent, nonprinting, non-programmable calculator may be used during the examination.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Master Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination is an open-book test. Candidates must bring their approved references to the testing center because the books are not provided at the examination site.

Approved reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed. Permanent tabs may be used to identify chapters, articles, tables, and other important sections. Temporary tabs, including removable notes and Post-it-style products, are not allowed. Books must otherwise remain unmarked and may not contain handwritten notes, loose papers, or attached additional sheets.

The open-book format rewards candidates who understand both the subject matter and the organization of the references. Searching every question from the beginning of a book is not an effective strategy for a timed contractor examination. Candidates should know which publication is most likely to contain the answer and how to reach the relevant section quickly.

Begin by learning the table of contents, index, chapter arrangement, article structure, definitions, major tables, and appendices in each book. Practice identifying whether a question relates to the NEC, OSHA construction regulations, OSHA general-industry standards, NFPA 70E, project management, energy requirements, business and law, field calculations, or electrical theory.

Permanent tabs should support an established navigation system. They are most useful when candidates have already practiced with the books and understand why each section matters. During study sessions, use the references exactly as they will be used on exam day and practice moving between multiple books without electronic search tools.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA examination does not automatically issue an electrical contractor, master electrician, or unlimited electrician license. The examination may satisfy the trade-testing requirement for participating regulatory agencies, but every applicant must complete the licensing process required by the state or jurisdiction where the credential will be used.

  1. Select the licensing jurisdiction. Identify the state or regulatory agency where you intend to apply for an electrical contractor, master electrician, or unlimited electrician license.
  2. Confirm examination acceptance. Verify that the jurisdiction accepts the NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors for the desired classification.
  3. Review eligibility requirements. Determine whether the agency requires documented electrical experience, supervisory experience, education, financial information, insurance, business registration, or other qualifications.
  4. Apply for NASCLA examination eligibility. Complete the current application process through the NASCLA National Examination Database and submit the required application materials.
  5. Receive examination approval. After approval, follow the instructions provided for scheduling the examination through the testing provider.
  6. Prepare with the approved books. Study the examination outline and become familiar with all nine references in this package.
  7. Schedule and take the examination. Follow the testing provider’s requirements for identification, calculators, reference books, arrival time, security, and prohibited materials.
  8. Access the examination record. After a passing result is processed, create or access the appropriate account in the NASCLA National Examination Database.
  9. Send the transcript. Purchase and electronically transmit the examination transcript to a participating state agency.
  10. Complete the state licensing application. Submit all additional forms, fees, business documents, experience records, and supporting materials required by the jurisdiction.

State Requirements

The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors is accepted by participating regulatory agencies as an alternative to certain state-specific trade examinations. Acceptance does not eliminate the remaining requirements for an electrical contractor or master electrician license.

Each state determines the classifications for which it accepts the examination. A jurisdiction may require applicants to document electrical work experience, supervisory experience, education, financial responsibility, insurance coverage, business registration, or the designation of a qualifying individual.

A separate state business and law examination may also be required. The business and project-management material included in the NASCLA electrical exam does not automatically replace a jurisdiction’s separate business-law testing requirement.

Some agencies issue individual master electrician credentials, while others regulate electrical contracting businesses and require a qualified individual to pass the trade examination. License names, scopes of work, renewal rules, continuing education requirements, and financial standards vary by jurisdiction.

After passing the examination, candidates can use the NASCLA National Examination Database to send their results electronically to participating agencies. The receiving agency evaluates the complete application and determines whether the applicant satisfies its licensing requirements.

Reference Books

  • National Electrical Code, 2023
    The 2023 National Electrical Code provides the principal installation requirements for electrical systems. It covers wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, and communication systems.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1926 - OSHA Construction Industry Regulations
    This OSHA reference addresses federal safety requirements for construction work. It supports preparation involving electrical hazards, jobsite conditions, employee protection, personal protective equipment, equipment use, and safe construction practices.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1910 - OSHA Occupational Safety and Health Standards
    This publication contains federal occupational safety and health standards for general industry. It addresses workplace hazards, electrical safety, employee protection, equipment, training, and employer responsibilities.
  • A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge, 2021, 7th Edition
    This project-management reference presents principles and performance areas that support planning, delivery, measurement, uncertainty management, stakeholder coordination, teamwork, and project value.
  • ANSI/ASHRAE/IES Standard 90.1, 2022 Energy Standard for Sites and Buildings Except Low-Rise Residential Buildings - I-P Edition
    This standard provides energy-efficiency requirements for applicable sites and buildings. It includes provisions affecting electrical power, lighting systems, equipment, controls, and energy-conscious building design.
  • NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Basic 14th Edition
    This guide supports contractor-level preparation involving business planning, project management, contracts, risk management, safety, estimating, scheduling, financial administration, and other responsibilities associated with operating a contracting business.
  • NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    NFPA 70E addresses electrical safety-related work practices, including risk assessment, shock protection, arc-flash protection, approach boundaries, personal protective equipment, energized work, and safe maintenance practices.
  • Ugly’s Electrical References, 2023
    This compact field reference contains commonly used electrical formulas, tables, conversions, conductor information, motor data, and practical information that supports calculation and field-knowledge review.
  • Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications
    This publication connects foundational electrical theory with practical NEC applications. It supports study involving voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, transformers, motors, calculations, and electrical problem-solving.

Build a study plan around the official examination content outline. These subjects deserve substantial preparation, but candidates should not ignore project management, safety, theory, energy standards, special installations, or communication systems.

Complete timed practice sessions with all nine references nearby. Track how long it takes to determine the subject, choose a book, locate the section, and confirm the answer. The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians evaluates the knowledge and skills associated with installing, maintaining, troubleshooting, and repairing electrical systems in accordance with applicable codes and accepted trade practices. Organizing study around the official subject areas can help candidates avoid spending all their preparation time in a single book. Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians contains 100 scored questions. Candidates must answer at least 70 questions correctly to achieve the minimum passing score. The examination allows 300 minutes, giving candidates five hours to work through the scored questions and any additional non-scored experimental items included for examination-development purposes.

The examination content is divided among ten subject areas:

  • Interpreting Plans and Specifications: 6 scored questions
  • Basic Electrical Safety: 8 scored questions
  • Electrical Theory and Principles: 10 scored questions
  • Testing and Troubleshooting: 7 scored questions
  • General Code Requirements: 15 scored questions
  • Wiring and Protection: 18 scored questions
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: 16 scored questions
  • Equipment for General Use: 10 scored questions
  • Special Occupancies and Special Equipment: 8 scored questions
  • Special Conditions and Communication Systems: 2 scored questions

Ten non-scored experimental questions may also be administered. These questions are used to support the development of future licensing examinations and do not count toward the candidate’s final score.

A physical diagram or blueprint packet is provided at the testing center. Candidates may also use a silent, nonprinting, non-programmable calculator during the examination. The testing format presents one question at a time, and candidates may return to previously answered questions while examination time remains.

Wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, and general code requirements represent a substantial portion of the scored examination. Candidates should dedicate meaningful preparation time to conductor requirements, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, raceways, cables, boxes, equipment installation, branch circuits, feeders, services, and other NEC-based subjects. Preparation should also cover safety, theory, plans, troubleshooting, special installations, and communication systems because every content area contributes to the final score.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing their permitted references to the testing center because the books are not supplied at the examination site.

Approved reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed. Permanent tabs may be used to organize sections and improve navigation. Temporary tabs, including removable notes such as Post-it products, are not permitted. References must otherwise remain unmarked and may not contain handwritten notes, loose sheets, attached papers, or other added material.

Open-book testing rewards preparation and familiarity. Five hours may sound generous, but looking up every answer from the beginning of a book can quickly consume valuable time. Candidates should practice identifying the correct reference, locating the applicable chapter or article, reading tables accurately, and confirming that exceptions or special conditions do not change the answer.

A practical preparation method is to study each reference individually before working with the entire package. Learn the table of contents, index, chapter structure, major articles, appendices, formulas, and frequently used tables. Once that foundation is established, complete mixed practice sessions that require movement among the NEC, OSHA standards, NFPA publications, and electrical theory material.

Permanent tabs should support navigation rather than replace knowledge. Tabs are most useful when they identify major divisions, frequently tested articles, calculation resources, safety sections, and other high-value locations. Candidates should confirm that all book preparation complies with the current testing-center rules before examination day.

The NASCLA examination is a trade examination used by participating regulatory agencies. Passing the examination does not automatically issue a journeyman electrician license. Licensing remains under the authority of the state or local agency to which the candidate applies.

  2. Confirm acceptance of the examination. Verify that the jurisdiction accepts the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians for the applicable license classification.
  3. Meet the jurisdiction’s eligibility rules. Complete any required experience, education, apprenticeship, documentation, or application requirements established by the licensing authority.
  4. Complete the examination application process. Follow the current NASCLA and testing-provider procedures for approval and scheduling.
  5. Prepare with the approved references. Study the examination content outline and become familiar with each permitted book.
  6. Schedule and take the examination. Follow the testing provider’s identification, security, calculator, reference-book, and examination-center rules.
  7. Access the examination record. After a passing result is processed, the candidate’s information is stored in the NASCLA National Examination Database.
  8. Send the transcript to an accepting agency. Candidates can use the database to purchase and electronically transmit examination results to participating regulatory agencies.
  9. Complete the licensing application. Submit all additional forms, fees, experience records, and supporting documents required by the chosen jurisdiction.

An agency may require documented electrical work experience, completion of an apprenticeship program, classroom education, employer verification, application approval, a background review, additional examinations, or other supporting materials.

Acceptance of a NASCLA examination result does not eliminate state-specific licensing requirements. A participating agency may use the NASCLA result to satisfy its trade-examination requirement while still requiring the applicant to complete the remainder of its licensing process. Candidates should review the rules for the exact jurisdiction and license classification in which they plan to work.

Some jurisdictions administer electrical licensing at the state level, while others may involve local authorities. The license classification, scope of permitted work, supervision rules, renewal requirements, and continuing education obligations can differ. Candidates should select the appropriate jurisdiction before registering so that the examination aligns with their licensing objective.

After passing the examination, candidates may use the NASCLA National Examination Database to transmit their results to agencies that accept the credential. The receiving agency evaluates the complete license application and determines whether the applicant satisfies its requirements.

Reference Books

  • National Electrical Code, 2023
    The 2023 National Electrical Code provides the core requirements for electrical installations. It addresses wiring and protection, wiring methods, equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, and communication systems. This is the principal code reference for a large portion of the examination.
  • Code of Federal Regulations – 29 CFR 1926 – OSHA Construction Industry Regulations
    This OSHA reference covers federal workplace safety requirements applicable to construction activities. It supports preparation for questions involving construction-site hazards, employee protection, electrical safety, personal protective equipment, and safe work practices.
  • Code of Federal Regulations – 29 CFR 1910 – OSHA Occupational Safety and Health Standards
    This reference contains federal occupational safety and health standards for general industry. It provides important safety information related to workplace conditions, electrical hazards, equipment, employee protection, and employer responsibilities.
  • NFPA 70E – Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    NFPA 70E addresses electrical safety-related work practices. It covers hazard assessment, shock and arc-flash protection, approach boundaries, personal protective equipment, energized work considerations, and procedures intended to reduce exposure to electrical hazards.
  • Ugly’s Electrical References, 2023
    Ugly’s Electrical References is a compact field resource containing commonly used electrical formulas, tables, conversion information, conductor data, motor information, and practical reference material. It can support efficient review of calculations and field-oriented electrical information.
  • NFPA 72 – National Fire Alarm and Signaling Code, 2022 Edition
    NFPA 72 provides requirements for fire alarm systems, emergency communication systems, signaling equipment, notification appliances, initiating devices, inspection, testing, and related system functions.
  • Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications
    This electrical theory reference connects foundational principles with practical NEC applications. It supports preparation involving voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, formulas, calculations, and the reasoning used to solve electrical problems.

Testing and troubleshooting preparation should reinforce meter use, systematic diagnosis, circuit behavior, and the identification of likely electrical faults.

The reference set includes the 2023 National Electrical Code, federal OSHA construction and general-industry regulations, the seventh edition of A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge, ANSI/ASHRAE/IES Standard 90.1, the NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, NFPA 70E, Ugly’s Electrical References, and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications.

Together, these publications support preparation for electrical installation rules, workplace safety, electrical hazards, energy-efficient building requirements, contractor operations, project delivery, calculations, and the principles behind electrical systems. The online course helps candidates organize this broad material into a practical study routine.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors is intended for individuals performing, supervising, or qualifying electrical contracting work. It evaluates knowledge related to the installation, maintenance, repair, management, and safe operation of electrical systems in accordance with applicable codes and standards.

The examination contains 100 scored questions. Candidates must answer at least 75 scored questions correctly to meet the minimum passing standard. The examination allows 270 minutes, which provides four hours and thirty minutes to complete the test.

Ten additional non-scored experimental questions may also be administered. These questions are used for future examination development and do not count toward the final score.

The examination content includes the following major areas:

  • Project Design and Management: Planning, coordination, project delivery, schedules, stakeholders, risk, quality, and contractor responsibilities.
  • Safety: Construction safety, general-industry safety, electrical hazards, protective equipment, and electrical safety-related work practices.
  • Electrical Theory and Principles: Voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, motors, transformers, formulas, and calculations.
  • General Code Requirements: NEC organization, definitions, general installation rules, and code interpretation.
  • Wiring and Protection: Branch circuits, feeders, services, grounding, bonding, conductors, and overcurrent protection.
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: Raceways, cables, boxes, fittings, conductor installation, support, and permitted uses.
  • Equipment for General Use: Motors, transformers, appliances, luminaires, switches, receptacles, and other electrical equipment.
  • Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: Requirements for specialized locations, systems, and installations.
  • Communication Systems: Code requirements affecting applicable communication circuits and systems.

General code requirements, wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, and equipment for general use represent a substantial portion of the contractor examination. Candidates should dedicate meaningful study time to these subjects while continuing to prepare for project management, safety, theory, energy requirements, and specialized electrical installations.

A physical diagram or blueprint packet may be provided at the testing center. Candidates should be prepared to interpret plans, specifications, equipment schedules, symbols, conductor information, notes, and project requirements. A silent, nonprinting, non-programmable calculator may be used during the examination.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Master Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing the permitted reference books to the testing center because the publications are not supplied onsite.

Approved reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed. Permanent tabs may be used to identify major chapters, articles, tables, and frequently referenced sections. Temporary tabs, removable notes, handwritten study notes, loose sheets, and attached additional papers are not permitted.

The open-book format places significant importance on reference familiarity. Candidates may need to move between the National Electrical Code, OSHA regulations, NFPA 70E, the energy standard, project-management guidance, contractor business material, field references, and electrical theory content during the same testing session.

A productive preparation method begins with learning the purpose and organization of each publication. Candidates should know which book is most likely to address a particular question before beginning to search. This reduces wasted time and helps create a more controlled examination strategy.

For the National Electrical Code, practice using the index, table of contents, definitions, chapters, articles, tables, exceptions, informational notes, and cross-references. For OSHA and NFPA 70E, learn how construction safety, general-industry safety, and electrical safety-related work practices differ.

For project management, contractor business, and energy-standard questions, become familiar with the chapters, subject divisions, terminology, and indexes within the applicable references. Repeated practice is more useful than attempting to memorize every page.

Candidates should study with the physical books they plan to use during the examination. The online course supports technical preparation and navigation practice, but it does not replace the approved references.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Master Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination does not automatically issue a contractor, master electrician, or unlimited electrician license. The exam may satisfy a trade-testing requirement for a participating jurisdiction, but applicants must still meet the licensing standards established by that agency.

  1. Select the licensing jurisdiction. Identify the state or regulatory authority where you intend to apply for an electrical contractor, master electrician, or unlimited electrician credential.
  2. Confirm examination acceptance. Verify that the agency accepts the NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors for the classification you are pursuing.
  3. Review eligibility requirements. Determine whether the jurisdiction requires documented electrical experience, supervisory experience, education, financial information, business registration, insurance, or a designated qualifying individual.
  4. Complete the applicable application. Submit the forms and supporting documents required for examination approval or licensing eligibility.
  5. Obtain the approved references. Purchase or otherwise obtain the listed editions before beginning intensive course study.
  6. Use the online exam prep course. Follow an organized plan for electrical code, safety, theory, project management, energy standards, business practices, calculations, and reference navigation.
  7. Register and schedule the examination. Follow the current scheduling instructions from the examination administrator.
  8. Take the examination. Comply with all testing-center rules concerning identification, calculators, references, arrival time, security procedures, and prohibited materials.
  9. Transmit the passing result. Complete the process for sending the examination transcript to a participating licensing agency.
  10. Finish the licensing application. Submit all remaining jurisdiction-specific forms, fees, experience records, financial documents, insurance information, and business credentials.

State Requirements

Electrical contractor licensing requirements vary by state and jurisdiction. A regulatory agency may accept the NASCLA examination while still requiring applicants to meet separate experience, education, financial, business, and administrative requirements.

Some jurisdictions issue individual master electrician or unlimited electrician licenses. Others license electrical contracting businesses and require a qualifying individual to pass the trade examination. Candidates should confirm the exact classification and scope of work associated with the credential they intend to obtain.

A separate state business and law examination may also be required. The inclusion of business and project-management subjects on the NASCLA electrical examination does not automatically replace a jurisdiction’s separate business-law testing requirement.

Applicants may need to document qualifying electrical work, supervisory experience, education, apprenticeship completion, financial responsibility, insurance coverage, or business registration. A licensing agency may also require application fees, background information, tax documentation, or other supporting records.

The NASCLA examination should not be treated as a national electrical contractor license. Passing results may be sent to participating agencies, but each agency independently decides whether an applicant meets its complete licensing requirements.

Reference Books

  • National Electrical Code, 2023
    The 2023 National Electrical Code contains requirements for electrical installations, including wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, special conditions, and communication systems.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1926 - OSHA Construction Industry Regulations
    This OSHA reference addresses federal workplace safety requirements for construction activities, including jobsite hazards, employee protection, electrical safety, personal protective equipment, and safe construction practices.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1910 - OSHA Occupational Safety and Health Standards
    This publication contains federal occupational safety and health standards for general industry, including workplace conditions, equipment, electrical hazards, employee protection, training, and employer responsibilities.
  • A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge, 2021, 7th Edition
    This project-management reference addresses principles and performance areas involving stakeholders, teams, planning, project work, delivery, measurement, uncertainty, adaptation, and value.
  • ANSI/ASHRAE/IES Standard 90.1, 2022 Energy Standard for Sites and Buildings Except Low-Rise Residential Buildings - I-P Edition
    This standard provides energy-efficiency requirements for applicable sites and buildings, including provisions involving electrical power, lighting, controls, equipment, and energy-conscious building systems.
  • NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Basic 14th Edition
    This contractor-focused publication supports study involving business organization, contracts, project management, estimating, scheduling, safety, risk, financial administration, and professional contractor responsibilities.
  • NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    NFPA 70E addresses electrical safety-related work practices, including shock protection, arc-flash protection, approach boundaries, risk assessment, personal protective equipment, and energized work considerations.
  • Ugly’s Electrical References, 2023
    This compact field reference includes commonly used electrical formulas, tables, conversions, conductor information, motor data, and practical trade information. References to highlighting or tabbing do not apply to this online-only course.
  • Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications
    This publication connects foundational electrical theory with practical NEC applications. It supports review involving voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, motors, transformers, formulas, and electrical calculations.

The listed publications are used alongside the online course and are not identified as included with course enrollment. Candidates should obtain the correct references separately and study with the physical books they intend to bring to the examination.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong preparation plan should combine course review, book navigation, calculations, code interpretation, and timed practice. Reading a reference from beginning to end without applying the material may not develop the speed needed for a contractor-level open-book exam.

For National Electrical Code study, focus on definitions, general requirements, conductor sizing, branch circuits, feeders, services, grounding, bonding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, boxes, raceways, cables, motors, transformers, equipment, special occupancies, emergency systems, and communication systems.

Practice reading complete code provisions rather than stopping after the first matching sentence. Exceptions, table notes, definitions, and related articles can change how a requirement applies.

For project management, review stakeholders, planning, schedules, project work, delivery, quality, procurement, communication, cost, uncertainty, and risk. Use both the PMBOK Guide and the NASCLA Contractors Guide to connect general management principles with contractor-focused responsibilities.

For safety preparation, compare OSHA construction regulations, OSHA general-industry standards, and NFPA 70E. Learn which publication applies to a particular work environment, hazard, or electrical safety practice.

For energy-standard preparation, become familiar with the organization of ANSI/ASHRAE/IES Standard 90.1. Practice locating requirements involving electrical power, lighting systems, controls, equipment, and applicable building-energy provisions.

Electrical theory study should include Ohm’s law, power relationships, series circuits, parallel circuits, alternating-current principles, motors, transformers, and common contractor calculations. Practice selecting the correct formula, maintaining consistent units, and checking whether the final result is reasonable.

Timed practice can help candidates identify whether difficulty comes from technical knowledge, reference navigation, calculation accuracy, or code interpretation. Keep all nine references nearby and practice moving between them as questions change subjects.

A useful exam process is to identify the topic, select the correct publication, locate the section, read the complete requirement, review exceptions or notes, complete any necessary calculation, and confirm the answer before moving forward.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps electrical contractor candidates build an organized study routine around the subjects measured by the NASCLA Master Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination. The online course supports trade-focused review, practical preparation, reference navigation, and confidence-building study structure.

The course helps candidates connect electrical code requirements with real trade applications. Students can review wiring and protection, installation methods, equipment, safety, theory, project management, business practices, and energy standards as related parts of contractor-level electrical work.

Organized study guidance can make a large reference list more manageable. Instead of moving through the books without a plan, candidates can study by subject, practice locating related requirements, review missed questions, and identify weaker knowledge areas.

Reference navigation is an essential part of open-book preparation. 1 Exam Prep encourages candidates to become familiar with indexes, tables of contents, code articles, tables, definitions, exceptions, and cross-references. Repeated use of the physical books can help students develop a faster and more consistent search process.

Practice-oriented preparation also helps candidates apply formulas and concepts rather than relying on memorization alone. Understanding the reason behind an electrical requirement or calculation can make it easier to recognize the correct approach during the examination.

The course is designed to support focused study and stronger familiarity with contractor-level electrical subjects. It does not guarantee a passing examination result, licensing approval, or acceptance by a regulatory agency.

Is the NASCLA Master Unlimited Electrical Contractor exam open book?

Yes. The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors is an open-book examination. Candidates must bring the permitted references and follow the current testing rules.

Are the nine reference books included with the online course?

No books are identified as included with this online course. Candidates should obtain the listed editions separately and use them throughout their preparation.

What subjects does the course cover?

The course supports preparation involving electrical code, wiring and protection, wiring methods, equipment, safety, electrical theory, calculations, project management, contractor business practices, energy standards, and reference navigation.

Why should I study for an open-book exam?

An open-book exam still requires technical knowledge, accurate interpretation, and efficient navigation. Candidates must know which book applies and how to locate the correct requirement within the testing period.

Does the online course replace the National Electrical Code?

No. The course is a preparation resource and does not replace the NEC or any other approved examination reference.

Does the exam include project-management material?

Yes. Project design and management is part of the examination content, and preparation should include planning, schedules, stakeholders, delivery, quality, risk, and contractor responsibilities.

Does passing the examination automatically provide a license?

No. A passing result may satisfy a trade-examination requirement for a participating agency, but applicants must complete all remaining licensing requirements.

Can this course guarantee that I will pass?

No exam prep course can guarantee a passing result. Performance depends on preparation, trade knowledge, reference familiarity, calculation skills, and the candidate’s work during the examination.

Who should take this online exam prep course?

This course is intended for experienced electrical professionals preparing for the NASCLA Master Unlimited Electrical Contractor examination and seeking organized review of technical, safety, management, business, energy, and code-navigation subjects.

Open Book Test

Prepare for the Georgia NASCLA – Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors with a faster, cleaner way to navigate your exam references. These pre-printed, permanent tabs are designed to help you organize your approved books so you can locate key chapters and sections more efficiently during an open-book, timed PSI exam.

On a long exam with more than one hundred questions, time management is everything. Pre-printed tabs help reduce the “where is it?” delay that can happen when you’re flipping through multiple references under pressure. Instead of searching from scratch, you can follow a consistent system that supports quicker lookups, steadier pacing, and more confident decision-making.

This product is for candidates taking the Georgia General Contractor or General Contractor Limited Tier licensing path where the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor exam is used as the trade exam portion in Georgia.

What You Get

  • Pre-Printed Permanent Tabs: A ready-to-apply tab set intended to help index and organize the reference materials used for the Georgia NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor exam.
  • Open-Book Navigation Support: A structured way to build faster “find-and-confirm” habits using the index and table of contents in your approved references.
  • Exam-Rule Friendly Organization: Designed specifically as permanent tabs to align with PSI’s reference-handling rules (temporary tabs like Post-It notes are not allowed).

Exam Details

The Georgia contractor Candidate Information Bulletin explains that for licensure in Georgia as a General Contractor or General Contractor Limited Tier (Individual or Qualifying Agent), candidates must pass:

  • NASCLA – Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors (trade exam portion)
  • Georgia Business & Law Exam (separate exam requirement)

For the Georgia NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor exam (as listed by PSI for Georgia):

  • Number of questions: 115
  • Minimum passing score: 70% (81 correct)
  • Time allowed: 330 minutes
  • Exam fee (Georgia – NASCLA General Contractor / Limited Tier): $106

These tabs are built to support your open-book workflow for the NASCLA portion of the Georgia licensing requirement by improving reference navigation and reducing wasted time during lookups.

Open Book Test

The Georgia NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor exam is listed by PSI as an OPEN BOOK examination. That means you can bring approved references into the testing center—but only if they follow the published rules.

PSI’s reference-handling rules for Georgia contractor exams emphasize:

  • Approved references only: You must use only the references permitted for the exam.
  • No extra inserts: References may not contain additional papers (loose or attached).
  • No writing in the books: References may be highlighted, underlined, and/or indexed, but must be otherwise unmarked.
  • Tabs must be permanent: References may be tabbed/indexed with permanent tabs only. Temporary tabs (such as Post-It notes) are not allowed and must be removed before the exam begins.
  • Bring your own references: PSI notes the references will not be available in the examination center.

How this relates to your tabs: These are pre-printed tabs intended to be used as a permanent indexing system. They help you stay organized without relying on removable notes or non-compliant paper inserts.

Licensing Steps

The exact application steps can vary depending on whether you are applying as an Individual or Qualifying Agent and whether you are applying as a General Contractor or General Contractor Limited Tier. That said, the Georgia PSI bulletin generally reflects the following exam pathway:

  1. Choose your license classification: General Contractor or General Contractor Limited Tier (based on the scope you plan to work under in Georgia).
  2. Submit your application to the state Board: PSI explains eligibility to test is determined by the Board.
  3. Receive approval to test: Once approved, you will receive instructions for PSI registration.
  4. Schedule your exams: You’ll schedule the NASCLA Commercial General Building exam and the Georgia Business & Law exam.
  5. Prepare and test with compliant materials: Bring only approved references, organized and compliant with PSI rules.

Pre-printed tabs support the last step by helping you keep references organized and ready for inspection on exam day.

State Requirements

Georgia requires contractors to be licensed and regulated through the state’s professional licensing structure. PSI’s bulletin explains that exam eligibility is determined by the Board and that candidates must follow the appropriate state application requirements in addition to passing the required exams.

This tabs product does not replace state requirements or application approvals. It is designed specifically to support the open-book portion of the testing process by improving reference navigation and time management.

Test Information and Study Materials

Pre-printed tabs are most effective when you use them as part of a real study system—not just as a last-minute organization tool. Here’s how to get the most value out of your tabs while staying exam-compliant:

  • Build a “find-and-confirm” habit: Don’t wait until exam day to learn where information lives. Practice locating key topics quickly using the table of contents and index.
  • Keep your tab system clean: A clear and consistent tab layout is typically faster than a cluttered one. Avoid adding extra materials that could slow you down or create check-in issues.
  • Use your tabs during timed drills: Set aside practice sessions where you answer questions under a countdown. This helps you learn pacing and reduces “panic searching.”
  • Know the code edition rule: PSI’s exam guidance explains that, for code questions, the exam is based only on the listed code edition. If a code book is part of your approved reference set, confirm you’re working from the correct edition for your test window.
  • Don’t rely on lookups for everything: PSI also notes the exam may include questions based on trade knowledge and general industry practices. Tabs help with navigation, but you still need concept mastery and real-world understanding.

Practical pacing tip: On a 115-question exam with 330 minutes, time can disappear quickly when you search too long. Tabs support a better strategy: answer what you know, confirm what needs verification, and avoid getting stuck flipping through pages for one question at the expense of many others.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep supports Georgia contractor candidates with structured preparation that fits the reality of trade testing: you need a plan, you need practice, and you need confidence built through consistent review. For an open-book NASCLA exam, that also includes the skill of navigating references efficiently without depending on searching for every answer.

  • Organized study guidance: Helps you focus your prep around the types of topic areas the exam covers so your time stays productive.
  • Practice-oriented preparation: Encourages repetition and application so you develop exam-ready judgment rather than relying on memorization alone.
  • Reference navigation support: Builds the habits that make open-book testing work—knowing where to look, confirming details efficiently, and managing time across a long exam.
  • Confidence-building structure: A consistent routine reduces overwhelm and helps you approach exam day with clearer pacing and less second-guessing.

FAQ

Are tabs allowed for the Georgia NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor exam?

Yes. PSI’s Georgia contractor bulletin explains that references may be tabbed/indexed with permanent tabs only. Temporary tabs (such as Post-It notes) are not allowed and must be removed before the exam begins.

Do these tabs include the books?

No. This product includes pre-printed tabs only. PSI notes that references will not be available in the examination center, so candidates must supply their own approved books.

Can I highlight or underline my references if they are tabbed?

PSI’s bulletin states reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and/or indexed, but they must be otherwise unmarked (not written in) and may not contain additional papers.

Can I add notes or extra pages inside my books?

No. PSI’s reference rules state references may not contain additional papers (loose or attached). Avoid inserts, taped notes, or any extra pages that could create a check-in problem.

Is the Georgia NASCLA exam open book?

Yes. PSI lists the NASCLA – Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors in Georgia as an OPEN BOOK examination and provides reference-handling rules for the exam.

How many questions are on the Georgia NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor exam?

PSI’s Georgia bulletin lists 115 questions with 330 minutes allowed, and a minimum passing score of 70% (81 correct).

Do I have to pass any other exam for Georgia General Contractor licensing?

Yes. PSI’s Georgia contractor bulletin explains that Georgia General Contractor and General Contractor Limited Tier candidates must pass the NASCLA Commercial General Building exam and the Georgia Business & Law exam.

Will tabs guarantee I pass?

No. Tabs are a navigation tool, not a substitute for understanding. They can help you move faster and confirm information more efficiently, but success still depends on learning the material, practicing under time, and building exam-ready judgment.

This Highlighted & Tabbed edition features the NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management — Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board (5th Edition), labeled for Plumbers, Conditioned Air, Low Voltage, Electrical and Utility Contractors.

When your Georgia exam allows references in the testing room, organization matters. Highlighting and permanent tabs can help you locate key sections faster and reduce time spent searching—so you can stay focused on answering questions accurately.

Exam Details

This NASCLA Georgia CILB 5th Edition reference is listed on official Georgia “Suggested Reference List” documents for multiple Construction Industry Licensing Board divisions. Exam format and permitted references vary by division and license class, so always match your exact exam to the current Georgia reference list.

Open Book Test

Open-book vs. reference-permitted testing depends on your specific Georgia exam. Georgia’s official reference lists may state whether the listed books can be used during the examination.

  • Conditioned Air Contractors: The official suggested reference list states that only the listed references may be used during the examination and includes a candidate notice about allowed highlighting and permanent tabs.
  • Plumbing: The official exam suggested reference list states the Journeyman Plumber exam is open-book format. The same document states that for all other plumbing exams, the listed references may not be used during the examination.

Candidate notice (when references are permitted): Georgia’s official reference list notice for Conditioned Air exams states you may bring only the listed references, you may not bring photocopied materials or handwritten notes (even if pasted into the book), and references may be highlighted, underlined, or tabbed with permanent tabs.

Licensing Steps

  1. Select your Georgia division and license class: Plumbing, Conditioned Air, Low Voltage, Electrical, or Utility (each has its own licensing path and exam requirements).
  2. Apply through Georgia’s licensing process: Follow the application instructions for your division under the Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board.
  3. Confirm exam references for your exact test: Use the official Georgia “Suggested Reference List” for your division and license class to verify required books/editions and whether references are allowed in the exam room.
  4. Prepare using compliant materials: Study with the correct edition and keep your reference materials within the published candidate rules.
  5. Test with approved items only: Bring only what your exam allows and keep your books free of prohibited inserts or notes.

State Requirements

The Georgia State Construction Industry Licensing Board includes five divisions: Conditioned Air Contractors, Electrical Contractors, Low Voltage Contractors, Master and Journeyman Plumbers, and Utility Contractors. Requirements can vary by division and license classification, so always follow the application checklist and exam guidance for your specific trade.

Reference Books

  • NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management — Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board (5th Edition)
    Georgia-specific NASCLA reference labeled for Plumbers, Conditioned Air, Low Voltage, Electrical and Utility Contractors. (ISBN: 978-1-934234-44-0)

  • Why highlighted & tabbed helps: When references are permitted, faster navigation can protect your pacing. A clean tab system and purposeful highlighting can reduce search time during practice.
  • Use permanent tabs only: Georgia’s candidate notice for Conditioned Air reference-permitted exams specifies permanent tabs and warns against extra materials that are not allowed.

  • Practice “find-and-confirm” lookups: Use the table of contents and index during timed drills so you build speed before exam day.

Who is this Georgia CILB 5th Edition NASCLA guide for?

This edition is labeled for Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board candidates, including Plumbers, Conditioned Air, Low Voltage, Electrical and Utility Contractors.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is an Open Book Test. South Carolina commercial contractor examinations administered through PSI are open book, with candidates responsible for bringing permitted references to the testing center.

Open-book testing should be approached strategically. The availability of reference books does not remove the need to understand the construction material. Searching through unfamiliar books for every answer can consume a substantial portion of the testing period.

A better approach is to determine what the question is testing, identify the reference most likely to contain the information, locate the relevant section, confirm the technical detail, and move forward. Practicing this process repeatedly can help make reference use more deliberate and efficient.

Reference materials used in South Carolina open-book commercial contractor examinations may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed according to applicable testing rules. References must otherwise remain free of prohibited writing and additional loose or attached papers. Permanent tabs may be used for indexing, while temporary removable tabs are not accepted.

Licensing Steps

  1. Determine the appropriate South Carolina classification or subclassification. South Carolina commercial contractor licenses are issued according to regulated construction classifications and subclassifications.
  2. Identify the Primary Qualifying Party. Applicants must designate a Primary Qualifying Party for each classification or subclassification for which licensure is requested.

  5. Pass the South Carolina Business Management and Law exam. Individuals seeking qualifying-party certification must complete this state-specific examination.
  6. Prepare the required licensing documentation. The application process includes the applicable contractor and qualifying-party documentation.
  7. Provide the required financial documentation or surety bond. South Carolina license group limitations are supported by applicable financial documentation or a qualifying surety bond.
  8. Complete the licensing application. After examination and qualification requirements are satisfied, submit the required materials to the South Carolina Contractor's Licensing Board.

State Requirements

Commercial contractor licensing in South Carolina is administered by the South Carolina Contractor's Licensing Board through the Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation. A General Contractor license is required for regulated commercial construction when the work falls within the state's applicable licensing requirements.

Federal construction-safety questions may require 29 CFR Part 1926, and stormwater-planning questions may involve Developing Your Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan.

  2. Determine the license type. Review whether the company needs a commercial contractor license and which classifications or subclassifications apply to the proposed work.
  3. Identify the qualifying party. The business must designate the individual responsible for qualifying the company for the requested classification.
  4. Submit the Louisiana license application. Provide the requested business, ownership, qualifying-party, classification, financial, and supporting information.
  5. Receive contractor portal access. Applicants and qualifying parties receive access to the Louisiana contractor portal after the application is submitted and processed.
  6. Apply for the NASCLA examination. Complete the NASCLA application process and receive authorization before scheduling the commercial general building examination.
  7. Prepare with the listed references. Study the technical subjects and practice locating information throughout the complete book set.
  8. Pass the NASCLA examination. The result may be transmitted to Louisiana through the NASCLA National Examination Database.
  9. Complete the Louisiana Business and Law requirement. Qualifying parties using NASCLA credit must complete the Louisiana online Business and Law course through the contractor portal.
  10. Submit remaining licensing documents. Provide financial information, insurance documentation, qualifying-party records, and other materials required for the requested license.
  11. Complete the Board’s review. The Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors evaluates the application, examination credit, and supporting documentation.
  12. Receive the license before contracting. The business must obtain the applicable Louisiana license before performing work that requires state contractor licensure.

State Requirements

The Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors regulates commercial, residential, mold remediation, and home improvement contractors in the state. Applicants must obtain the appropriate license and classification before performing covered contracting work.

A commercial license applies to qualifying commercial construction projects that fall within Louisiana’s contractor licensing laws. The applicant should select the classification that accurately describes the work the company intends to perform.

The contractor license is issued to the business entity. A qualifying party is connected with the license and demonstrates the applicable technical knowledge for the requested classification.

Louisiana accepts the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors as a trade-examination option. A candidate who has already passed the NASCLA examination may transmit the result to the Louisiana Board through the National Examination Database.

Using a NASCLA examination result does not replace the Louisiana license application. The company must still provide all required business, ownership, financial, qualifying-party, insurance, and classification information.

Qualifying parties using NASCLA or reciprocity credit must complete Louisiana’s online Business and Law course. The course is accessed through the LSLBC contractor portal after the application process has been initiated.

Applicants should submit complete and accurate documents. Missing financial information, incomplete qualifying-party records, unresolved ownership details, or missing insurance materials may delay the licensing process.

The Louisiana Board makes the final licensing decision. Passing an examination or purchasing this complete book set does not independently authorize the applicant to perform licensed contracting work.

Practice using each book’s index and table of contents. Read a sample question, identify the central construction subject, select the likely publication, and locate the relevant material. Repeat this process until choosing a reference becomes more automatic.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors contains 115 questions. Candidates are allowed 5-1/2 hours to complete the exam, and the minimum passing score is 81 correct answers.

The exam content outline includes the following subject areas:

  • General Requirements
  • Site Construction
  • Concrete
  • Masonry
  • Metals
  • Wood
  • Thermal and Moisture Protection
  • Doors, Windows, and Glazing
  • Finishes
  • Mechanical and Plumbing Systems
  • Electrical Systems
  • Procurement and Contracting Requirements

The exam may include questions based on listed references, trade knowledge, and general construction industry practices. Code questions are based on the code edition listed for the examination. For non-code references, candidates may study from later editions as they become available, but edition differences can affect how a topic is presented, so candidates should prepare from the references required for their exam whenever possible.

The exam measures broad commercial construction knowledge rather than a single specialty trade. Candidates should understand how a commercial project is planned, estimated, contracted, scheduled, managed, built, inspected, and closed out. The questions may require practical construction knowledge, code lookup, reference navigation, plan interpretation, project coordination, and management judgment.

Because the exam is timed, candidates should practice pacing. With 115 questions and 5-1/2 hours, candidates have less than three minutes per question on average. Some questions may be answered from knowledge, while others require looking up information in the correct reference. A strong preparation plan includes learning when to answer immediately, when to look up a question, and when to mark a question and return later.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for bringing their own approved references to the examination center. The references are not provided at the testing center.

Reference materials may be highlighted, underlined, and indexed before the examination session. They must otherwise be unmarked and may not contain additional papers, whether loose or attached. Candidates may not write, highlight, underline, or index references during the examination.

References may be tabbed or indexed with permanent tabs only. Permanent tabs are the type of tabs that would tear the page if removed. Temporary tabs, including removable sticky notes or Post-It style tabs, are not allowed and must be removed before the exam begins.

Candidates may use a silent, non-printing, non-programmable calculator in the examination center. A physical diagram or blueprint packet may also be issued at the testing center for use during the exam.

Because this is an open-book exam with a large reference set, organization is a major part of preparation. Candidates should become familiar with the book titles, table of contents, indexes, topic sections, charts, tables, definitions, and code provisions before exam day. The goal is to reduce search time and increase confidence when moving from a question to the correct book.

Arizona contractor licensing is handled by the Arizona Registrar of Contractors. Applicants pursuing a commercial general building license should review the current Arizona classification requirements and choose the exam path that matches the license classification they plan to obtain.

Arizona applicants applying for the B-1 or B-2 General Commercial classifications may elect to take the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors as an option in place of the Arizona-specific trade examination. Passing the NASCLA exam does not automatically issue an Arizona contractor license. Once the required examination and application requirements are complete, the applicant submits the contractor license application to the Arizona Registrar of Contractors for review. The license is issued only after the state approves the application for the applicable classification.

State Requirements

Arizona uses contractor license classifications to define the work a contractor may legally contract for and perform. The B-1 General Commercial Contractor classification is connected to general commercial building work, while the B-2 General Small Commercial Contractor classification is connected to smaller commercial projects within the state’s classification limits.

The NASCLA commercial general building exam may be used as an alternative trade exam option for Arizona B-1 and B-2 General Commercial applicants. Candidates should apply for the classification that matches the work they intend to perform and should operate only within the scope of the license issued by the Arizona Registrar of Contractors.

Commercial general building contractors coordinate multiple trades and construction disciplines. A general building license can involve project management responsibilities, subcontractor coordination, code compliance, safety responsibilities, scheduling, procurement, contract administration, and quality control. Concrete study should include ACI requirements, reinforcing bars, post-tensioning fundamentals, precast concrete erection, concrete quality, placement, finishing, curing, tolerances, forms, reinforcement, inspection, and field procedures. What is included in the Arizona NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractors Complete Book Set?

Yes. The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is an open-book exam. Candidates must bring their own approved references to the examination center.

The exam contains 115 questions. Candidates are allowed 5-1/2 hours, and the minimum passing score is 81 correct answers.

No. Passing the NASCLA exam supports the trade-exam portion of the process. Applicants must still meet Arizona Registrar of Contractors licensing requirements and receive approval for the appropriate license classification.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is a standardized technical examination accepted by participating contractor licensing agencies. Utah is a participating jurisdiction through the Utah Division of Professional Licensing.

The examination is designed to evaluate knowledge used to plan, supervise, coordinate, and complete commercial building projects involving multiple construction trades. Its broad scope reflects the responsibilities of a commercial general building contractor rather than a contractor working in one specialty area.

The listed references address project management, jobsite operations, estimating, scheduling, contracts, safety, structural concrete, reinforcing steel, precast construction, post-tensioning, steel decking, steel joists, wood trusses, masonry, excavation, carpentry, roofing, accessibility, building codes, environmental controls, exterior systems, and mechanical and electrical coordination.

Specialty structural references cover precast concrete erection, unbonded post-tensioning, steel deck installation, steel joist handling, and metal plate connected wood-truss restraint and bracing. Other books address masonry, gypsum systems, excavation, carpentry, roofing, accessibility, stormwater planning, exterior insulation and finish systems, and building-service coordination.

Utah accepts a passing NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination result as part of its contractor licensing framework. The examination result may also be used by other participating jurisdictions that accept the NASCLA examination.

After passing the examination, candidates may use the NASCLA National Examination Database to send an official transcript to Utah or another participating licensing agency. The agency pairs the transcript with the candidate’s contractor license application.

A passing NASCLA result does not independently issue a Utah contractor license. Applicants must complete the state application process and satisfy the applicable business, ownership, experience, classification, insurance, financial-responsibility, and supporting-document requirements.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for obtaining and bringing permitted reference materials to the testing location. The examination center does not provide the complete technical library.

Open-book testing allows candidates to consult approved publications, but it does not eliminate the need for preparation. The NASCLA reference library contains thousands of pages across construction textbooks, codes, standards, manuals, and specialty technical guides.

A practical open-book strategy begins with identifying the primary subject of a question. The candidate should then choose the publication most likely to contain the answer and use the index, table of contents, chapter headings, definitions, diagrams, code sections, or technical tables to locate the relevant information.

Structural concrete questions may require ACI 318-19, while questions involving reinforcing-bar placement may require Placing Reinforcing Bars. Concrete field-practice questions involving preparation, placement, consolidation, finishing, curing, testing, or quality control may be addressed in The Contractor’s Guide to Quality Concrete Construction.

Steel-deck questions may require the Steel Deck Institute Manual of Construction with Steel Deck, while steel-joist and joist-girder questions may involve Technical Digest No. 9. Questions involving wood-truss handling, installation, restraint, and bracing may require the BCSI guide.

Precast concrete erection questions may be addressed in the Erectors’ Manual. Unbonded post-tensioning questions may require the Level 1 Field Fundamentals publication. Masonry questions may involve Modern Masonry, while excavation and underground utility questions may require Pipe and Excavation Contracting.

Accessibility questions may involve ICC A117.1, while broader commercial building-code questions may require the International Building Code. Federal construction-safety questions may require 29 CFR Part 1926, and stormwater-planning questions may involve Developing Your Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan.

Candidates should practice using the listed editions because code provisions, page numbers, technical requirements, illustrations, and publication organization may differ between editions. Working directly with the correct books helps build familiarity before examination day.

All books brought into the testing room must comply with current examination rules. Candidates should review the applicable candidate bulletin and avoid unauthorized loose pages, removable notes, inserts, or other prohibited materials.

Licensing Steps

  1. Select the appropriate Utah classification. Candidates seeking broad commercial building authority should review the B100 General Building Contractor classification and confirm that it matches the work the business intends to perform.
  2. Choose the business structure. Determine whether the contractor will operate as a sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, or another eligible business entity.
  3. Identify the qualifying individual. The contractor business must identify the person whose experience and qualifications support the requested classification.
  4. Prepare for the Utah Business and Law examination. Study the Utah Contractors’ Guide to Business Law and Project Management and review state contractor responsibilities.
  5. Complete the Utah Business and Law requirement. Follow the current examination and application procedures established for Utah contractor applicants.
  6. Prepare for the NASCLA examination. Study the technical construction subjects and practice locating information throughout the complete reference library.
  7. Apply for the NASCLA examination. Complete the current NASCLA examination application and testing-registration process.
  8. Pass the NASCLA examination. The passing result may be transmitted to Utah through the NASCLA National Examination Database.
  9. Document the applicable experience. Provide the employment and construction-experience records required for the requested Utah classification.
  10. Complete the contractor application. Submit the business, ownership, qualifying-individual, classification, and contact information requested by Utah.
  11. Provide supporting documents. Submit the applicable insurance, financial-responsibility, registration, and business records required for the license.
  12. Receive the license before contracting. The business must obtain the applicable Utah contractor license before performing work that requires state licensure.

State Requirements

The Utah Division of Professional Licensing regulates contractor licensing through its Construction Trades Bureau. Businesses performing work that requires a Utah contractor license must obtain the appropriate classification before offering or completing regulated contracting services.

Utah’s B100 General Building Contractor classification covers general building work within the scope established by the state’s contractor licensing laws and rules. Applicants should review the classification and confirm that it corresponds with the projects the company intends to undertake.

The contractor license is issued to the business entity. The application must identify the company’s legal structure, ownership, qualifying individual, requested classification, and other information required by the Division.

Utah does not use the NASCLA examination as a mandatory state trade examination for every general building applicant. A passing NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination result may be applied toward Utah’s experience-related licensing pathway under current state acceptance policies.

The NASCLA examination does not replace the Utah Business and Law requirement. Applicants should prepare from the Utah contractor business reference and complete the applicable state examination or approved requirement connected with their license application.

Contractor applicants must document the experience required for the requested classification. Records should accurately describe the qualifying individual’s work history and connection with the applicant business.

The application process may also include business registration, financial responsibility, insurance, ownership information, qualifying-individual records, and other supporting documents. Requirements may vary according to the classification and business structure.

The Utah business name should remain consistent across the contractor application, registration records, insurance materials, and other supporting documents. Incomplete or inconsistent information may delay the licensing review.

Passing an examination or purchasing this complete book set does not independently authorize contracting work. The applicant must complete the Utah licensing process and receive the appropriate contractor license before performing regulated construction services.
