Prepare for the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors with a complete reference-book set covering construction management, building codes, safety, accessibility, concrete, masonry, structural systems, carpentry, roofing, excavation, exterior systems, and mechanical and electrical coordination.

This commercial general building contractor book set includes the listed references used to study the broad technical subjects addressed by the NASCLA examination. The collection is designed for experienced contractors and examination candidates who need an organized library for commercial construction review and open-book reference practice.

California recognizes the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination for a specific trade-examination waiver pathway. An out-of-state contractor may request a waiver of the California B – General Building trade examination when the applicant has passed the NASCLA commercial building examination, holds an eligible out-of-state contractor license in good standing, and meets the experience and reciprocity conditions established by the California Contractors State License Board.

The NASCLA examination is not a California contractor license, and purchasing this book set does not establish eligibility for the California waiver. California residents generally follow the state-specific examination process. Applicants seeking the NASCLA waiver must complete the California application process, request the waiver, share their NASCLA examination result with California, and satisfy all additional requirements imposed by the Contractors State License Board.

The reference library contains thousands of pages of technical material. Effective preparation involves learning more than construction concepts. Candidates must understand which publication covers each subject and how to locate information through indexes, tables of contents, chapters, definitions, code provisions, diagrams, and technical tables.

Studying with the complete book set helps candidates develop a consistent navigation method before test day. The books can be organized into subject groups such as management, safety, codes, accessibility, concrete, metals, masonry, carpentry, roofing, excavation, environmental controls, and building systems. This structure makes a large examination library easier to review.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is a standardized technical trade examination accepted by participating contractor licensing agencies. It addresses knowledge used to plan, supervise, coordinate, and complete commercial building projects.

The examination covers a broad range of subjects represented by the books in this set. Candidates should be prepared to review jobsite management, project management, estimating, contracts, safety, structural concrete, reinforcing steel, precast concrete, post-tensioning, steel decking, steel joists, wood trusses, masonry, excavation, carpentry, roofing, accessibility, building codes, exterior insulation systems, stormwater controls, green construction, and mechanical and electrical systems.

After passing, a candidate may use the NASCLA National Examination Database to send an official result to participating licensing agencies. Each agency applies its own licensing laws, classifications, financial requirements, experience standards, examinations, and application procedures.

California’s Contractors State License Board recognizes the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination for qualifying out-of-state applicants seeking a waiver of the B – General Building trade examination. The waiver is not automatic. The applicant must request it as part of the California application and satisfy the conditions established by CSLB.

A qualifying applicant must hold an out-of-state commercial building contractor license in good standing for the required period and have passed the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination. CSLB retains authority over the waiver decision and may require additional information or examinations.

The NASCLA examination does not replace California’s Law and Business examination when that examination is required. It also does not replace experience verification, fingerprinting, bonding, insurance, application, business-entity, personnel, or license-issuance requirements.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is an open-book examination. Candidates are responsible for obtaining and bringing permitted references to the testing location. The testing center does not provide the complete book library.

Open-book testing requires strong subject recognition and reference-navigation skills. The candidate must read the question carefully, identify the construction topic, choose the most relevant publication, and locate the supporting information within the available examination period.

A concrete question may require ACI 318, the quality concrete guide, or the reinforcing-bar reference. A structural-system question may involve the wood-truss guide, precast erection manual, post-tensioning publication, steel-deck manual, or steel-joist digest. Accessibility and general code questions may require ICC A117.1 or the International Building Code.

Candidates should practice directly with the listed editions. Page numbers, chapter organization, code provisions, definitions, and technical requirements can change between editions. Using the correct books during preparation helps the candidate build familiarity with the same reference structure expected for the examination.

All materials brought into the examination room must comply with the current testing rules. Candidates should review the applicable NASCLA candidate bulletin before test day and avoid loose papers, unauthorized inserts, removable notes, or other prohibited materials.

Licensing Steps

  1. Determine whether the California NASCLA waiver pathway applies. The pathway is intended for qualifying out-of-state contractors who have passed the NASCLA commercial building examination and meet CSLB’s licensing and experience conditions.
  2. Confirm the appropriate California classification. The comparable California classification is B – General Building Contractor.
  3. Review the qualifying experience requirement. California applicants must document the experience required for the requested contractor classification.
  4. Complete the NASCLA examination process. Candidates must apply for, schedule, and pass the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors.
  5. Maintain the eligible out-of-state license. The contractor must hold the qualifying license in good standing for the period required by CSLB.
  6. Submit the California contractor license application. The applicant must provide the required business, personnel, classification, experience, and supporting information.
  7. Request the NASCLA trade-examination waiver. The application must include the required signed request for waiver consideration.
  8. Share the NASCLA result with California. The applicant must use the NASCLA account and examination database to transmit the official result to CSLB.
  9. Complete the California Law and Business examination when required. A NASCLA trade-exam waiver does not automatically waive the California Law and Business examination.
  10. Complete the remaining issuance requirements. These may include fingerprinting, bonding, insurance documentation, fees, and other materials required for the applicant’s business structure and license.

State Requirements

The California Contractors State License Board licenses and regulates contractors operating in the state. A contractor must hold the appropriate California license before performing work that requires licensure. An out-of-state license or NASCLA examination result does not independently authorize contracting in California.

The California B – General Building classification applies to contractors whose principal business involves structures built for the support, shelter, and enclosure of persons, animals, property, or movable items when the construction requires the use of at least two unrelated building trades or crafts.

California began recognizing the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination for an expanded reciprocity and trade-waiver pathway in 2025. The pathway allows qualifying contractors licensed outside California to request waiver consideration for the B – General Building trade examination.

The applicant must have passed the NASCLA examination and held the eligible out-of-state commercial building contractor license in good standing for at least five years. The applicant must also complete California’s original-license application and submit a signed request for the NASCLA examination waiver.

The official NASCLA result must be shared with California through the NASCLA examination database. CSLB evaluates the application and determines whether the trade-examination waiver is approved. The Board retains the right to require an examination when appropriate.

Applicants must still satisfy California requirements that are not covered by the waiver. These may include the Law and Business examination, qualifying experience, business and personnel disclosures, fingerprinting, contractor bond, workers’ compensation documentation, application fees, and initial license requirements.

California residents who do not qualify through the out-of-state NASCLA waiver pathway generally must complete the California state-specific B – General Building trade examination. Candidates should choose study products that correspond with the examination and licensing pathway that applies to their circumstances.

The examination evaluates knowledge used to plan, supervise, coordinate, and complete commercial building projects involving multiple construction trades. Its broad scope reflects the responsibilities of a commercial general building contractor rather than the work of one specialty contractor.

Open Book Test

The candidate should then select the publication most likely to contain the answer and use the index, table of contents, chapter headings, definitions, code sections, diagrams, or technical tables to locate the applicable material.

Precast erection questions may be located in the Erectors’ Manual, while unbonded post-tensioning questions may require the Level 1 Field Fundamentals publication. Masonry questions may involve Modern Masonry, and excavation or underground utility questions may require Pipe and Excavation Contracting.

Licensing Steps

  1. Determine the appropriate Oregon contractor endorsement. Review the available residential, commercial, and combined endorsement options and choose the endorsement that matches the work the business intends to perform.
  2. Select the business structure. Determine whether the contractor will operate as a sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, or another approved business form.
  3. Designate a Responsible Managing Individual. The RMI must be an owner or employee of the business and must manage or supervise its construction activities.
  4. Prepare for the NASCLA examination. Study the commercial construction subjects and practice locating information throughout the listed technical reference library.
  5. Apply for the NASCLA examination. Complete the current NASCLA application and examination-registration process.
  6. Pass the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination. The passing result may be transmitted to Oregon through the NASCLA National Examination Database.
  7. Prepare for the Oregon examination. Study the Oregon Contractors’ Guide to Business Law and Project Management and review state laws, rules, licensing responsibilities, and business practices.
  8. Pass the Oregon laws, rules, and business-practices examination. Applicants using a NASCLA result remain responsible for completing this Oregon-specific examination.
  9. Register the business when applicable. File the corporation, limited liability company, partnership, or assumed business name with the Oregon Secretary of State when required.
  10. Obtain the required contractor bond. Secure the bond amount associated with the selected endorsement and business structure.
  11. Obtain general liability insurance. Provide a company-specific certificate showing the insurance coverage required for the selected endorsement.
  12. Submit the Oregon CCB application. Upload the examination records, bond, insurance certificate, business information, RMI information, and other required materials.

State Requirements

The Oregon Construction Contractors Board licenses and regulates construction contractors in the state. Contractors performing covered construction work must obtain the appropriate CCB license and endorsement before advertising, bidding, contracting, or performing work that requires licensure.

The contractor license is issued to the business entity. The business must identify a Responsible Managing Individual who is connected with the company and manages or supervises its construction activities.

The RMI must satisfy the applicable education and examination requirements. Under the standard pathway, the RMI completes at least 16 hours of approved pre-license training and passes the Oregon examination covering laws, rules, and business practices.

An applicant who has passed the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is exempt from the 16-hour pre-license training requirement. The applicant must still pass the Oregon examination and complete the remaining licensing steps.

The Oregon examination is based on the Oregon version of the NASCLA Contractors’ Guide to Business, Law and Project Management. The examination is open book and focuses on state laws, rules, business practices, licensing responsibilities, contracts, employment matters, safety, insurance, and related contractor obligations.

Applicants must select the correct endorsement type. Oregon contractor endorsements distinguish between residential, commercial, and combined contracting activity and may also include different commercial levels based on the type and size of work performed.

The selected endorsement affects the contractor’s bond and insurance requirements. Applicants should obtain coverage in the exact business name shown on the CCB application and confirm that the policy and bond satisfy the current requirements for the requested endorsement.

Corporations, limited liability companies, partnerships, and businesses using an assumed business name must complete the applicable registration with the Oregon Secretary of State. The legal name and registration details should remain consistent throughout the licensing documents.

The CCB application may require proof of examination completion, RMI information, business-structure records, bond documentation, general liability insurance, ownership information, and other supporting materials.

Passing the NASCLA examination and purchasing this complete book set do not guarantee license approval. The Oregon Construction Contractors Board determines whether an applicant has completed the legal, examination, business, bonding, insurance, and administrative requirements for the requested license.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is a standardized technical trade examination used by participating contractor licensing agencies. It evaluates knowledge involved in planning, supervising, coordinating, and completing commercial building projects that include multiple construction trades.

The examination has a broader scope than a single-trade test. Candidates should be prepared to review project management, jobsite operations, estimating, scheduling, contracts, structural systems, safety, accessibility, building codes, site construction, exterior systems, finishes, and building-service coordination.

Construction Jobsite Management and Construction Project Management support preparation involving field supervision, project organization, communication, documentation, scheduling, estimating, cost control, quality management, risk, safety, and project closeout.

Concrete subjects are represented by ACI 318-19, Placing Reinforcing Bars, and The Contractor’s Guide to Quality Concrete Construction. Together, these references address structural concrete requirements, reinforcement, placement, consolidation, finishing, curing, testing, durability, inspection, and quality control.

Specialty structural references address precast concrete erection, unbonded post-tensioning, steel deck installation, steel joist handling, and metal plate connected wood-truss restraint and bracing. Candidates may also encounter subjects involving excavation, masonry, carpentry, gypsum construction, roofing, accessibility, stormwater controls, exterior insulation systems, and mechanical and electrical coordination.

The International Building Code supports review of commercial building requirements involving occupancy, construction types, fire protection, means of egress, accessibility, structural provisions, and coordinated building systems. ICC A117.1 provides technical criteria for accessible and usable buildings and facilities.

Federal construction-safety material is addressed through 29 CFR Part 1926. Candidates may use this reference when reviewing fall protection, excavation, scaffolding, electrical safety, equipment, personal protective measures, and other construction-site requirements.

Virginia contractor licenses are divided into Class A, Class B, and Class C. The class determines the level of contracting activity permitted under the license, while the classification or specialty identifies the type of construction work the business is authorized to perform.

The Virginia Commercial Building Contractor classification applies to qualifying commercial, industrial, institutional, governmental, and related building work. Applicants should select the license class and classification that correspond with the business’s intended contracting activity.

Passing the NASCLA examination does not complete the entire Virginia licensing process. The contractor business must satisfy the applicable requirements of the Virginia Board for Contractors, including the requirements related to responsible management, pre-license education, business examinations, the designated employee, the qualified individual, experience, financial responsibility, and the license application.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for obtaining and bringing permitted reference materials to the testing location. The testing center does not provide the complete technical reference library.

Open-book testing allows approved publications to be used during the examination, but it does not remove the need for technical study. The reference library contains thousands of pages, and searching every book for every question is not an effective testing strategy.

A productive reference-navigation process begins by identifying the primary subject of the question. The candidate should then select the publication most likely to contain the answer and use the index, table of contents, chapter headings, definitions, diagrams, code provisions, or technical tables to find the relevant information.

Structural concrete questions may require ACI 318-19, while reinforcing-bar placement questions may involve Placing Reinforcing Bars. Concrete field-practice questions involving preparation, placement, consolidation, finishing, curing, testing, or quality control may be addressed in The Contractor’s Guide to Quality Concrete Construction.

Steel-deck questions may require the SDI Manual of Construction with Steel Deck. Questions involving steel joists and joist girders may require Technical Digest No. 9, while wood-truss handling, installation, restraint, and bracing questions may involve the BCSI guide.

Precast concrete erection questions may be addressed in the Erectors’ Manual. Unbonded post-tensioning questions may require the Level 1 Field Fundamentals publication. Masonry questions may involve Modern Masonry, while excavation and underground utility questions may require Pipe and Excavation Contracting.

Accessibility questions may involve ICC A117.1, while broader commercial building-code questions may require the International Building Code. Construction-safety questions may require 29 CFR Part 1926, and stormwater-planning questions may involve Developing Your Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan.

The course helps candidates practice making these connections before examination day. Students can work on recognizing key terms, selecting the appropriate publication, locating the supporting information, and evaluating the available answer choices.

All materials brought into the testing room must comply with the current examination rules. Candidates should use the approved editions and avoid unauthorized loose pages, removable notes, inserts, or other prohibited materials.

Licensing Steps

  1. Select the appropriate Virginia license class. Review the requirements for Class A, Class B, and Class C and choose the class that matches the business’s intended level of contracting activity.
  2. Select the Commercial Building Contractor classification. Confirm that the classification corresponds with the commercial construction work the company intends to perform.
  3. Establish the business entity. Organize the contractor as a sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, or another eligible business form.
  4. Identify responsible management. List the owners, officers, managers, members, partners, or other individuals who meet Virginia’s responsible-management requirements.
  5. Complete contractor pre-license education. An eligible member of the applicant organization must complete the Board-approved pre-license education requirement.
  6. Identify the designated employee when required. Class A and Class B applicants must designate the individual responsible for satisfying the applicable Virginia contractor business-examination requirement.
  7. Identify the qualified individual. The business must designate a qualified individual whose experience and examination credentials support the Commercial Building Contractor classification.
  8. Prepare for the NASCLA examination. Use the online course with the listed references to review commercial construction topics and practice open-book navigation.
  9. Apply for and take the NASCLA examination. Complete the current application, approval, registration, and scheduling procedures.
  10. Transmit the examination result. Follow the applicable process for providing the official NASCLA result to the Virginia Board for Contractors.
  11. Complete the Virginia business requirements. Satisfy the business-examination and application requirements associated with the selected license class.
  12. Submit the contractor license application. Provide the requested business, ownership, classification, financial, examination, experience, and organizational information.
  13. Receive the license before contracting. The business must obtain the appropriate Virginia contractor license before performing work that requires state licensure.

State Requirements

The Virginia Board for Contractors licenses contractor businesses and regulates contractor classifications and specialties within the Commonwealth. The license belongs to the business entity rather than solely to the individual who passes an examination.

A Virginia contractor license includes both a class and a classification or specialty. The class establishes the permitted level of contracting activity, while the classification identifies the type of work the business may perform.

Class A, Class B, and Class C applicants have different application, financial, experience, and examination requirements. Candidates should select the class that accurately reflects the scope and size of the company’s intended projects.

The Commercial Building Contractor classification applies to qualifying construction, remodeling, repair, improvement, removal, and demolition involving commercial, industrial, institutional, governmental, and related buildings or structures. This classification does not automatically authorize every separately regulated specialty trade.

Virginia requires contractor pre-license education for new license applicants. This education addresses contractor regulations and business responsibilities and is separate from the technical preparation provided by this NASCLA online course.

Class A and Class B applicants must identify a designated employee who satisfies the applicable Virginia business-examination requirements. The designated employee must remain properly associated with the licensed business.

The applicant must also identify a qualified individual for the Commercial Building Contractor classification. The qualified individual is the person whose experience and examination qualifications support the classification shown on the license.

Experience requirements vary according to the license class. The applicant should provide complete and accurate records describing the qualified individual’s relevant construction experience.

The licensing application may require organizational records, financial information, responsible-management details, designated-employee information, qualified-individual information, examination records, and other supporting documentation.

Passing the NASCLA examination or completing this course does not independently authorize construction work. The business must complete the Virginia licensing process and receive the appropriate contractor license before performing regulated contracting services.

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is a standardized technical trade examination accepted by participating contractor licensing agencies. The examination covers a broad range of topics rather than focusing on one specialty. Candidates should be prepared to review project management, jobsite operations, estimating, scheduling, contracts, safety, structural concrete, reinforcing steel, precast construction, post-tensioning, steel decking, steel joists, wood trusses, masonry, excavation, carpentry, roofing, accessibility, building codes, environmental controls, exterior systems, and mechanical and electrical coordination.

Construction Jobsite Management and Construction Project Management support preparation involving field supervision, project organization, communication, documentation, scheduling, estimating, cost control, safety, risk, quality management, and project closeout.

Concrete subjects are represented by ACI 318-19, Placing Reinforcing Bars, and The Contractor’s Guide to Quality Concrete Construction. Together, these references address structural requirements, reinforcement, placement, consolidation, finishing, curing, inspection, testing, durability, and quality control.

Specialty structural references address precast concrete erection, unbonded post-tensioning, steel deck installation, steel joist handling, and metal plate connected wood-truss restraint and bracing. Other books cover masonry, gypsum construction, excavation, carpentry, roofing, accessibility, stormwater planning, exterior insulation systems, and building-service systems.

The International Building Code supports review of commercial building requirements involving occupancy, construction types, fire protection, means of egress, accessibility, structural provisions, and coordinated building systems. ICC A117.1 provides technical accessibility criteria for buildings and facilities.

Oregon is a participating jurisdiction for the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination. After passing, a candidate may use the NASCLA National Examination Database to send an official transcript to the Oregon Construction Contractors Board.

A passing NASCLA result does not independently issue an Oregon contractor license. The applicant must still identify a Responsible Managing Individual, pass the Oregon contractor examination, choose the proper endorsement, register the business when required, obtain the applicable contractor bond and general liability insurance, and submit a complete CCB license application.

The Oregon examination is separate from the NASCLA technical examination. It is based on the Oregon version of the NASCLA Contractors’ Guide to Business, Law and Project Management and covers Oregon contractor laws, rules, licensing responsibilities, and business practices.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is an open-book test. Candidates are responsible for obtaining and bringing permitted references to the testing location. The testing center does not provide the complete technical library.

Oregon’s contractor examination covering laws, rules, and business practices is also open book. Candidates may use the approved Oregon reference manual during the examination under the current testing rules.

Open-book testing allows candidates to consult approved publications, but it does not eliminate the need for study. The NASCLA library contains thousands of pages across construction textbooks, codes, standards, manuals, and specialty technical guides.

A practical reference-navigation method begins with identifying the primary subject of a question. The candidate should then select the publication most likely to contain the answer and use the index, table of contents, chapter headings, definitions, diagrams, code sections, or technical tables to locate the relevant information.

Structural concrete questions may require ACI 318-19, while questions involving reinforcing-bar placement may require Placing Reinforcing Bars. Concrete field-practice questions involving preparation, placement, consolidation, finishing, curing, testing, or quality control may be addressed in The Contractor’s Guide to Quality Concrete Construction.

Steel-deck questions may require the Steel Deck Institute Manual of Construction with Steel Deck, while steel-joist and joist-girder questions may involve Technical Digest No. 9. Questions involving wood-truss handling, installation, restraint, and bracing may require the BCSI guide.

Precast concrete erection questions may be addressed in the Erectors’ Manual. Unbonded post-tensioning questions may require the Level 1 Field Fundamentals publication. Masonry questions may involve Modern Masonry, while excavation and underground utility questions may require Pipe and Excavation Contracting.

Accessibility questions may involve ICC A117.1, while broader commercial building-code questions may require the International Building Code. Federal construction-safety questions may require 29 CFR Part 1926, and stormwater-planning questions may involve Developing Your Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan.

The online exam prep course helps candidates practice connecting these topics with the appropriate references. Students can build a repeatable process for recognizing a subject, selecting the correct publication, locating the supporting information, and evaluating the available answer choices.

Licensing Steps

  1. Determine the appropriate Oregon contractor endorsement. Review the residential, commercial, and combined endorsement options and select the endorsement that matches the work the business intends to perform.
  2. Select the business structure. Decide whether the contractor will operate as a sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, limited liability company, or another eligible business form.
  3. Designate a Responsible Managing Individual. The RMI must be an owner or employee of the business and must manage or supervise its construction activities.
  4. Prepare for the NASCLA examination. Use the online course with the listed references to review technical construction subjects and practice open-book navigation.
  5. Apply for the NASCLA examination. Complete the current NASCLA application and examination-registration process.
  6. Pass the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination. The passing result may be transmitted to Oregon through the NASCLA National Examination Database.
  7. Prepare for the Oregon contractor examination. Study the Oregon business-law reference and review contractor laws, rules, licensing duties, and business practices.
  8. Pass the Oregon examination. NASCLA candidates remain responsible for completing the Oregon contractor examination even though they are exempt from the standard 16-hour pre-license training requirement.
  9. Register the business when required. Complete the applicable corporation, limited liability company, partnership, or assumed business-name registration.
  10. Obtain the required contractor bond. Secure the bond required for the selected endorsement and business structure.
  11. Obtain general liability insurance. Provide proof of the coverage required for the selected Oregon contractor endorsement.
  12. Submit the Oregon CCB application. Include the examination records, bond, insurance certificate, RMI information, business records, and other required documents.

State Requirements

The Oregon Construction Contractors Board licenses and regulates construction contractors in the state. Contractors performing covered construction work must obtain the appropriate CCB license before advertising, bidding, contracting, or performing work that requires licensure.

The contractor license is issued to the business entity. Each applicant must identify a Responsible Managing Individual who is an owner or employee and who manages or supervises the company’s construction activities.

Under the standard Oregon licensing pathway, the Responsible Managing Individual completes at least 16 hours of approved pre-license training and passes the Oregon contractor examination. A candidate who has passed the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is exempt from the standard 16-hour pre-license training requirement.

The NASCLA exemption does not eliminate the Oregon examination requirement. The Responsible Managing Individual must still pass the Oregon open-book examination covering contractor laws, rules, and business practices.

The Oregon contractor examination is based on the Oregon version of the NASCLA Contractors’ Guide to Business, Law and Project Management. The examination covers licensing responsibilities, business organization, contracts, financial management, employment matters, insurance, safety, liens, and other contractor obligations.

Applicants must choose the correct endorsement for the work they intend to perform. Oregon distinguishes among residential, commercial, and combined contracting activity. Commercial endorsements may also have different levels based on the type and scope of projects performed.

Corporations, limited liability companies, partnerships, and businesses operating under an assumed business name must complete the applicable registration with the Oregon Secretary of State. Organizational information should remain consistent throughout the application and supporting documents.

The CCB license application may require examination records, RMI information, business-structure details, ownership information, bond documentation, general liability insurance, and other materials associated with the requested endorsement.

The qualifying party must have a relationship with the applicant that meets the Board’s requirements. Depending on the business structure, the qualifying party may be an owner, officer, executive staff member, or responsible managing employee.

The contractor application may require business-registration records, ownership information, qualifying-party documentation, detailed electrical experience, references, financial information, insurance records, and other supporting materials. Application information should be accurate and consistent with the company’s official records.

Mississippi applicants are required to complete the Law and Business Management examination. A trade examination may also be required unless the Board accepts an approved examination result or grants an applicable waiver.

A passing NASCLA electrical examination result may be used to satisfy the trade-examination requirement when accepted by the licensing authority. Candidates must still complete the Mississippi application, Business and Law examination, documentation, and final approval process.

Passing the NASCLA examination does not authorize the candidate or business to begin regulated electrical contracting work. The applicable Mississippi contractor credential must be issued before the company performs work requiring the license.

Electrical contractors may also be responsible for local permits, inspections, utility requirements, adopted electrical codes, employee safety, tax registrations, insurance, and project-specific approvals.

Reference Books

The following references support the Mississippi NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors - Online Exam Prep Course. They are not included with the online course unless purchased separately.

  • National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023
    The primary electrical code reference covering services, feeders, branch circuits, conductors, wiring methods, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, motors, transformers, equipment, calculations, and specialized installations.
  • Code of Federal Regulations—29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    A federal construction-safety reference covering electrical hazards, temporary power, personal protective equipment, fall protection, ladders, tools, equipment, material handling, and construction operations.
  • Code of Federal Regulations—29 CFR Part 1910
    A federal general industry safety reference addressing workplace conditions, electrical safety, machinery, personal protective equipment, hazardous materials, emergency planning, and employer responsibilities.
  • A Guide to the Project Management Body of Knowledge
    A project-management reference addressing principles, stakeholders, teams, planning, project work, delivery, measurement, uncertainty, performance, and project outcomes.
  • ANSI/ASHRAE/IES 90.1-2022, Energy Standard for Sites and Buildings Except Low-Rise Residential Buildings—I-P Edition
    An energy-efficiency standard addressing applicable commercial building requirements for electrical power, lighting, controls, equipment, energy monitoring, and building performance.
  • NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Basic, 14th Edition
    A contractor business reference covering company organization, licensing, estimating, contracts, project management, financial management, employment responsibilities, safety, and risk management.
  • NFPA 70E—Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    An electrical workplace-safety standard covering shock and arc-flash hazards, risk assessments, protective equipment, approach boundaries, electrically safe work conditions, and safety-related work practices.
  • Ugly’s Electrical References
    A compact field reference containing electrical formulas, calculations, conversions, conductor information, diagrams, tables, and frequently used technical data.
  • Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications
    A technical reference connecting electrical theory, circuit behavior, calculations, and fundamental electrical principles with practical National Electrical Code applications.

Test Information and Study Materials

Create a study schedule that separates preparation into National Electrical Code navigation, electrical theory, calculations, construction safety, general industry safety, electrical workplace safety, energy standards, project management, and contractor business law.

Practice NEC navigation by article, definition, table, and index term. Review services, feeders, branch circuits, wiring methods, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, motors, transformers, equipment, and common calculations.

Study OSHA and NFPA 70E as connected but distinct resources. OSHA references address regulatory workplace responsibilities, while NFPA 70E provides detailed practices for controlling shock and arc-flash hazards.

Use the energy standard to review lighting power, controls, electrical distribution, equipment, and applicable commercial energy requirements. Use the PMBOK Guide to study planning, stakeholders, teams, delivery, performance, measurement, and uncertainty.

Complete timed reference searches while progressing through the course. Identify the primary subject, select the appropriate book, locate an effective search term, and find the supporting provision. Repeat slow lookups until navigation becomes more efficient.

When reviewing a missed practice question, determine whether the difficulty resulted from limited electrical knowledge, selecting the wrong reference, using an ineffective index term, overlooking an exception, misreading the question, or making a calculation error.

How 1 Exam Prep Helps You Reach Your Goal

1 Exam Prep helps electrical contractor candidates organize a broad accredited examination into manageable study areas. The online course provides trade-focused review, practice-oriented preparation, reference-navigation guidance, and a structured approach to the listed technical and business subjects.

The course helps connect practical electrical experience with the formal terminology used in codes, safety standards, energy requirements, project-management materials, formulas, and contractor examination questions.

Reference-navigation exercises encourage active preparation. Candidates practice identifying the correct book, selecting an effective search term, locating the applicable provision, interpreting technical information, and completing calculations.

Open-book examination confidence develops through repeated practice. Becoming familiar with indexes, article structures, tables, definitions, formulas, diagrams, and related search terms can help candidates approach the examination with a clearer strategy.

Results depend on the candidate’s electrical experience, preparation, technical understanding, reference-navigation ability, examination performance, and completion of all licensing requirements.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the online exam prep course cover?

The course supports preparation involving the National Electrical Code, electrical theory, calculations, OSHA safety, NFPA 70E, energy standards, project management, contractor business topics, and reference navigation.

Are the reference books included with the course?

No. The listed references support the course and examination preparation but must be purchased separately unless another package specifically includes them.

Is the NASCLA Electrical Contractor examination open book?

Yes. The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors is open book. Candidates must follow the current examination rules for permitted references and materials.

Does the course teach electrical work from the beginning?

No. The course is designed for contractor examination preparation and complements practical electrical experience rather than replacing trade education or field training.

Does this course include Mississippi Business and Law preparation?

No. This product focuses on the NASCLA electrical trade examination. Mississippi-specific Business and Law preparation is separate.

Should I study with the books while taking the course?

Yes. Using the listed references alongside the course helps develop practical lookup skills and familiarity with code articles, safety requirements, formulas, tables, and technical terminology.

Does passing the NASCLA examination create a national electrical license?

No. Candidates must apply for and satisfy the licensing requirements of each jurisdiction where they plan to perform regulated electrical contracting work.

How should I prepare for the open-book examination?

Learn the purpose of every reference, practice timed lookups, review code organization, complete calculations, and become familiar with related technical search terms.

Can I use a NASCLA examination result for Mississippi licensing?

A passing NASCLA result may satisfy the trade-examination requirement when accepted by Mississippi, but the applicant must still complete the state application and remaining licensing requirements.

No. Examination results depend on the candidate’s electrical experience, preparation, technical knowledge, calculation skills, reference-navigation ability, and performance on test day.

Does passing the examination automatically issue a Mississippi contractor license?

No. Passing the trade examination is one part of the licensing process. The state application, Business and Law examination, supporting documentation, and final approval requirements must also be completed.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Electrical Contractor examination contains 110 questions and allows 4.5 hours of testing time. Ten questions are experimental items and do not count toward the candidate's score.

The published examination subject areas include:

  • Project Design and Management: 8 questions
  • Safety: 9 questions
  • Electrical Theory & Principles: 11 questions
  • General Code Requirements: 17 questions
  • Wiring and Protection: 17 questions
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: 16 questions
  • General Equipment Use: 13 questions
  • Special Occupancies, Special Equipment, and Special Conditions: 8 questions
  • Communication Systems: 1 question
  • Experimental Items: 10 questions

General code requirements and wiring and protection each account for 17 questions, while wiring methods and materials accounts for another 16. These categories make familiarity with the National Electrical Code especially important. General equipment use, electrical theory and principles, safety, project design and management, and specialized electrical installations also represent meaningful portions of the examination.

Alabama currently offers the NASCLA Electrical Contractors Exam and the Alabama Electrical Contractor Exam through Prov. Candidates choosing the NASCLA Electrical Contractor route must also satisfy the applicable Alabama Business and Law examination requirement before licensure is issued.

The Alabama Electrical Contractor Business and Law examination contains 40 questions and allows 2 hours. Its subject areas include business organization, contracts, estimating, financial management, labor laws, licensing laws, lien laws, payroll and employment taxes, project management, risk management, safety, and environmental topics.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Electrical Contractor examination and the applicable Alabama Electrical Contractor Business and Law examination are open-book and timed examinations. Candidates should prepare by learning how each approved reference is organized and which books apply to particular subject areas.

Open-book testing rewards candidates who can combine technical knowledge with efficient reference navigation. Looking up every question from the beginning can consume valuable testing time. A stronger approach is to understand the underlying subject, identify the correct reference, locate the applicable section, and confirm the answer efficiently.

The National Electrical Code will be particularly important for subjects involving wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, general equipment, special occupancies, and general code requirements. OSHA and NFPA 70E support safety-related preparation, while electrical theory resources can help with calculations and electrical principles.

Project management and Business and Law preparation require familiarity with a different group of books. Candidates should become comfortable moving between technical electrical references and contractor-management material so they can quickly identify where relevant information is located.

Licensing Steps

Alabama Electrical Contractor licensing is administered by the Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors. Candidates seeking licensure through examination must complete the appropriate application process and receive approval before scheduling the required examination.

  1. Review the Electrical Contractor qualification requirements. Applicants should confirm that their electrical experience satisfies the Board's contractor-level requirements.
  2. Complete the Electrical Contractor Examination Application. Submit the current application and required supporting documentation to the Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors.
  3. Document qualifying electrical experience. Applicants must provide the employment, affidavit, or other documentation required by the Board.
  4. Receive authorization to test. The Board reviews the candidate's application and qualifications before examination approval is issued.
  5. Schedule the applicable examination. Approved candidates follow the current testing instructions for the NASCLA Electrical Contractor examination.
  6. Complete the required Business and Law examination. Alabama requires the applicable Business and Law examination before the Electrical Contractor license is issued.
  7. Complete the licensing process. After satisfying the examination requirements, candidates submit the applicable Electrical Contractor licensing forms and required documentation.

Candidates should use the current forms required by the Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors when applying. The Board maintains separate examination and licensing stages, so successfully completing an examination is only one part of obtaining the license.

State Requirements

Applicants seeking an Alabama Electrical Contractor license by examination must satisfy the experience and application requirements established by the Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors. Qualifying applicants must demonstrate substantial electrical construction experience appropriate to contractor-level responsibilities.

The Board requires applicants to document qualifying work experience through the applicable forms and supporting records. Electrical Contractor experience may involve planning, layout, supervision, installation, and other electrical construction responsibilities consistent with the scope of contractor-level work.

Alabama currently uses the 2023 NFPA 70 National Electrical Code for electrical examinations. The Board has announced that testing will move to the 2026 NFPA 70 National Electrical Code beginning January 1, 2027. This book package contains the 2023 NEC.

Candidates should make sure their examination application is approved before attempting to schedule the trade examination. After successfully completing the required examinations, the applicant must complete the appropriate licensing forms with the Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors.

A successful study plan should combine subject review with consistent book-navigation practice. This examination uses a large reference library, so candidates should avoid waiting until test day to become familiar with the books.

Begin with the 2023 National Electrical Code. Learn how it is organized and practice locating information through the index, chapters, articles, tables, and definitions. The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is accepted by the North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors for the Building classification. The NASCLA examination contains 115 scored questions. Candidates must answer at least 81 questions correctly to pass. Candidates receive 330 minutes, or 5 hours and 30 minutes, to complete the examination.

Licensing Steps

The North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors administers general contractor licensing. Applicants using the NASCLA examination must still complete the Board's application and qualification requirements before receiving a North Carolina license.

  1. Determine the appropriate classification. North Carolina accepts the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination for the Building classification.
  2. Select the desired license limitation. Applicants choose Limited, Intermediate, or Unlimited based on the size of projects the business intends to undertake and the financial qualification it can meet.
  3. Identify a qualifier. The applicant must identify an individual who holds an examination credential accepted by the Board and who will serve as the qualifier for the license.
  4. Complete the NASCLA examination. Candidates choosing the NASCLA pathway take the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination before using the result for North Carolina qualification.
  5. Submit the North Carolina license application. New license applications are submitted through the Board's licensing system with the required business, qualifier, financial, and supporting information.
  6. Complete the North Carolina state-specific examination requirement. Applicants using NASCLA must pass the Board's North Carolina law, rule, and building code examination before licensure.
  7. Meet financial responsibility requirements. The applicant must satisfy the financial standards associated with the selected Limited, Intermediate, or Unlimited limitation.
  8. Complete applicable background requirements. New applicants and qualifying individuals are subject to the background-check provisions established by the Board.
  9. Complete Board review. The North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors reviews the application and supporting qualifications before issuing the license.

State Requirements

North Carolina requires a general contractor license when the value of a covered construction project is $40,000 or more. The licensing requirement applies to covered building, highway, public utilities, grading, and other qualifying construction work.

The North Carolina Building Contractor classification includes commercial, industrial, institutional, public, private, and residential building construction. Its scope also includes qualifying sitework, grading, paving, storm drainage, retaining and screen walls, accessory structures, recreational facilities, and several specialty construction areas identified by Board rules.

North Carolina licenses are also divided by monetary limitation. A Limited License permits projects valued up to $750,000 each. An Intermediate License permits projects valued up to $1,500,000 each. An Unlimited License does not restrict the value of an individual project.

Financial requirements differ by limitation. Limited applicants must have current assets exceeding current liabilities by at least $17,000 or total net worth of at least $80,000. Intermediate applicants must demonstrate at least $75,000 in working capital. Unlimited applicants must demonstrate at least $150,000 in working capital. North Carolina rules also provide qualifying surety-bond alternatives for these financial requirements.

Applicants must be at least 18 years old, demonstrate financial responsibility, submit the appropriate application, and satisfy the Board's character and background requirements.

NASCLA qualification does not itself authorize contracting in North Carolina. The examination credential is used as part of the licensing process, and the contractor must receive the appropriate North Carolina license before undertaking work that requires licensure.

Exam Details

Oregon contractor licensing is administered by the Oregon Construction Contractors Board, commonly known as the CCB. Most Oregon contractor licenses require a Responsible Managing Individual (RMI) who manages or supervises the construction activities of the business.

For most applicants, the RMI completes 16 hours of approved Oregon pre-license education and then passes the Oregon contractor examination. Candidates who have already passed the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors do not have to complete the 16-hour Oregon pre-license training. They must provide their NASCLA transcript to the CCB and still pass the Oregon examination covering laws, rules, and business practices.

The Oregon contractor examination contains 80 multiple-choice questions. Candidates have 3 hours to complete the exam and must achieve a 70% passing score, which equals 56 correct answers.

The Oregon examination is based on the Oregon edition of the contractor business, law, and project-management reference. Candidates should study subjects involving contractor licensing, business practices, contracts, employment responsibilities, financial management, insurance, bonds, project management, and Oregon construction requirements.

The NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination is a separate national trade examination covering broad commercial construction knowledge. Major preparation areas include:

  • General construction requirements
  • Planning and estimating
  • Procurement and contracting
  • Financial and project management
  • Construction safety
  • Site construction
  • Concrete
  • Masonry
  • Metals
  • Wood construction
  • Thermal and moisture protection
  • Doors, windows, and glazing
  • Finishes
  • Mechanical and plumbing systems
  • Electrical systems

Candidates using NASCLA for Oregon licensing should treat the NASCLA trade examination and Oregon state examination as separate study areas. NASCLA focuses on commercial construction knowledge, while the Oregon examination focuses on Oregon contractor law, rules, and business practices.

The NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination is also an open-book examination using its designated commercial construction reference library. Licensing Steps

The Oregon Construction Contractors Board establishes the licensing process for construction contractors operating in Oregon. NASCLA candidates still complete the Oregon-specific steps required for a CCB license.

  1. Identify the Responsible Managing Individual. Most Oregon contractor endorsements require an RMI who manages or supervises the company's construction activities. The RMI may be an owner, officer, partner, or employee of the business.
  2. Use the NASCLA pathway when applicable. An applicant who has passed the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors can use that credential instead of completing Oregon's standard 16-hour pre-license education requirement.
  3. Provide the NASCLA transcript to the Oregon CCB. NASCLA candidates must provide proof of passing the accredited commercial examination so they can become eligible for Oregon's state examination.
  4. Pass the Oregon contractor examination. NASCLA applicants must still pass the Oregon examination covering contractor laws, rules, and business practices.
  5. Choose the correct Oregon endorsement. Oregon offers residential and commercial endorsements with different scopes and requirements. Commercial contractors should select the endorsement that matches their intended business activities.
  6. Register the business entity. Corporations, LLCs, and assumed business names must be properly filed through Oregon's business registration system when applicable.
  7. Obtain the required CCB surety bond. The bond amount depends on the endorsement selected.
  8. Obtain general liability insurance. Oregon requires proof of general liability coverage in an amount corresponding with the contractor's endorsement.
  9. Obtain workers' compensation coverage when applicable. Contractors hiring employees must comply with Oregon workers' compensation requirements.
  10. Complete and submit the CCB license application. The application must include the required bond, insurance, business, RMI, and supporting information.

Applicants must apply for the Oregon CCB license within 24 months of passing the Oregon contractor examination. The Application Service included with The 1 Package supports candidates with organizing the licensing process while they complete exam preparation and business setup.

State Requirements

Oregon requires construction contractors performing qualifying work for compensation to hold the appropriate Construction Contractors Board license. The license is issued to the contracting business and must correspond with the endorsement under which the contractor intends to operate.

Most licenses require a Responsible Managing Individual. The RMI must be an owner or employee of the business and have management or supervisory authority over the company's construction activities. An individual may not serve as an RMI employee for multiple CCB licenses at the same time.

Oregon contractors must select an appropriate residential or commercial endorsement. Commercial general and commercial specialty endorsements are divided into Level 1 and Level 2 categories, with requirements that vary according to the business and endorsement selected.

A CCB surety bond is required, and the applicable bond amount depends on the endorsement. Contractors must also maintain the general liability insurance required for their endorsement and provide the necessary certificate of coverage with the licensing application.

Businesses employing workers must comply with Oregon workers' compensation requirements. Contractors may also need state and federal tax accounts and employer identification numbers depending on their business structure and workforce.

Commercial contractors have continuing education obligations during the license cycle. Oregon bases commercial continuing education requirements on whether the contractor is Level 1 or Level 2 and, for Level 1 contractors, the number of key employees.

Virginia contractor licenses are divided into Class A, Class B, and Class C. The class determines the monetary size of work the business may undertake.

Class A applies when a single contract or project is valued at $150,000 or more, or when the total value of construction undertaken during a 12-month period is $1 million or more.

Class B applies when a single contract or project is valued at $30,000 or more but less than $150,000, or when the total value of construction during a 12-month period is $250,000 or more but less than $1 million.

Applicants must still satisfy the licensing requirements established by West Virginia.

West Virginia regulates contractor businesses and individual electricians through separate state programs. Contractor licensing is administered through the West Virginia Division of Labor and Contractors Licensing Board, while individual electrician licensing is administered by the West Virginia State Fire Marshal's Office. Understanding this distinction is important because passing a NASCLA examination does not automatically create either a contractor license or an individual West Virginia master electrician license.

The NASCLA electrical examination is designed for Electrical Contractors, Master Electricians, and Unlimited Electricians. It evaluates a broad range of knowledge needed by experienced electrical professionals, including electrical theory, Code application, wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, equipment, workplace safety, project design and management, special electrical conditions, and communication systems.

Because the examination is open book, effective preparation should include consistent work with the approved reference materials. Open-book testing rewards candidates who understand the organization of their references and can move efficiently between books, chapters, Code articles, tables, formulas, and safety standards. The goal is not simply to know that information exists in a book, but to know where to find it when time matters.

The West Virginia NASCLA Master Electrical Contractor - Online Exam Prep provides an organized approach to preparing for this advanced electrical examination. Study can focus on strengthening technical knowledge, practicing calculations, improving NEC navigation, reviewing safety requirements, and developing a repeatable method for solving exam-style questions.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors is part of the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program. It is intended for Electrical Contractors, Master Electricians, and Unlimited Electricians whose work involves electrical installation, maintenance, repair, and related responsibilities governed by electrical codes and industry standards.

The examination content is based on an occupational analysis developed with electrical industry subject matter experts. Candidates should expect the exam to evaluate both technical knowledge and the practical application of electrical standards rather than simple memorization of Code article numbers.

Major examination areas include:

  • Project Design and Management: Planning, coordination, professional responsibilities, and project-related electrical work.
  • Safety: Construction safety and electrical workplace safety requirements.
  • Electrical Theory: Electrical principles, relationships, calculations, and practical applications.
  • General Code Requirements: Broad National Electrical Code requirements applying to electrical installations.
  • Wiring and Protection: Branch circuits, feeders, services, overcurrent protection, grounding, bonding, and related requirements.
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: Conductors, cables, raceways, boxes, fittings, installation methods, and permitted applications.
  • Equipment for General Use: Motors, transformers, appliances, luminaires, equipment connections, and other commonly installed electrical equipment.
  • Special Occupancies, Equipment, and Conditions: NEC requirements applying to specialized locations, systems, and installations.
  • Communication Systems: Requirements associated with applicable communications wiring and systems.

A strong exam preparation plan should address every content area while giving additional attention to topics that require frequent Code navigation or multi-step calculations. Candidates should be comfortable determining whether a problem calls for direct trade knowledge, a mathematical calculation, an NEC lookup, or information from another reference.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program uses open-book electrical trade examinations. Candidates preparing for the Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination should build reference navigation into their regular study routine.

An open-book examination can still be challenging because the amount of material available is substantial. The National Electrical Code alone contains hundreds of sections, tables, definitions, exceptions, and specialized requirements. Additional books cover electrical theory, OSHA requirements, NFPA 70E safety practices, project management, energy standards, and contractor-related concepts.

Practice locating information rather than simply reading the references from beginning to end. When working through a practice question, identify the subject first. Determine whether it involves conductors, overcurrent protection, grounding, motors, transformers, wiring methods, safety, electrical theory, project management, or another topic. Then select the most appropriate reference and locate the controlling information.

NEC navigation deserves particular attention. Become comfortable using the index, Article 100 definitions, chapter structure, tables, exceptions, informational notes, and cross-referenced sections. Learn where commonly tested electrical subjects are located so that you can begin searches in the correct part of the Code.

Candidates should also follow the current NASCLA and testing-provider rules governing reference books, markings, tabs, and other materials permitted in the examination room. Studying with books prepared in accordance with current testing rules can make practice more realistic and help avoid relying on materials that cannot be used on exam day.

Licensing Steps

  1. Determine which West Virginia credential you need. Contractor licensing and individual electrician licensing are separate. The West Virginia Contractors Licensing Board regulates contractor businesses, while the West Virginia State Fire Marshal's Office regulates individual electricians.
  2. Review the electrical contractor licensing pathway. Contractors performing qualifying construction work in West Virginia must obtain the appropriate contractor license and classification through the Division of Labor.
  3. Determine whether the NASCLA examination fits your contractor application. West Virginia's Contractors Licensing Board participates in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program and accepts the Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination.
  4. Apply for the NASCLA electrical examination. Candidates using the NASCLA route complete the applicable NASCLA examination application before scheduling.
  5. Schedule the examination after authorization. Approved NASCLA candidates receive instructions for scheduling the examination through the designated testing provider.
  6. Prepare for the open-book examination. Study electrical theory, Code requirements, wiring methods, protection, equipment, safety, project management, and reference navigation.
  7. Pass the NASCLA examination. Passing results can be maintained through the NASCLA National Examination Database and transmitted to participating state agencies as applicable.
  8. Complete the West Virginia contractor application process. Submit the required contractor licensing application and supporting documentation to the West Virginia Division of Labor.
  9. Complete individual electrician licensing separately when required. Electricians performing regulated electrical work must follow the licensing requirements administered by the West Virginia State Fire Marshal's Office.

State Requirements

West Virginia uses separate regulatory systems for contractor businesses and individual electricians. A business performing construction work that meets the state's contractor licensing threshold must obtain the appropriate contractor license through the West Virginia Contractors Licensing Board, Division of Labor. Electrical contractor is one of the classifications regulated through that program.

The West Virginia Contractors Licensing Board participates in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program and accepts the NASCLA Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination. This allows an applicant to use an accepted NASCLA examination result in place of the applicable state trade examination requirement for the participating contractor licensing pathway.

NASCLA examination acceptance should not be confused with individual master electrician licensure. The West Virginia State Fire Marshal's Office, Regulatory and Licensing Division, administers electrician licenses statewide. Its programs include master electrician, journeyman electrician, and specialty electrician licensing.

West Virginia's electrician licensing rules establish experience requirements for individuals seeking a master electrician license. The current rules require a master electrician applicant to have two years of experience as a journeyman electrician in electrical work demonstrating the breadth, independence, and quality necessary to perform electrical work and direct other electricians.

The State Fire Marshal's current electrical examination application describes the master electrician experience standard as at least two years, or 4,000 hours, of qualifying hands-on electrical work experience. Individual applicants pursuing the West Virginia master electrician credential must follow the State Fire Marshal's licensing and examination requirements.

As of January 1, 2026, West Virginia's state-administered electrical examinations through the State Fire Marshal are based on the 2023 edition of NFPA 70, the National Electrical Code. This state examination update is separate from the NASCLA contractor examination program but is important for applicants who also need an individual West Virginia electrician license.

Passing a NASCLA examination does not issue a West Virginia contractor license, master electrician license, or other professional credential. Applicants must complete the relevant state applications and satisfy the licensing requirements associated with the work they intend to perform.

As your preparation progresses, use timed practice sessions. Contractor businesses are licensed through the West Virginia Contractors Licensing Board, Division of Labor. Electrical contractor is one of the contractor classifications regulated by that agency.

Who licenses individual master electricians in West Virginia?

The West Virginia State Fire Marshal's Office, Regulatory and Licensing Division, administers individual electrician licensing, including master electrician licenses.

West Virginia's electrician licensing rules require a master electrician applicant to have two years of qualifying journeyman-level electrical experience demonstrating the ability to perform and supervise electrical work. Beginning January 1, 2026, West Virginia's State Fire Marshal electrical examinations are based on the 2023 edition of NFPA 70, the National Electrical Code.

Test Information and Study Materials

Preparation for the Virginia NASCLA Master Electrical Contractor exam should combine technical knowledge, calculations, Code application, and reference navigation. Reading alone may not provide enough practice for a professional open-book examination. Candidates benefit from actively solving questions and locating supporting information.

Begin with the highest-volume Code subjects. General Code Requirements, Wiring and Protection, Wiring Methods and Materials, and Equipment for General Use represent a large portion of the examination. Review topics involving branch circuits, feeders, services, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, raceways, cables, boxes, motors, transformers, and commonly encountered equipment.

Electrical Theory should be studied through problem solving. Practice identifying the values provided in a question, selecting the appropriate relationship or formula, maintaining correct units, completing the calculation, and determining whether an NEC requirement affects the final answer. Understanding the underlying electrical principle makes it easier to recognize how a problem should be approached.

Safety preparation should include familiarity with both construction workplace requirements and electrical safety practices. Learn which reference is likely to contain the information requested so that you can navigate directly to the appropriate source during study and testing.

Project Design and Management should also be part of the study schedule. Electrical contractors work within broader construction projects that involve planning, coordination, documentation, scheduling, risk management, communication, and project execution. These professional responsibilities are represented in the NASCLA examination blueprint.

Timed practice can help bring these skills together. Set aside blocks of time to answer questions while using the reference materials. Track how long you spend on calculations and searches. If a question becomes time-consuming, practice moving forward and returning to it later. Developing a consistent approach to pacing can make the examination environment more manageable.
