Trade-focused review helps strengthen understanding of electrical theory, wiring requirements, protection methods, electrical equipment, safety, project management, and special electrical conditions. Building that foundation can make Code questions easier to interpret and help candidates recognize which reference applies to a particular problem.

Practice-oriented preparation also helps identify areas that need additional attention. One candidate may need more work with electrical calculations, while another may need to improve Code-navigation speed. Others may be strong in installation requirements but need additional review of safety standards or project-management concepts. A structured study process makes those differences easier to identify.

Reference navigation is especially important for an open-book examination. 1 Exam Prep supports candidates in becoming more familiar with the organization of the NEC and supporting references so they can practice locating information with greater efficiency. Knowing where to search can be just as valuable as knowing what to search for.

The objective is to help candidates build technical knowledge, improve reference familiarity, reinforce trade concepts, and develop confidence through organized preparation. Examination success and Virginia licensing depend on the candidate's performance and satisfaction of all applicable state requirements.

FAQ Section

Does Virginia participate in the NASCLA Electrical Examination Program?

Yes. The Virginia Board for Contractors and Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation are listed as participating agencies in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program.

Is the NASCLA Electrical Contractor exam open book?

Yes. NASCLA identifies the Electrical Contractor examination as an open-book examination. Candidates should become familiar with the reference materials and current testing rules before exam day.

How many scored questions are on the NASCLA Electrical Contractor exam?

The NASCLA examination blueprint contains 100 scored items distributed across nine electrical and professional content domains.

What subjects are most heavily represented on the exam?

General Code Requirements and Wiring and Protection each contain 17 items, Wiring Methods and Materials contains 16 items, and Equipment for General Use contains 13 items. Electrical Theory, Safety, Project Design and Management, Special Occupancies and Conditions, and Communication Systems make up the remaining content.

How can I qualify for a Virginia master electrician examination?

Virginia's current regulations provide qualification paths that include holding a valid journeyman license in the trade for at least one year or documenting nine years of practical experience in the applicable trade. Applicants must provide the documentation required by the Board.

Is a Virginia master electrician license the same as a Virginia electrical contractor license?

No. A master electrician license is an individual tradesman credential. A Virginia contractor license applies to the contracting business. Electrical contractors must meet the contractor licensing requirements and identify the appropriately qualified individual for the electrical specialty.

Does an electrical contractor's qualified individual need a Virginia master electrician license?

Virginia contractor regulations identify a master electrician tradesman license issued by the Board for Contractors as the qualification associated with the Electrical Contractors specialty.

Does passing the NASCLA exam automatically give me a Virginia license?

No. The NASCLA examination is not a national license. Candidates must complete the Virginia licensing process and satisfy the applicable requirements established by the Virginia Board for Contractors.

Why is reference navigation important for this exam?

The examination is open book, but the references contain a large amount of material. Practicing navigation can help candidates identify the correct book, section, table, formula, or standard more efficiently during testing.

Does Virginia require continuing education for master electricians?

Yes. Virginia requires licensed master electricians to complete approved electrical continuing education as a condition of renewal. The required electrical continuing education course is three hours and addresses the applicable National Electrical Code update.

  5. Complete the North Carolina license application. Submit the application for the electrical contracting classification requested.

State Requirements

Electrical contracting in North Carolina is regulated by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors.

North Carolina law defines electrical contracting as engaging or offering to engage in the business of installing, maintaining, altering, or repairing electrical work, wiring, devices, appliances, or equipment. A business performing electrical contracting must hold the applicable license classification.

North Carolina issues three principal electrical contracting classifications: Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited. It also offers several Special Restricted classifications for more limited types of electrical work.

The Limited classification requires at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 2,000 hours of primary experience involving direct installation of electrical wiring and equipment governed by the National Electrical Code.

The Intermediate classification requires at least 5,750 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 5,000 hours of primary electrical experience.

The Unlimited classification requires at least 9,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 8,000 hours of primary experience. Unlimited applicants must also provide statements from individuals knowledgeable about the applicant's electrical experience and ability to supervise and direct electrical installation work.

The Unlimited classification permits the licensee to engage in electrical contracting projects without a project-value limit. Limited and Intermediate licenses are subject to the project-value limits established for those classifications.

Applicants who pass this NASCLA examination may apply for Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, or applicable Special Restricted classifications, subject to the requirements of the classification selected.

North Carolina requires NASCLA-qualified applicants to have their examination transcripts sent to the Board through the NASCLA National Examination Database.

Passing NASCLA does not create a national license and does not automatically produce a North Carolina electrical contractor license. A strong Louisiana NASCLA Electrical study plan should begin with the largest exam areas: General Code Requirements, Wiring and Protection, and Wiring Methods and Materials. Together, these three categories account for half of the scored examination.

General Code Requirements preparation should include broad NEC rules involving equipment, installation, working space, conductor identification, listing and labeling concepts, and general provisions that apply across multiple electrical systems.

Wiring and Protection should include branch circuits, feeders, services, conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, grounding, bonding, load calculations, and protection requirements.

Wiring Methods and Materials should include conduit, raceways, cable systems, conductors, boxes, fittings, supports, conduit fill, box fill, and installation conditions.

Equipment for General Use accounts for 13 questions. Candidates should review motors, transformers, generators, appliances, luminaires, equipment connections, controllers, and other commonly encountered electrical equipment.

Electrical Theory and Principles contributes 11 questions. Practice Ohm's Law, series and parallel circuits, power formulas, alternating current, voltage, current, resistance, impedance, motors, and transformer relationships.

Reference navigation should be practiced with every question set. Before opening a book, decide what kind of question you are answering. An NEC installation question, electrical theory problem, workplace-safety question, and project-management question should not all be approached with the same reference.

For NEC questions, identify the primary electrical term and use the index strategically. Move to the referenced article or table, then confirm whether exceptions, notes, or related sections change the answer.

For calculation questions, identify the electrical relationship before searching. Knowing whether the problem involves voltage, current, resistance, power, conductor sizing, motors, or transformers helps narrow the search and improve efficiency.

Because the examination allows 270 minutes for 100 scored questions, timed practice is important. Candidates should learn when to mark a difficult question and move on rather than spending an excessive amount of time on one reference search.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Trade Examination for Electrical Contractors is designed for Electrical Contractors, Master Electricians, and Unlimited Electricians. The content distribution shows why strong National Electrical Code knowledge is important. NASCLA examination guidance permits approved references to be highlighted, underlined, and permanently indexed while otherwise remaining unmarked. Additional loose or attached papers are not permitted, and temporary indexing materials such as Post-it notes are not allowed.

An open-book examination still requires extensive preparation. The references contain a large amount of information, and searching every question from the beginning of a book can consume valuable testing time. Candidates should develop familiarity with the organization of each major reference before taking the examination.

National Electrical Code navigation should receive particular attention. Become comfortable locating definitions, tables, conductor requirements, branch-circuit provisions, feeder and service requirements, grounding and bonding provisions, wiring methods, overcurrent protection rules, motor requirements, transformer provisions, and requirements for specialized installations.

Practice with supporting references as well. Safety questions may involve OSHA construction regulations or NFPA 70E. Electrical theory may require textbook knowledge or calculation references. State Requirements

An individual electrical contractor may serve as the contractor's own supervising master electrician when that individual holds the required valid master electrician license. Business entities must satisfy the applicable contractor application and supervisory requirements established by the Idaho Electrical Board.

Idaho requires an electrical contractor license before a person or business acts or attempts to act as an electrical contractor within the scope regulated by the state. Electrical contracting includes covered installation, maintenance, and repair activities.

The Electrical major classification covers the installation, construction, alteration, improvement, movement, maintenance, repair, or demolition of wiring, cabling, fixtures, appliances, equipment, and hardware used for supplying electricity to a structure, building, or project when the work falls within Louisiana's licensing requirements.

Louisiana requires a commercial contractor license for electrical projects exceeding $10,000 in value, including labor and materials. This electrical threshold is different from the general commercial construction threshold that applies to many other types of contracting work.

Louisiana requires contractor applicants to designate a qualifying party. The qualifying party is the individual who represents the licensed entity for purposes of complying with licensing law, satisfying the Business and Law requirement, and meeting the requirements associated with the contractor classifications carried on the license.

Qualifying parties can include a sole proprietor, certain owners or officers, partners, members or managers of a limited liability company, or qualifying full-time employees when the relationship satisfies the Board's requirements. Supporting documentation may be required to verify the qualifying party's relationship to the contracting business.

The qualifying party must meet the examination or credential requirements associated with the classification being requested. Louisiana requires the contractor to maintain an eligible qualifying party for Business and Law and for each classification carried on the license.

Louisiana's licensing application specifically allows applicants to request credit from a passing NASCLA examination for Electrical. When this option is selected, the applicant is directed to use the NASCLA National Examination Database to send the transcript to the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors.

The Business and Law requirement is separate from the NASCLA electrical trade examination. Louisiana contractor applicants must complete the applicable Business and Law requirement through the state's licensing process.

Passing the NASCLA examination does not automatically create a Louisiana electrical contractor license. The applicant must still satisfy the qualifying-party requirements, Business and Law requirements, application requirements, and other licensing conditions established by the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors.

    Federal construction-safety regulations addressing workplace hazards, employee protection, electrical safety considerations, jobsite practices, and other occupational safety requirements associated with construction work.

Begin with the 2023 National Electrical Code. Practice locating requirements for services, feeders, branch circuits, conductor sizing, ampacity, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, raceways, cables, boxes, motors, transformers, and equipment. Electrical theory should be studied through calculations and applied problem solving. Use the theory references to reinforce voltage, current, resistance, power, circuit relationships, motors, transformers, and other core concepts. For calculation questions, identify the information given, determine what must be solved, choose the appropriate formula, and evaluate whether an NEC requirement affects the final answer.

Project-management preparation should include planning, communication, coordination, estimating, risk, scheduling, documentation, and other responsibilities associated with professional electrical contracting. A master electrician, journeyman electrician, residential electrician, or limited electrical installer may serve as a supervising electrician when the contractor's work falls within that person's licensed scope of practice.

Idaho rules also specify that the contractor's allowable scope of electrical work follows the scope of its licensed supervising employee. This makes the supervising electrician an important part of the contractor licensing structure and distinguishes the business license from the individual electrical credential.

Passing the NASCLA examination does not automatically create an Idaho Master Electrician or Electrical Contractor license. Candidates must still apply through the Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses and satisfy the experience, supervision, application, and other requirements associated with the credential they are pursuing.

Electrical contracting in North Carolina is regulated by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. The Limited classification requires at least 3,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 2,000 hours of primary experience involving direct installation of electrical wiring and equipment governed by the National Electrical Code.

The Intermediate classification requires at least 5,750 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 5,000 hours of primary electrical experience. The current Board licensing information limits an Intermediate license holder to a single electrical contracting project valued at no more than $150,000.

The Unlimited classification requires at least 9,000 hours of qualifying experience, including at least 8,000 hours of primary electrical experience. Unlimited applicants must also submit written statements from at least two people familiar with the applicant's electrical experience attesting to the applicant's ability to supervise and direct electrical wiring or installation work performed by an electrical contracting business.

The Unlimited classification allows the licensee to engage in electrical contracting projects regardless of project value. NASCLA's electrical program includes separate examinations for Electrical Contractors/Master Electricians, Journeyman Electricians, and Residential Electrical Contractors. The Journeyman Electrician examination is specifically designed around the knowledge and skills associated with journeyman-level electrical work.

The Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors defines a Journeyman Electrician as an individual with the qualifications, training, and technical knowledge necessary to install electrical wiring, apparatus, equipment, lighting, heating, power, or controls. An Alabama Journeyman Electrician works under a master electrician or state-certified electrical contractor and must be capable of performing electrical work according to plans, specifications, applicable rules, and regulations.

This online exam prep program helps candidates organize their preparation around important areas such as the 2023 National Electrical Code, electrical theory, workplace and construction safety, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, circuit protection, troubleshooting, special occupancies, fire alarm systems, and electrical calculations. The goal is to build both trade knowledge and the reference-navigation skills needed for an open-book NASCLA electrical examination.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians is one of three examinations offered through the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program. NASCLA developed the examination content through an occupational analysis involving electrical subject matter experts from across the United States.

The examination focuses on the knowledge and skills expected of a journeyman electrician rather than the business-management responsibilities associated with an electrical contractor or master-level contractor examination. NASCLA's published Journeyman Electrician content domains include:

  • Interpreting Plans and Specifications
  • Basic Electrical Safety
  • Electrical Theory and Principles
  • Testing and Troubleshooting
  • General Code Requirements
  • Wiring and Protection
  • Wiring Methods and Materials
  • Equipment for General Use
  • Special Occupancies and Special Equipment
  • Special Conditions and Communication Systems

These subject areas reflect the broad range of knowledge journeyman electricians use in the field. Preparation should therefore include more than memorizing NEC article numbers. Candidates benefit from understanding electrical theory, calculations, installation requirements, safety practices, equipment operation, troubleshooting methods, and how different sections of the electrical code work together.

Alabama currently bases its electrical examinations on the 2023 NFPA 70 National Electrical Code. The Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors has announced that its examinations will begin referencing the 2026 National Electrical Code on January 1, 2027. Candidates preparing under the current testing cycle should therefore develop strong familiarity with the 2023 NEC.

The Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors currently uses Prov for electrical licensing examinations and application-related testing processes. Candidates pursuing Alabama licensure should complete the applicable Board examination application and receive authorization according to the state's current procedures.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Journeyman Electrician examination is an open book test. NASCLA's Accredited Electrical Examination Program consists of open-book electrical trade examinations using authorized reference materials under the applicable examination rules.

Open-book testing rewards preparation and reference familiarity. The ability to bring approved books into an examination does not eliminate the need to understand electrical concepts. Candidates still need to recognize what a question is asking, determine which reference applies, find the correct section, interpret the requirement, and choose the best answer while managing exam time.

Reference navigation should therefore become part of your study routine. Practice using indexes, tables of contents, NEC article organization, tables, definitions, informational notes, and cross-references. When working through a practice question, first identify the electrical topic and then decide where the information is most likely located before beginning your search.

The more frequently you use the actual references during preparation, the more familiar their organization becomes. This can be especially valuable for questions involving wiring methods, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, motors, special occupancies, communications, fire alarms, or safety requirements.

Licensing Steps

The NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination is an examination credential, not a license by itself. Alabama licenses Journeyman Electricians through the Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors, and candidates must satisfy the Board's application and licensing requirements.

  1. Review the Alabama Journeyman Electrician qualification requirements. Determine whether your electrical experience meets the Board's eligibility requirements before applying for examination approval.
  2. Submit the Electrical Journeyman Examination Application. Alabama requires candidates to apply to the Board for the applicable examination process.
  3. Prepare for the electrical examination. Study the 2023 NEC, electrical theory, safety, wiring methods, troubleshooting, equipment, special occupancies, and other journeyman-level subjects.
  4. Schedule the authorized examination. Follow the scheduling instructions provided after your examination application and eligibility are processed.
  5. Take and pass the applicable examination. Follow all examination-center rules concerning identification, approved references, calculators, prohibited materials, and testing procedures.
  6. Apply for Alabama Journeyman Electrician licensure. After successfully satisfying the examination requirement, complete the applicable Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors licensing application.
  7. Work within the scope of the Journeyman Electrician license. Alabama Journeyman Electricians perform qualifying electrical work under a master electrician or state-certified electrical contractor.

State Requirements

The Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors regulates electrical contractor and Journeyman Electrician licensing in Alabama. The Board distinguishes between an Electrical Contractor and a Journeyman Electrician.

An Electrical Contractor possesses the qualifications, training, and technical knowledge necessary to plan, lay out, and supervise electrical installations and may conduct business involving electrical power or control systems. A Journeyman Electrician performs electrical installation work under a master electrician or state-certified electrical contractor and must be capable of completing work according to plans, specifications, codes, and applicable regulations.

Alabama requires candidates to complete an examination application before proceeding through the traditional examination pathway. After successful examination completion, Journeyman Electrician applicants use the applicable Board licensing application to obtain their license.

Because NASCLA examination passage is not itself a license or certification, candidates must still meet the Alabama Board of Electrical Contractors' requirements. NASCLA examination participation can provide a standardized electrical examination pathway, while Alabama remains responsible for issuing and regulating the actual state license.

Alabama currently references the 2023 National Electrical Code for its electrical examination program. Candidates studying for current examinations should therefore practice code navigation using the 2023 NEC rather than an older edition.

Reference Books

The following references are included in the study materials identified for this Alabama NASCLA Journeyman Electrician Contractor - Online Exam Prep product:

  • NFPA 70 - National Electrical Code 2023
    The primary electrical code reference covering conductors, wiring methods, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, communications systems, and other requirements for electrical installations.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    A federal construction-safety reference addressing occupational safety and health requirements applicable to construction workplaces, including requirements relevant to electrical jobsite activities.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1910
    A federal occupational safety and health reference covering general industry standards, including requirements associated with workplace safety and electrical hazards.
  • NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    An electrical workplace safety standard focused on practices and procedures designed to reduce exposure to electrical hazards while employees perform electrical work.
  • Ugly's Electrical References, 2023
    A compact electrical field reference containing commonly used formulas, calculations, tables, conversions, and practical electrical information useful when reviewing trade concepts.
  • NFPA 72 - National Fire Alarm Code, 2022
    A fire alarm and signaling systems reference addressing requirements associated with fire detection, alarm, signaling, notification, and related systems.
  • Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications
    A study reference focused on strengthening electrical theory knowledge and connecting fundamental electrical principles with practical National Electrical Code applications.

Test Information and Study Materials

Effective NASCLA Journeyman Electrician exam preparation should combine code study with practical electrical knowledge. A strong study routine should cover the NEC, theory, calculations, troubleshooting, safety, wiring methods, equipment, special occupancies, and plans and specifications.

Start with the 2023 National Electrical Code. Learn how the NEC is organized rather than trying to memorize every rule. Practice using Article 100 definitions, locating requirements through the index, identifying chapters associated with specific equipment or occupancies, and following references from one code section to another.

Wiring and protection is a major journeyman-level knowledge area. Study services, feeders, branch circuits, conductor protection, overcurrent devices, grounding, bonding, and related requirements. Work through practice problems that require both calculation and code navigation.

Wiring methods and materials should also receive substantial attention. Become familiar with conductors, cables, raceways, boxes, fittings, installation conditions, conductor fill, ampacity considerations, and installation rules. Rather than studying each topic in isolation, practice recognizing which NEC article applies to a particular installation scenario.

Electrical theory provides the foundation for many journeyman questions. Review voltage, current, resistance, power, series and parallel circuits, alternating current concepts, transformers, motors, loads, and common electrical calculations. Understanding the underlying principles makes it easier to solve unfamiliar questions instead of relying only on memorized formulas.

Testing and troubleshooting should be included in your preparation as well. Journeyman electricians need to understand how electrical systems behave, how measurements are interpreted, and how problems can be isolated logically. Study the relationships among voltage, current, resistance, continuity, equipment operation, and circuit conditions.

Safety preparation should extend beyond a few memorized OSHA rules. The OSHA construction standards, OSHA general industry standards, and NFPA 70E help candidates study jobsite safety, electrical hazards, safe work practices, and workplace responsibilities. Understanding the purpose behind a safety requirement can make it easier to identify the correct response to scenario-based questions.

Special occupancies and equipment can involve code requirements that candidates do not encounter every day. Regular practice with these sections can prevent unfamiliar NEC articles from consuming too much time during an open-book examination. Fire alarm and signaling systems should also be reviewed using NFPA 72 and applicable NEC requirements.

Interpreting plans and specifications is another important journeyman skill. Practice identifying circuit information, symbols, equipment, locations, and installation requirements from electrical plans. Journeyman-level work frequently requires translating plans and specifications into safe, code-compliant installations.

The course brings electrical code review, theory, safety, trade knowledge, and practice-oriented preparation together in a structured online learning experience.

Trade-focused review helps you concentrate on areas that matter to journeyman electrical work. Instead of treating the NEC as a book to memorize from beginning to end, preparation emphasizes understanding the code's organization and learning how to identify where specific electrical requirements are located.

Practice-oriented preparation helps reinforce electrical calculations, code application, safety concepts, and troubleshooting skills. Repeated exposure to exam-style subjects can also help identify weaker areas that deserve additional study before testing.

Reference navigation is particularly important because the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination is open book. 1 Exam Prep encourages candidates to use their references actively while studying, building familiarity with indexes, articles, tables, and subject organization instead of waiting until examination day to navigate the books under pressure.

The course also supports confidence-building through structured preparation. A consistent routine of studying electrical concepts, reviewing reference material, working practice questions, and revisiting weaker subjects can help candidates approach the examination with greater familiarity with the material and the testing process.

The NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination covers major areas of professional electrical work, including interpreting plans and specifications, basic electrical safety, electrical theory and principles, testing and troubleshooting, general code requirements, wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, equipment for general use, special occupancies and equipment, and special conditions and communication systems.

Virginia is listed by NASCLA as an accepting agency for the Journeyman Electrician examination. A passing NASCLA result may be transmitted through the NASCLA National Examination Database for use by participating agencies. The examination result itself is not a license; Virginia retains authority over the actual Journeyman Electrician licensing process.

Virginia's Board for Contractors regulates individual tradesmen, including electricians. The Board requires pre-approval before candidates sit for Virginia-administered tradesman examinations. PSI is Virginia's current examination vendor for individual tradesman testing, and the Board's current testing program includes Journeyman Electrician and Master Electrician examinations.

Candidates preparing specifically through the NASCLA pathway should study the NASCLA examination blueprint and the reference materials associated with the accredited Journeyman Electrician exam. The strongest preparation plans balance National Electrical Code work with electrical theory, safety, calculations, troubleshooting, and practical application.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Journeyman Electrician examination is an open book test. Authorized reference materials may be used according to the examination rules in effect for the NASCLA testing appointment.

Open-book testing makes reference navigation an important part of preparation. Candidates need to recognize what a question is asking, decide which reference contains the relevant information, locate the appropriate section, and apply the rule or technical concept efficiently. Simply having the books available does not eliminate the need to understand the material.

The 2023 National Electrical Code should become one of your most familiar study tools. Practice using the NEC index, Article 100 definitions, tables, article organization, chapter structure, informational notes, and cross-references. Learn how general requirements interact with more specific rules for equipment, occupancies, and wiring systems.

Safety references should also be used throughout preparation. OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 focuses on construction-industry safety requirements, while OSHA 29 CFR 1910 addresses general-industry workplace requirements. NFPA 70E focuses specifically on electrical safety in the workplace.

NFPA 72 supports preparation involving fire alarm and signaling systems. Ugly's Electrical References provides formulas, tables, calculations, and practical electrical information. Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications supports the electrical principles behind many code and calculation questions.

A useful study routine is to identify the topic before opening a reference. Decide which book should contain the answer, navigate to the correct section, and then confirm the solution. Repeating that process helps develop a more efficient open-book testing strategy.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination does not automatically issue a Virginia Journeyman Electrician license. Candidates must complete the licensing requirements administered by the Virginia Board for Contractors.

  1. Choose the Journeyman Electrical designation. Virginia licenses Journeyman Electricians as individual tradesmen through the Board for Contractors.
  2. Review Virginia's qualification pathways. Determine which combination of practical experience, vocational training, education, apprenticeship, or other approved pathway applies to you.
  3. Document your experience and education. Virginia requires supporting documentation such as experience verification forms and training or education records when applicable.
  4. Complete the applicable exam and license application process. Submit the information required by the Virginia Board for Contractors for the licensing pathway you are using.
  5. Prepare for the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination. Study the 2023 NEC, electrical theory, safety, troubleshooting, wiring methods, equipment, special occupancies, fire alarms, and communication systems.
  6. Take and pass the accepted examination. Follow the current NASCLA and testing-provider rules for scheduling, identification, authorized references, and examination-day procedures.
  7. Complete Virginia licensure. After satisfying the examination requirement, complete the Board's remaining licensing requirements before working under the Virginia Journeyman Electrician designation.
  8. Maintain the license. Virginia Journeyman Electricians must comply with renewal and continuing-education requirements.

State Requirements

Virginia Journeyman Electrician licensing is administered through the Virginia Board for Contractors within the Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation. The Board regulates individual tradesmen engaged in electrical, plumbing, HVAC, gas fitting, and other regulated trades.

Virginia provides several qualification combinations for applicants seeking a Journeyman tradesman license by examination. One pathway requires four years of practical experience in the trade plus 240 hours of formal vocational training.

Another pathway allows five years of practical experience plus 160 hours of formal vocational training. Applicants may also qualify with six years of practical experience plus 80 hours of formal vocational training, or seven or more years of practical experience plus 40 hours of formal vocational training.

Virginia also recognizes qualifying education-based pathways. An applicant may qualify with an associate degree or certificate from at least a two-year tradesman-related program from an accredited community college or technical school together with two years of practical trade experience.

A qualifying bachelor's degree or certificate of completion from an accredited college or university in an engineering curriculum related to the trade can also be used with the applicable practical-experience requirement.

Journeyman applicants who successfully complete an approved apprenticeship program may qualify through that pathway. Virginia's application also provides procedures for applicants who completed an apprenticeship program in another state, provided the required documentation from the regulating entity and apprenticeship sponsor is submitted.

Applicants must be at least 18 years old. Virginia requires supporting documentation that verifies the experience, training, education, or apprenticeship pathway being used to qualify for licensure.

Virginia also requires pre-license education for tradesmen. Candidates should complete the Board-approved education requirements that apply to their licensing method before the license can be issued.

After licensure, Virginia Journeyman Electricians are subject to continuing-education requirements. Electricians must complete an approved three-hour continuing-education course in the applicable electrical code as a condition of renewal.

Virginia Journeyman Electrician licensure applies to an individual tradesman. Contractor business licensing is a separate matter. An individual who performs work that requires a Virginia contractor license must also comply with the Board for Contractors' business licensing rules.

  • NFPA 70 - National Electrical Code 2023
    The primary electrical code reference covering branch circuits, feeders, services, conductors, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, and communication systems.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    A federal construction-industry safety reference addressing occupational safety and health requirements applicable to construction jobsites and electrical work performed in construction environments.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1910
    A federal general-industry safety reference covering workplace requirements, including provisions relevant to electrical hazards and electrical work environments.
  • NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    An electrical workplace safety standard addressing practices and procedures intended to reduce exposure to electrical hazards.
  • Ugly's Electrical References, 2023
    A compact electrical reference containing commonly used formulas, calculations, tables, conversions, and practical electrical field information.
  • NFPA 72 - National Fire Alarm Code, 2022
    A fire alarm and signaling systems reference addressing detection, initiating devices, notification, signaling functions, and related system requirements.
  • Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications
    A study reference focused on strengthening electrical theory and connecting fundamental electrical principles with National Electrical Code applications and calculations.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive Virginia NASCLA Journeyman Electrician study plan should combine National Electrical Code navigation with electrical theory, safety, troubleshooting, calculations, plans, equipment, and specialty electrical work. The NASCLA examination blueprint covers a wide range of journeyman responsibilities, so preparation should not be limited to memorizing NEC articles.

Start with the 2023 National Electrical Code. Practice locating requirements for branch circuits, feeders, services, conductors, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, boxes, raceways, equipment, and special occupancies. Learn to use the index efficiently and practice following cross-references between related articles.

Electrical theory should receive regular study time. Review voltage, current, resistance, power, series circuits, parallel circuits, alternating-current concepts, transformers, motors, loads, conductor calculations, and other principles commonly used in electrical work. Understanding the theory behind a calculation can make unfamiliar questions easier to solve.

Testing and troubleshooting are also important journeyman-level skills. Practice interpreting voltage, resistance, current, continuity, circuit behavior, and equipment operation. A systematic troubleshooting method can help with questions that require reasoning rather than direct code lookup.

Safety preparation should include OSHA construction standards, OSHA general-industry standards, and NFPA 70E. Study both general workplace safety requirements and electrical-specific hazard controls.

Plans and specifications should be part of the study schedule. Practice recognizing symbols, circuits, equipment, locations, and installation requirements from electrical drawings. Journeyman electricians must often translate plans into compliant field installations.

Special occupancies, special equipment, communication systems, and fire alarm systems should also receive attention. These subjects may involve code sections that candidates encounter less frequently, making advance navigation practice especially valuable.

Use the references while studying rather than waiting until the final review period. When you work a practice question, identify the subject first, select the most likely reference, locate the applicable section, and then confirm the answer. This reinforces both trade knowledge and open-book exam skills.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians is designed around the competency expected of an individual performing electrical installation, maintenance, and repair work in accordance with applicable standards and codes. NASCLA developed the examination through a national occupational analysis involving electrical subject matter experts and electricians from multiple jurisdictions.

The current NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination contains 100 scored questions. Candidates must achieve a minimum passing score of 70. The current candidate information published for the examination allows 300 minutes for completion.

In addition to the scored questions, NASCLA may administer non-scored experimental questions. These questions are used for future examination development and are not included when calculating the candidate's final examination score.

The Journeyman Electrician examination content outline covers the following major subject areas:

  • Interpreting Plans and Specifications
  • Basic Electrical Safety
  • Electrical Theory and Principles
  • Testing and Troubleshooting
  • General Code Requirements
  • Wiring and Protection
  • Wiring Methods and Materials
  • Equipment for General Use
  • Special Occupancies and Special Equipment
  • Special Conditions and Communication Systems

The examination places substantial emphasis on code-based electrical work. Candidates should be prepared to locate and apply requirements for branch circuits, feeders, services, conductor protection, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, equipment, special installations, and other National Electrical Code subjects.

Electrical theory, safety, plans, troubleshooting, and specialty systems remain important parts of preparation. A candidate who concentrates only on NEC lookup may leave significant areas of the examination insufficiently reviewed.

NASCLA examination applications are handled through the NASCLA National Examination Database. Once an application is approved, candidates receive examination scheduling information for the NASCLA testing program. NASCLA currently provides approved candidates with up to three examination attempts during the one-year eligibility period associated with an approved application.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Journeyman Electrician examination is an open book test. Candidates may use authorized reference materials in accordance with NASCLA and testing-center rules.

Open-book testing does not remove the need for preparation. Candidates still need to identify the electrical concept involved, select the appropriate reference, locate the correct section or table, interpret the information, and apply it accurately within the available testing time.

The 2023 National Electrical Code should become one of the most familiar references in your library. Practice using the NEC index, Article 100 definitions, chapters, articles, tables, informational notes, and cross-references. Learn where commonly tested subjects are located rather than attempting to memorize every code number.

NASCLA testing rules permit qualifying reference materials to be highlighted, underlined, and indexed. Permanent tabs may be used under the published testing rules. Temporary tabs such as Post-it notes are not allowed. References must otherwise remain unmarked and cannot contain additional loose or attached papers.

The reference books are not supplied at the examination center, so candidates using permitted books must bring their own approved materials. Preparing with the same references before testing helps build familiarity with each book's organization and reduces the need for random searching.

A useful practice technique is to read a question, identify the topic before opening a book, choose the reference most likely to contain the answer, and then locate the applicable information. Repeating that process develops both technical knowledge and practical reference-navigation skills.

Licensing Steps

Tennessee's electrical licensing structure includes state contractor licensing, the Limited Licensed Electrician program, and local electrical licensing requirements. Tennessee does not treat passing the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination by itself as permission to perform unrestricted electrical contracting work throughout the state.

  1. Identify the Tennessee license or local credential required for your work. Determine whether the work falls under Tennessee contractor licensing, Limited Licensed Electrician requirements, or a municipality's local electrical licensing rules.
  2. Review the applicable licensing authority's requirements. The Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors regulates contractor licenses and the state Limited Licensed Electrician program, while local jurisdictions may impose their own requirements.
  3. Prepare for the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination. Study the 2023 NEC, electrical theory, workplace safety, wiring methods, troubleshooting, equipment, calculations, and specialty systems.
  4. Apply for the NASCLA examination. Complete the NASCLA Accredited Examination application process through the National Examination Database.
  5. Schedule and take the examination. Follow the NASCLA testing instructions and examination-center rules for identification, references, permanent tabs, calculators, and prohibited materials.
  6. Pass the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination. After passing, the examination result is recorded in NASCLA's National Examination Database.
  7. Submit the examination result when applicable. NASCLA transcripts can be transmitted electronically to participating agencies that accept the examination.
  8. Complete the applicable Tennessee or local licensing process. Meet all additional application, examination, financial, business, permit, or local requirements associated with the credential needed for the work you intend to perform.

State Requirements

The Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors is the state agency responsible for contractor licenses and the Limited Licensed Electrician program. NASCLA currently lists the Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors as an agency that accepts the Journeyman Electrician examination.

Tennessee's electrical licensing structure is different from states that issue a single statewide Journeyman Electrician license covering electrical work everywhere in the state. Candidates should distinguish between the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination and the particular Tennessee credential required for the work they plan to perform.

For larger contracting projects, Tennessee contractor licensing requirements may apply. A Tennessee contractor license is generally required before bidding, offering to perform, or contracting for projects of $25,000 or more. Electrical subcontractors are also subject to contractor licensing requirements when the electrical portion of the project meets the applicable threshold.

Tennessee's full electrical contractor classification is designated CE – Electrical Contracting. The CE classification covers electrical work for buildings and structures and requires a trade examination. Tennessee contractor applicants are also required to complete the state's Business and Law examination.

The Limited Licensed Electrician, or LLE, is a separate Tennessee credential. The LLE applies in municipalities that use the Tennessee Division of Fire Prevention for permits or inspections and covers qualifying electrical work costing less than $25,000 per project. Local governments may maintain their own licensing requirements, so the applicable local authority determines what credential is required in a particular area.

For this reason, a NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination result should not be confused with a Tennessee LLE license, a Tennessee CE contractor license, or a local journeyman credential. These are separate regulatory pathways.

Tennessee also requires contractors to hold the appropriate classification before performing work that falls within state contractor licensing requirements. The classification determines the type of contracting work the license authorizes, while the contractor license also carries a monetary limit.

The Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors changed its trade examination provider in 2026. Candidates planning to use NASCLA results in Tennessee should match the examination to the specific licensing or credentialing pathway they are pursuing and complete all remaining requirements imposed by the appropriate state or local authority.

Understanding the differences among these sources can make safety-related reference navigation more efficient.

NFPA 72 supports preparation involving fire alarm and signaling systems. Candidates should become familiar with how fire alarm requirements are organized and where to locate information involving initiating devices, notification, system functions, and related electrical requirements.

Testing and troubleshooting should also receive regular study attention. Review voltage, resistance, current, continuity, circuit behavior, equipment operation, and the logical use of electrical test instruments. Journeyman-level questions may require practical reasoning in addition to code lookup.

Plans and specifications are another important part of electrical exam preparation. Practice interpreting symbols, circuits, equipment locations, and installation information shown on electrical drawings. Understanding how design information translates into field installation supports both exam preparation and practical trade knowledge.

Use the reference package actively. This routine builds familiarity with the books while reinforcing the electrical principles behind the question.

The Virginia NASCLA Journeyman Electrician Exam Book Package brings together essential references for studying National Electrical Code requirements, electrical theory, workplace safety, troubleshooting, wiring methods, equipment, calculations, fire alarm systems, and other knowledge areas associated with journeyman-level electrical work.

The Virginia Board for Contractors participates in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program and accepts the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians. This gives qualified Virginia applicants an accepted NASCLA electrical examination pathway while Virginia continues to establish and administer the education, practical experience, application, licensing, and continuing-education requirements for individual Journeyman Electricians.

This package includes the 2023 National Electrical Code, OSHA construction and general-industry regulations, NFPA 70E, Ugly's Electrical References, NFPA 72, and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications. Together, these books support preparation across many of the technical subjects found on the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination.

Because the NASCLA examination is open book, successful preparation involves more than reading. Candidates should learn how the references are organized, become familiar with commonly used NEC articles and tables, practice finding safety requirements, and know which source is most likely to contain the information needed for a particular question.

A well-organized electrical reference library can also support preparation beyond the examination itself. The NEC, OSHA regulations, electrical safety standards, theory materials, and practical field references reinforce concepts used throughout professional electrical work.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians is a standardized electrical trade examination created around the knowledge and skills used by journeyman electricians. NASCLA developed the examination through a national occupational analysis involving electrical subject matter experts from multiple jurisdictions.

The current NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination contains 100 scored questions. Candidates must answer at least 70 questions correctly to achieve the current minimum passing score. Candidates are allowed 300 minutes, or 5 hours, to complete the examination.

NASCLA also administers 10 non-scored experimental questions. These questions are used for examination development and do not count toward the candidate's final score.

The current scored examination content is distributed across the following subject areas:

  • Interpreting Plans and Specifications: 6 questions
  • Basic Electrical Safety: 8 questions
  • Electrical Theory and Principles: 10 questions
  • Testing and Troubleshooting: 7 questions
  • General Code Requirements: 15 questions
  • Wiring and Protection: 18 questions
  • Wiring Methods and Materials: 16 questions
  • Equipment for General Use: 10 questions
  • Special Occupancies and Special Equipment: 8 questions
  • Special Conditions and Communication Systems: 2 questions

Wiring and Protection represents the largest portion of the scored examination, followed by Wiring Methods and Materials and General Code Requirements. Those categories make strong National Electrical Code navigation especially important. Candidates should also devote meaningful study time to theory, troubleshooting, safety, equipment, plans, and specialty systems.

Virginia is currently listed by NASCLA as an accepting agency for both the Electrical Contractor/Master Electrician examination and the Journeyman Electrician examination. Passing a NASCLA examination can satisfy an accepted examination requirement, but the Virginia Board for Contractors remains responsible for determining whether an applicant qualifies for the Virginia Journeyman Electrician license.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Journeyman Electrician examination is an open book test. Candidates may use authorized reference materials that comply with the current examination rules.

The examination format makes reference-navigation practice a major part of preparation. Candidates should be able to identify the subject of a question, determine which reference is most likely to contain the answer, locate the appropriate section or table, and correctly apply the information.

The 2023 National Electrical Code deserves substantial study time. Practice using the NEC index, Article 100 definitions, chapter organization, individual articles, tables, notes, and cross-references. Become comfortable moving between general provisions and rules that apply to a particular wiring method, occupancy, piece of equipment, or installation condition.

Current NASCLA examination rules allow qualifying reference materials to be highlighted, underlined, and indexed. Permanent tabs may be used. Temporary tabs such as Post-it notes are not permitted. Books must otherwise remain unmarked and may not contain additional loose or attached papers.

The authorized reference materials are not supplied by the testing center, so candidates using permitted books must bring their own qualifying references. Preparing with your books in advance helps make the reference library familiar before examination day.

A useful study technique is to work practice questions with the books beside you. First determine what the question is testing. Then select the appropriate reference and locate the supporting information. This method helps develop electrical knowledge and reference-navigation skills at the same time.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination does not automatically issue a Virginia Journeyman Electrician license. Virginia licenses individual electrical tradesmen through the Board for Contractors, and applicants must satisfy the state's qualification requirements.

  1. Review the Virginia Journeyman Electrician qualification pathways. Determine which combination of practical experience, vocational education, apprenticeship training, or qualifying education applies to your background.
  2. Gather your supporting documentation. Virginia requires documentation verifying the practical experience and education used to establish eligibility.
  3. Complete the applicable Virginia application process. Submit the required information to the Virginia Board for Contractors for the Journeyman Electrician licensing pathway.
  4. Prepare for the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination. Study electrical code requirements, theory, calculations, safety, wiring methods, troubleshooting, plans, equipment, and specialty systems.
  5. Take and pass the accepted examination. Follow NASCLA and testing-provider requirements for scheduling, identification, authorized references, and examination procedures.
  6. Complete the remaining Virginia licensing requirements. Passing the examination is one component of eligibility for the individual tradesman license.
  7. Receive the applicable Virginia credential. The Board for Contractors issues the license after the applicant has met the applicable statutory and regulatory requirements.
  8. Maintain the license. Virginia Journeyman Electricians must comply with renewal and continuing-education requirements.

State Requirements

The Virginia Board for Contractors regulates individual tradesmen who work in electrical, plumbing, HVAC, gas fitting, and several other regulated trades. A Virginia Journeyman Electrician license is issued to an individual rather than a business entity.

Virginia provides multiple education-and-experience pathways for candidates seeking authorization to take the Journeyman Electrician examination. One pathway requires a qualifying bachelor's degree in an engineering curriculum related to the trade together with one year of practical experience.

Another pathway allows an applicant with an associate degree or certificate of completion from at least a two-year tradesman-related program to qualify with two years of practical experience in the trade.

Virginia also recognizes combinations of formal vocational training and practical electrical experience. These pathways include:

  • 240 hours of formal vocational training plus four years of practical experience.
  • 160 hours of formal vocational training plus five years of practical experience.
  • 80 hours of formal vocational training plus six years of practical experience.
  • 40 hours of formal vocational training plus seven years of practical experience.

Virginia's rules also provide pathways involving qualifying apprenticeship training and other recognized education or training. Applicants must furnish the documentation required to support the pathway they use.

The Virginia Board for Contractors currently requires pre-approval before a candidate sits for the state-administered tradesman examination. The Board reviews the application and qualification documentation before examination eligibility is granted.

Virginia's state tradesman examinations are currently administered by PSI. The NASCLA Accredited Examination is a separate examination program that Virginia accepts for Journeyman Electrician purposes. Candidates should make sure the examination pathway selected matches the licensing application they intend to use.

Virginia Journeyman Electricians are also subject to continuing education. Electrical tradesmen must complete an approved three-hour continuing-education course covering the applicable electrical code as part of the renewal requirements.

A Virginia individual Journeyman Electrician license should not be confused with a Virginia contractor business license. Contractors are licensed separately by the Board for Contractors, and businesses performing work that falls under contractor licensing laws must satisfy the applicable contractor-class and specialty requirements.

Reference Books

The Virginia NASCLA Journeyman Electrician Exam Book Package includes the following electrical study and reference materials:

  • NFPA 70 - National Electrical Code 2023
    The primary electrical code reference for studying branch circuits, feeders, services, conductors, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, electrical equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, and communication systems.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    A federal construction-industry safety reference covering occupational safety and health requirements applicable to construction work, including hazards and practices relevant to electrical jobsites.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1910
    A federal general-industry safety reference addressing workplace safety standards, including requirements associated with electrical hazards and electrical work environments.
  • NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    An electrical workplace safety standard addressing safe work practices and procedures designed to reduce exposure to electrical hazards.
  • Ugly's Electrical References, 2023
    A compact electrical field reference containing commonly used formulas, tables, conversions, calculations, and practical technical information for electrical work.
  • NFPA 72 - National Fire Alarm Code, 2022
    A reference for fire alarm and signaling systems covering detection, initiating devices, notification, signaling functions, and related system requirements.
  • Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications
    A technical study reference focused on electrical theory and the application of fundamental electrical principles to calculations and National Electrical Code topics.

Test Information and Study Materials

A productive Virginia NASCLA Journeyman Electrician preparation plan should be based on the examination blueprint rather than random reading. The content outline provides a practical guide for deciding where to invest study time.

Wiring and Protection accounts for 18 scored questions. Review branch circuits, feeders, services, overcurrent protection, conductor requirements, grounding, bonding, and related NEC provisions. Practice locating code requirements quickly and recognizing when multiple articles apply to the same problem.

Wiring Methods and Materials accounts for 16 scored questions. Study conductors, cables, raceways, boxes, fittings, conduit systems, installation requirements, fill calculations, and the rules associated with specific wiring methods.

General Code Requirements contains 15 scored questions. Become familiar with broadly applicable NEC requirements, including definitions, installation rules, equipment requirements, working spaces, and other provisions used throughout electrical installations.

Electrical Theory and Principles contains 10 scored questions. Review voltage, current, resistance, power, series and parallel circuits, alternating-current concepts, transformers, motors, loads, conductor relationships, and electrical calculations. Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications and Ugly's Electrical References can support this portion of preparation.

Equipment for General Use also contains 10 scored questions. Candidates should review the NEC requirements that apply to commonly used electrical equipment and understand how equipment rules connect with wiring, protection, grounding, and installation requirements.

Basic Electrical Safety accounts for 8 scored questions. OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926, OSHA 29 CFR 1910, and NFPA 70E provide resources for studying construction safety, general workplace safety, and electrical safe-work practices.

Testing and Troubleshooting contains 7 questions. Review voltage, resistance, current, continuity, equipment behavior, test instruments, and systematic troubleshooting. These questions may require practical reasoning rather than simply locating a single code rule.

Plans and specifications, special occupancies, special equipment, communication systems, and fire alarm systems should also be included in the study schedule. NFPA 72 supports preparation involving fire alarm and signaling-system topics.

The best way to become comfortable with an open-book examination is to use the references continuously. Practice identifying the subject, selecting the correct book, finding the relevant information, and applying it to the problem. Repeating this process can make reference navigation more organized and deliberate.

  3. Prepare for the examination. Study the 2023 NEC, electrical theory, OSHA requirements, NFPA safety standards, calculations, troubleshooting, wiring methods, equipment, and specialty systems.
  4. Apply for and take the NASCLA examination. Complete the applicable NASCLA examination process and schedule through PSI after approval.
  5. Pass the Journeyman Electrician examination. Initial Idaho applicants must pass the applicable examination before applying for the Journeyman Electrician license.
  6. Apply for Idaho licensure. Submit the Journeyman Electrician license application to the Idaho Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses.
  7. Provide supporting documentation. Submit work verification, apprenticeship completion records, license verification, test results, or other documentation required for the pathway being used.

State Requirements

Idaho Journeyman Electrician licensing is regulated by the Idaho Electrical Board through the Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses. Applicants must satisfy both examination and experience requirements before the Journeyman Electrician license is issued.

Idaho provides an apprenticeship-school pathway that combines completion of a Board-approved electrical apprenticeship program with 8,000 hours of supervised electrical installation work. Work verification is required as part of the licensing documentation.

Idaho also provides a work-experience pathway for applicants who do not qualify through the approved apprenticeship-school route. That pathway requires documentation of 16,000 hours of supervised electrical installation work.

Certain types of work do not count toward the Journeyman Electrician experience requirement. Idaho specifically excludes work experience in appliance repair, motor winding, and communications from the qualifying experience used to obtain a Journeyman Electrician license.

Idaho's application materials also provide reciprocal licensing pathways for qualifying electricians licensed in participating jurisdictions. Reciprocity is separate from taking the NASCLA examination and has its own license-verification and eligibility requirements.

Initial applicants must pass the applicable NASCLA examination before applying for licensure. Idaho's Journeyman Electrician application specifically asks whether the applicant has taken and passed the NASCLA examination through PSI and whether the examination was taken through Idaho. Applicants who tested outside Idaho are instructed to provide a copy of their test scores with the application.

Electrical examinations are currently offered through PSI. Idaho's Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses directs candidates to PSI for exam registration and scheduling.

Idaho's electrical licensing rules also require continuing education for journeyman and master electricians. Continuing education helps licensed electricians remain familiar with electrical-code changes and other technical developments that affect professional practice.

Journeyman electrical certification in New Mexico is administered through the Construction Industries Division of the New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department. The Division regulates construction trades and issues certificates of competence for applicable journeyman classifications.

The principal New Mexico journeyman electrical classification used for residential and commercial electrical work is EE-98J. New Mexico identifies this classification as residential and commercial electrical journeyman work.

New Mexico's journeyman certification rules require applicants to document qualifying work experience or approved training for the classification being sought. The Construction Industries Division evaluates the applicant's experience and supporting documentation as part of the certification process.

New Mexico also recognizes qualifying technical training from accredited educational institutions, approved apprenticeship programs, and other recognized training sources according to the state's certification rules. For the NASCLA pathway, New Mexico accepts the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination in lieu of the trade examination for the Journeyman Certificate. The NASCLA examination should not be confused with a national electrical license. NASCLA provides an accredited examination accepted by participating agencies. New Mexico remains responsible for issuing the actual certificate and determining whether an applicant meets its certification requirements.

New Mexico also maintains journeyman reciprocity for the EE-98J classification with qualifying electricians from participating states. The current reciprocal jurisdictions include Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming. Reciprocity has its own application and eligibility requirements and is separate from the NASCLA examination pathway.

New Mexico requires continuing education for renewal of journeyman electrician certificates. The current requirement includes at least 16 hours of continuing education during each three-year period between electrical code updates. Eight hours must consist of code-change instruction, and eight hours may consist of other approved industry-related instruction.

Journeyman certification is also different from a New Mexico contractor license. Electrical subcontractors are also subject to contractor licensing requirements when the electrical portion of a qualifying project reaches the applicable state threshold.

Tennessee also offers a separate Limited Licensed Electrician, or LLE, credential. The LLE applies to electricians performing qualifying work in municipalities that use the Tennessee Division of Fire Prevention for permits or inspections and is limited to projects costing less than $25,000.

The LLE credential is not the same as a journeyman or master electrician examination. Tennessee's own licensing materials specifically distinguish the Limited Licensed Electrician examination from journeyman and master electrician credentials.

Tennessee regulates electrical work through several licensing pathways. A NASCLA examination result by itself does not automatically authorize electrical work throughout Tennessee.

State Requirements

The Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors regulates contractors and Limited Licensed Electricians at the state level. Tennessee's electrical licensing structure differs from states that issue one statewide journeyman electrician license covering every jurisdiction.

A Tennessee contractor license is generally required before bidding, offering to perform, or contracting for construction projects of $25,000 or more. Electrical subcontractors are also subject to contractor licensing requirements when the electrical portion of a qualifying project reaches the applicable $25,000 threshold.

Tennessee's full electrical contractor classification is CE – Electrical Contracting. The full CE classification requires a trade examination and covers electrical work for buildings and structures. Tennessee's contractor licensing process also requires new contractor applicants to pass the Tennessee Business and Law examination.

Tennessee also issues the Limited Licensed Electrician, or LLE, credential. The LLE applies to electricians performing work in municipalities that use the Tennessee Division of Fire Prevention for permits or inspections and covers qualifying projects costing less than $25,000.

Local requirements remain important. Tennessee directs electricians to check with the local government where the work will be performed because a municipality may accept the state LLE license or may require its own local electrical license for permits and inspections.

The LLE license is issued to individuals who pass the applicable LLE trade examination and complete the state's application process. The LLE examination is separate from a NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination and from Tennessee's CE Electrical Contractor examination.

For contractor examinations, Tennessee changed trade examination providers in 2026. Beginning July 1, 2026, Prov began administering trade examinations for the Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors. New trade-exam scheduling beginning on that date is handled through Prov. The Tennessee Board's contractor examinations are open book.

Contractor applicants should also understand the role of the Qualifying Agent. The Qualifying Agent is the individual designated to take the applicable examination for the entity obtaining the contractor license. The person taking the Business and Law examination does not have to be the same person who takes the required trade examination.

A Tennessee contractor license is issued with both a classification and a monetary limit. The classification determines the type of work the contractor may perform, while the monetary limit controls the maximum project amount for which the contractor is authorized to contract.

An applicant with an associate degree or certificate of completion from at least a two-year tradesman-related program may qualify with two years of practical experience.
