Exam Details

The Idaho Electrical Board accepts the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians as part of its participation in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program. NASCLA's electrical examination program provides standardized trade examinations that participating licensing agencies may use as an alternative to their own trade examinations.

The NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination is intended to evaluate technical knowledge associated with journeyman-level electrical work. Preparation should cover a broad range of subjects involving electrical installations, code compliance, calculations, workplace safety, troubleshooting, equipment, wiring systems, and electrical theory.

Major study areas include:

  • Interpreting plans and specifications
  • Basic electrical safety
  • Electrical theory and principles
  • Testing and troubleshooting
  • General electrical code requirements
  • Wiring and protection
  • Wiring methods and materials
  • Equipment for general use
  • Special occupancies and special equipment
  • Special conditions and communication systems

National Electrical Code preparation should include services, feeders, branch circuits, conductors, conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, raceways, cables, boxes, fittings, motors, transformers, electrical equipment, special occupancies, and communication systems. Candidates should also understand common electrical formulas, calculations, testing procedures, and troubleshooting methods.

NASCLA examination applications are submitted through the NASCLA National Examination Database. An approved NASCLA application is currently valid for one year. Candidates must complete the applicable NASCLA examination process and separately satisfy Idaho's licensing requirements.

Passing a NASCLA examination does not create a national electrician license. The Idaho Electrical Board remains responsible for determining whether an applicant has met the qualifications required for an Idaho Journeyman Electrician license.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Journeyman Electrician examination is an open book test. Authorized reference materials may be used in accordance with the examination rules that apply to the candidate's testing appointment.

Open-book testing requires more than simply bringing reference books into the examination room. Candidates should know how the references are organized, which book is likely to contain a particular answer, and how to move efficiently between indexes, articles, tables, formulas, definitions, and technical standards.

Every rental book included in this Ultimate package is highlighted and permanently tabbed. Highlighting helps identify important material, while permanent tabs create clear navigation points throughout the references. Candidates can use these prepared books throughout their study period to become familiar with their organization before examination day.

The 2023 National Electrical Code should receive substantial attention during preparation. Practice using Article 100 definitions, the NEC index, chapters, articles, tables, exceptions, notes, and cross-references. Learn where major subjects are located so you can navigate based on the type of problem rather than relying only on memorized section numbers.

OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 supports study involving construction-industry safety, while OSHA 29 CFR 1910 covers general-industry workplace requirements. NFPA 70E supports preparation involving electrical workplace safety and safe work practices.

Ugly's Electrical References provides frequently used formulas, conversions, calculations, and practical field information. Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications supports electrical theory and the application of fundamental concepts to NEC-related problems. NFPA 72 supports preparation involving fire alarm and signaling systems.

A productive open-book routine is to work practice questions while using the references. Identify the topic, select the appropriate book, navigate to the relevant material, and then apply the rule, formula, or concept. Repeating this process strengthens both technical knowledge and book-navigation skills.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination does not automatically issue an Idaho Journeyman Electrician license. Applicants must complete the licensing process administered by the Idaho Electrical Board and Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses.

  1. Choose the applicable Idaho qualification pathway. Determine whether you qualify through the approved apprenticeship pathway or the electrical work-experience pathway.
  2. Document the required training and experience. Idaho requires evidence supporting the experience and education used for journeyman eligibility.
  3. Submit the required application materials. Complete the Idaho electrical journeyman application and provide the required supporting documentation.
  4. Complete the applicable examination requirement. Idaho accepts the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Journeyman Electricians as an examination option.
  5. Prepare for the examination. Study the 2023 NEC, electrical theory, calculations, OSHA requirements, NFPA safety standards, troubleshooting, wiring methods, equipment, and fire alarm systems.
  6. Provide required examination documentation. Follow the applicable NASCLA and Idaho procedures for reporting the examination result.
  7. Complete Idaho's licensing requirements. The Idaho Electrical Board reviews whether the applicant satisfies the applicable experience, training, examination, and documentation requirements.
  8. Receive the journeyman license. A license is issued only after the applicable Idaho requirements have been satisfied.

State Requirements

Idaho provides two primary qualification pathways for a Journeyman Electrician applicant. The first combines an approved four-year sequence of electrical instruction with supervised electrical installation experience. The second is based on a higher amount of qualifying electrical work experience.

Under the apprenticeship pathway, an applicant must successfully complete an approved four-year electrical apprenticeship program and document 8,000 hours of supervised electrical installation work.

Idaho allows an applicant who has completed the approved four-year sequence of instruction to sit for the journeyman examination before all 8,000 work hours are completed. However, the Journeyman Electrician license is not issued until the applicant provides documentation showing completion of the required 8,000 hours of supervised electrical installation work.

The alternative work-experience pathway requires 16,000 hours of qualifying electrical experience. Applicants using this pathway must provide work verification supporting the required experience.

Idaho specifically excludes certain types of work from the journeyman experience requirement. Experience involving appliance repair, motor winding, or communications does not count toward the experience required to take the journeyman examination or obtain a Journeyman Electrician license.

Idaho also limits how much experience obtained while working as a limited electrical installer or trainee can be applied toward journeyman licensure. No more than 2,000 hours of qualifying limited electrical installer or trainee experience may be applied toward the journeyman experience requirement.

Applicants should maintain complete records of apprenticeship registration, supervised electrical installation work, training, and employer verification. Accurate documentation is an important part of demonstrating eligibility to the Idaho Electrical Board.

The Idaho Journeyman Electrician license is an individual electrical license. Holding or passing the NASCLA examination does not eliminate the requirement to satisfy Idaho's licensing standards. Applicants must meet the Board's applicable experience, education, examination, application, and documentation requirements.

Review voltage, current, resistance, power, series and parallel circuits, alternating-current principles, transformers, motors, loads, and common calculations. Testing and troubleshooting should also receive regular attention. Review voltage, current, resistance, continuity, test instruments, circuit operation, equipment behavior, and systematic fault diagnosis. Journeyman-level preparation involves knowing how systems operate as well as understanding applicable code requirements.

NFPA 72 provides focused support for fire alarm and signaling-system study. Ugly's Electrical References and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications can be used for calculations, formulas, theory concepts, and practical electrical problem solving.

The Nebraska State Electrical Division administers examinations for Journeyman Electricians and participates in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program. Nebraska requires the applicable NASCLA examination date to be after August 1, 2025 for acceptance. Candidates should complete Nebraska's eligibility process before scheduling their examination.

  • National Electrical Code - 2023
  • Basic Electricity and Electrical Theory
  • Nebraska State Electrical Act
  • Emergency Circuits, including Fire Alarm Circuits

Passing the examination does not automatically create a Nebraska Journeyman Electrician license. The Nebraska State Electrical Board remains responsible for determining whether the applicant satisfies the experience, education, application, examination, and other requirements for licensure.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination is only one part of obtaining a Nebraska Journeyman Electrician license. Applicants must complete the licensing process through the Nebraska State Electrical Division.

  1. Review Nebraska's journeyman qualifications. Determine whether your electrical work experience and any qualifying electrical education satisfy the State Electrical Board's requirements.
  2. Document qualifying experience. Nebraska generally requires four years, or 8,000 hours, of verifiable electrical trade experience acceptable to the Board.
  3. Submit the Nebraska examination application. Complete the required application and provide the supporting documentation requested by the State Electrical Division.
  4. Receive approval to test. Nebraska reviews the application before sending examination eligibility to PSI.
  5. Prepare for the examination. Study the 2023 NEC, basic electricity and theory, the Nebraska State Electrical Act, emergency circuits, fire alarm circuits, safety, troubleshooting, wiring methods, and equipment.
  6. Schedule through PSI. Approved candidates receive scheduling information after Nebraska submits their eligibility.
  7. Take the NASCLA examination through Nebraska. For Nebraska acceptance, the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination must be taken through the Nebraska State Electrical Division and must meet the applicable examination-date requirement.
  8. Complete the licensing process. Submit any remaining documentation and licensing requirements after successful examination completion.
  9. Maintain the license. Follow Nebraska's applicable renewal and continuing-education requirements after licensure.

State Requirements

The Nebraska State Electrical Division administers statewide electrical licensing. A Nebraska Journeyman Electrician may install electrical wiring, apparatus, and equipment and may supervise apprentice electricians within the scope authorized by the state license.

An applicant for a Nebraska Journeyman Electrician license must generally have at least four years, or 8,000 hours, of verifiable experience acceptable to the Board in the electrical trade. Registration as an apprentice electrician during those years may constitute evidence of the required experience when approved by the Board.

Nebraska provides an education-based experience credit. Successful completion of an approved two-year post-high-school electrical course resulting in an Associate's degree in Electrical Technology may provide one year of work-experience credit. This can allow an applicant to qualify with three years of acceptable verifiable experience together with the qualifying degree.

Qualified electrical experience gained during military service may also receive work-experience credit when accepted by the Nebraska State Electrical Board.

Nebraska also distinguishes between unrestricted and restricted Journeyman Electrician licenses based on in-state experience. If an applicant has fewer than 4,000 hours of verifiable electrical experience in Nebraska, the resulting journeyman license is restricted and cannot be used for reciprocity with another state.

The Nebraska State Electrical Board maintains reciprocal Journeyman Electrician agreements with Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Idaho, Minnesota, Montana, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming. Reciprocity has its own requirements and should be treated separately from the NASCLA examination pathway.

Nebraska currently lists a $90 application fee for the Journeyman Electrician license. License purchase fees depend on the year in which the license is issued. These government licensing charges are separate from the price of this Ultimate Exam Prep Rental Package.

Nebraska also requires electrical license and apprenticeship applicants to complete the applicable lawful-presence attestation associated with the state's licensing process.

The available electrical examinations include the NASCLA Electrical Contractor examination for Master Electrician or Unlimited Electrician candidates and the NASCLA Journey-level Electrician examination for journeyman candidates.

The current Vanderburgh County NASCLA Journey-level Electrician examination contains 110 questions and allows 5 hours for completion. The 110 questions include 100 scored questions and 10 experimental items. Journey-level examinations are currently graded against a 70% passing score.

The current examination content is distributed among the following subject areas:

  • Interpreting Plans & Specifications: 6 questions
  • Basic Electrical Safety: 8 questions
  • Electrical Theory and Principles: 10 questions
  • Testing and Troubleshooting: 7 questions
  • General Code Requirements: 15 questions
  • Wiring and Protection: 18 questions
  • Selects and Installs Cabinets, Boxes, Fittings, Conduit: 16 questions
  • Equipment for General Use: 10 questions
  • Special Occupancies and Special Equipment: 8 questions
  • Special Conditions and Communication Systems: 2 questions
  • Experimental Items: 10 questions

Wiring and Protection is the largest scored category, followed by cabinets, boxes, fittings and conduit, and General Code Requirements. Candidates should also dedicate meaningful preparation time to electrical theory, equipment, safety, troubleshooting, plans, specifications, and special electrical systems.

The current Prov examination fee is $125 per examination attempt. This testing fee is separate from the price of the Ultimate Exam Prep Rental Package.

Vanderburgh County does not currently accept NASCLA transcripts from examinations completed in another participating jurisdiction. Candidates must take the examination in Evansville for this local licensing pathway.

Open Book Test

The Vanderburgh County NASCLA Journey-level Electrician examination is an open book test. Candidates may use authorized reference materials listed for the examination, provided the books comply with current Prov reference-material rules.

Prov permits approved reference books to contain highlighting, underlining in pen, and permanent tabs. Handwritten notes are not permitted. Moveable tabs and Post-it notes are prohibited, and candidates cannot add photocopied documents to reference books. Reference materials are checked before candidates enter the testing room.

All seven rental books included in this Ultimate package are highlighted and permanently tabbed. This preparation helps candidates organize their study and become familiar with navigation points throughout the references before exam day.

The 2023 National Electrical Code is a central reference for the examination. Candidates should practice using Article 100 definitions, the NEC index, chapter organization, individual articles, tables, exceptions, and cross-references. Efficient navigation can be particularly valuable in categories such as Wiring and Protection, General Code Requirements, wiring methods, equipment, and special occupancies.

OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 supports construction-safety preparation, while OSHA 29 CFR 1910 covers general-industry workplace requirements. NFPA 70E supports preparation involving electrical workplace safety and safe work practices.

Ugly's Electrical References and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications support calculations, formulas, electrical theory, and practical problem solving. NFPA 72 provides reference material for fire alarm and signaling-system topics.

A useful preparation routine is to work a practice-oriented question, identify its subject, select the correct reference, use the permanent tabs to reach the relevant area, locate the supporting rule or formula, and then solve the problem. Repeating this process helps combine technical learning with open-book navigation practice.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Journey-level Electrician examination does not automatically issue a Vanderburgh County journeyman electrician license. Candidates must complete the local licensing process and satisfy the requirements established for the trade.

  1. Review the journeyman qualification requirements. Vanderburgh County requires a journeyman applicant to establish at least four years of practical experience in the applicable trade.
  2. Prepare the local application. Complete the application materials required by the Evansville-Vanderburgh County licensing authority.
  3. Provide the required recommendations. Local application requirements include three letters of recommendation from qualifying business or professional references who are not related to the applicant by blood or marriage.
  4. Document practical electrical experience. Provide information supporting the required four years of trade experience.
  5. Receive examination eligibility. Complete the local approval process before scheduling the licensing examination.
  6. Schedule the NASCLA Journey-level Electrician examination through Prov. Candidates must take the examination in Evansville because Vanderburgh County does not currently accept NASCLA transcripts from outside examinations.
  7. Prepare with the course and rental references. Study the NEC, safety requirements, theory, calculations, troubleshooting, wiring methods, equipment, plans, and specialty systems.
  8. Take and pass the examination. The current journey-level passing standard is 70%.
  9. Complete the remaining licensing requirements. Follow the local process for issuance of the journeyman license after satisfying the examination and application requirements.

State Requirements

Electrical journeyman licensing in Vanderburgh County is a local licensing process. Indiana does not use one single statewide journeyman electrician license that replaces all municipal or county electrical licensing requirements. The local rules governing work in Vanderburgh County and Evansville therefore play a central role for electricians working in this jurisdiction.

Under the Vanderburgh County licensing ordinance, a person cannot be issued a journeyman license unless the applicant establishes at least four years of practical experience in the applicable trade.

The local ordinance also establishes supervision requirements. An apprentice may not install regulated work except under the supervision of a licensed journeyman or master employed on the same job. These provisions help distinguish apprentice-level work from the responsibilities associated with journeyman licensing.

The Vanderburgh County application requirements include information identifying the license being sought, the applicant's identifying and business information where applicable, proof of applicable fees, and three letters of recommendation. The recommendation letters must come from reputable business or professional individuals who are not related to the applicant by blood or marriage and must address the applicant's honesty, integrity, and good character.

Electrical applicants are examined through the local licensing process, and the applicable board determines eligibility. For the current NASCLA Journey-level Electrician pathway, Prov administers the examination.

After a candidate completes the examination, Prov scores the test and reports the result. The current journey-level cut score is 70%. If a candidate does not pass, the candidate must return to the Board for a new eligibility before retesting.

Each examination eligibility is valid for one examination attempt. The current process permits the examination to be administered up to three times per year, with a new eligibility required for each attempt.

NASCLA specifically identifies Vanderburgh County as a participating electrical examination agency but states that the jurisdiction does not currently accept transcripts. Candidates seeking the Vanderburgh County credential must therefore take the examination in Evansville instead of relying on a passing NASCLA result obtained elsewhere.

The current Vanderburgh County ordinance lists a new Journeyman license fee of $35 and a renewal fee of $25. These local licensing fees are separate from the Prov examination fee and separate from the price of this 1 Exam Prep package.

State Requirements

The Virginia Board for Contractors regulates individual tradesman licenses, including Journeyman and Master Electricians. Virginia provides several different combinations of practical experience and formal education or vocational training that can qualify an applicant for a Journeyman Electrician license.

An applicant with a bachelor's degree or certificate of completion from an accredited college or university in an engineering curriculum related to the electrical trade may qualify with one year of practical experience in the trade.

An applicant with an associate degree or certificate of completion from at least a two-year tradesman-related program at an accredited community college or technical school may qualify with two years of practical experience.

Virginia also recognizes several combinations of formal vocational training and practical electrical experience:

  • 240 hours of formal vocational training plus four years of practical experience.
  • 160 hours of formal vocational training plus five years of practical experience.
  • 80 hours of formal vocational training plus six years of practical experience.
  • 40 hours of formal vocational training plus seven or more years of practical experience.

Applicants using one of these pathways must provide the supporting experience verification and training or education documentation required by the Board.

Virginia also provides additional routes to eligibility through recognized apprenticeship and other qualifying education or experience established in the Board's regulations. Applicants should select the pathway that accurately reflects their training and practical electrical background.

Virginia's individual Journeyman Electrician license is different from a Virginia contractor business license. The tradesman license identifies the individual's qualification in the electrical trade. Businesses contracting for regulated construction work must separately comply with Virginia's contractor licensing requirements when those requirements apply.

Virginia electrician licenses are currently issued on a three-year license cycle. As a condition of renewal, Journeyman and Master Electricians must complete an approved three-hour electrical continuing-education course. The continuing-education requirement must be completed before the license expires.

The required continuing education must be provided by a Board-approved provider and relate to the applicable electrical code changes. Electricians holding both Journeyman and Master designations in the same electrical trade need only complete the applicable electrical continuing-education requirement for that trade during the renewal period.

Practice recognizing the subject first, determining where it is addressed, locating the supporting material, and then applying it to the problem.

Licensing Steps

Florida's acceptance of the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination applies to an endorsement pathway rather than serving as the standard examination route for every new Florida applicant.

  1. Confirm that the Florida endorsement pathway applies to you. Applicants using the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination for Florida must hold a license from another jurisdiction that is similar in scope to the Florida classification being requested.
  2. Review Florida certification qualifications. Florida requires applicants for electrical contractor certification to satisfy statutory experience, character, and licensing requirements.
  3. Apply for the NASCLA examination. Submit the NASCLA examination application through the National Examination Database and complete the applicable application requirements.
  4. Prepare for the Residential Electrical Contractor examination. Study the National Electrical Code, residential code provisions, OSHA safety, electrical workplace safety, theory, calculations, fire alarm systems, product safety markings, and business and project management subjects.
  5. Take and pass the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination. Follow all current examination rules concerning approved reference materials and testing procedures.
  6. Request the appropriate NASCLA examination documentation. NASCLA provides electronic transcript services for participating licensing agencies.
  7. Complete the Florida endorsement application. Submit the application and documentation required by the Florida Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.
  8. Document your out-of-state license. The license must be from another jurisdiction and similar in scope to the Florida certification being pursued.
  9. Complete Florida's remaining certification requirements. The Board determines whether all applicable statutory and regulatory requirements have been satisfied before issuing certification.

State Requirements

Florida electrical contractor certification is regulated by the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board within the Department of Business and Professional Regulation. Florida law provides both examination and endorsement pathways for electrical and specialty electrical contractor certification.

A person must be at least 18 years old to take the Florida electrical contractor certification examination. An applicant seeking certification must also satisfy Florida's good-moral-character requirement and meet one of the experience or education pathways established under Florida law.

One pathway requires at least three years of proven management experience in the trade during the six years immediately preceding the application. Education may substitute for part of this requirement, but no more than one-half of the required experience may be satisfied through educational equivalency.

Another pathway allows qualification based on at least four years of experience as a supervisor or contractor in the trade during the eight years immediately preceding the application. Florida also recognizes qualifying supervisory electrical or alarm-system experience obtained through the United States Armed Forces.

Florida also provides a pathway based on at least six years of comprehensive training, technical education, or supervisory experience associated with an electrical or alarm-system contracting business during the 12 years immediately preceding the application. Qualifying technical electrical experience, education, or training obtained through the United States Armed Forces or a governmental entity may also be considered under this pathway.

A qualifying professional engineer may use another statutory pathway when the individual has been licensed for at least three years and is qualified by education, training, or experience to practice electrical engineering. Florida also permits certain combinations of qualifying experience, education, and training.

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor specialty scope includes the installation, repair, alteration, addition to, replacement of, or design of electrical wiring, fixtures, appliances, apparatus, raceways, conduit, or related electrical components in one-, two-, three-, or four-family residences not exceeding two stories in height, together with accessory-use structures associated with those residences. The electrical service within this specialty scope is limited to single-phase, 400-ampere single service.

For NASCLA specifically, Florida currently accepts the Residential Electrical Contractor examination for endorsement. NASCLA states that the applicant must hold a license from another jurisdiction that is similar in scope to the Florida classification being requested.

An applicant who has never previously held a license cannot use the NASCLA examination as a substitute for Florida's initial examination pathway. For an initial applicant with no prior qualifying license, Florida requires the applicable Florida examination.

Reference Books

The following references support preparation for the Florida NASCLA Residential Electrician - Online Exam Prep:

  • National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023
    The primary electrical code reference for residential wiring, services, feeders, branch circuits, grounding and bonding, conductor requirements, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, equipment, and special electrical installations.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    A construction-industry safety reference covering occupational safety and health requirements applicable to construction jobsites, electrical work, tools, equipment, and workplace hazards.
  • NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, 14th
    A contractor-focused reference addressing business organization, project management, contracts, estimating, financial management, employment considerations, safety, and other business topics relevant to professional contracting.
  • NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    An electrical safety reference focused on workplace practices and procedures designed to reduce exposure to electrical hazards.
  • Ugly's Electrical References
    A compact electrical field reference containing commonly used formulas, tables, calculations, conversions, and practical electrical information useful for theory and problem-solving review.
  • NFPA 72 - National Fire Alarm Code, 2022
    A reference for fire alarm and signaling systems, including initiating devices, notification appliances, detection, signaling functions, and related installation requirements.
  • Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications
    A study reference focused on strengthening fundamental electrical theory and connecting concepts such as voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, and calculations with practical NEC applications.
  • ANSI Z535.4-2023, Product Safety Signs and Labels
    A safety standard addressing the design, application, and use of product safety signs and labels intended to communicate hazards and safety information.
  • International Residential Code (IRC), 2024
    A residential construction code reference addressing requirements for one- and two-family dwellings and townhouses, supporting study of residential construction conditions that interact with electrical installations.

Test Information and Study Materials

Residential electrical exam preparation is most effective when candidates combine code study, electrical theory, calculations, safety, and repeated reference navigation. The goal is to understand both why an electrical requirement applies and where to find the supporting rule.

Begin with the 2023 National Electrical Code. Concentrate on dwelling-unit branch circuits, required receptacle and lighting outlets, services, feeders, conductor sizing, load calculations, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, boxes, raceways, equipment, appliances, motors, and special systems.

Electrical theory should be studied alongside NEC requirements. Review Ohm's law, power formulas, series and parallel circuits, conductor relationships, voltage drop concepts, alternating-current fundamentals, and practical calculations. Understanding theory helps candidates recognize what a calculation question is asking before selecting a formula.

The International Residential Code adds broader residential construction context. Candidates should understand how electrical installations interact with residential building conditions and how code requirements affect work in houses, townhouses, and related structures.

Safety preparation should include construction-jobsite requirements from OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 and electrical safe-work practices from NFPA 70E. ANSI Z535.4 provides additional preparation involving product safety signs and hazard communication.

NFPA 72 supports review of residential fire alarm and signaling concepts. Ugly's Electrical References can reinforce frequently used formulas and field calculations, while Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications can help connect electrical principles directly to code-based problem solving.

Business and project management should not be neglected. The NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management supports study of contractor operations, estimating, contracts, project administration, safety management, financial topics, and other business responsibilities.

A strong preparation routine combines topic review with practice-oriented questions. After answering a question, locate the supporting information in the applicable reference even when the answer seems familiar. This reinforces technical understanding and improves open-book navigation.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination does not automatically issue a North Carolina electrical contractor license. Candidates must complete the licensing process through the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors.

  1. Identify the SP-SFD classification. North Carolina accepts the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination for the Special Restricted Single-Family Residential Dwelling license.
  2. Review the experience requirements. Applicants must satisfy the Board's qualifying experience requirements for the SP-SFD classification.
  3. Prepare the license application. Applicants must submit the required application and supporting documentation to the Board.
  4. Provide character documentation. Examination applicants must submit written statements from at least two people attesting to the applicant's good character.
  5. Complete the NASCLA examination process. Apply for and pass the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination.
  6. Send the NASCLA transcript to North Carolina. Applicants using the NASCLA pathway must have the examination transcript transmitted to the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors.
  7. Document qualifying electrical experience. Provide the experience information needed to establish eligibility for the SP-SFD classification.
  8. Complete the Board's licensing review. The Board determines whether the applicant satisfies all licensing requirements before issuing the SP-SFD credential.

State Requirements

Electrical contractor licensing in North Carolina is regulated by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. The Board issues several electrical contractor classifications, including Limited, Intermediate, Unlimited, and special restricted classifications.

For the SP-SFD Single-Family Detached Residential Dwelling classification, current Board rules require at least 3,000 hours of qualifying electrical experience. At least 2,000 hours must be primary experience, while the remaining qualifying hours may be primary experience, secondary experience, or a combination of both.

North Carolina defines primary experience as work directly involving the installation of electrical wiring and equipment governed by the National Electrical Code or activities directly related to that work. Qualifying primary experience can include work as a journeyman electrician, electrical mechanic, electrical foreman, electrical superintendent, electrical estimator for a licensed contractor, and other qualifying electrical roles recognized by the Board.

Applicants for an electrical contracting examination must also be at least 18 years of age, submit the required application, and provide written statements from at least two people attesting to good character.

The SP-SFD classification authorizes the licensee to install, maintain, or repair electrical wiring and devices that are in or on a single-family residential dwelling or ancillary to that dwelling.

For purposes of the SP-SFD classification, North Carolina defines a single-family residential dwelling as a building or manufactured home designed and used for habitation by one family and not physically attached to another building or structure. Qualifying cabanas, porches, room additions, and ancillary structures can be treated as part of the single-family dwelling when they are designed and used for residential purposes.

Ancillary structures associated with the dwelling can include detached residential garages or carports, household or farm equipment storage buildings, barns, pump houses, electric fences, and yard lighting when the work falls within the authorized residential scope.

The SP-SFD classification is more limited than North Carolina's broader Limited, Intermediate, and Unlimited electrical contractor licenses. Candidates pursuing the residential classification should understand the specific scope of work authorized by the SP-SFD credential before contracting for electrical projects.

Florida currently accepts the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination for endorsement toward the Florida Certified Specialty Electrical Contractor classification. NASCLA acceptance serves as a trade-examination waiver pathway for an eligible endorsement applicant. It does not automatically issue a Florida license.

NASCLA examination applications are submitted through the NASCLA National Examination Database. The current application fee is $65. Approved applications are valid for one year from the approval date, and candidates currently receive up to three examination attempts during that eligibility period.

NASCLA examination applications are generally processed within seven business days. Once approved, candidates receive scheduling information from the testing provider. The examination may be scheduled at a PSI location offering the applicable NASCLA test.

Open Book Test

Open-book testing makes familiarity with the reference library an important part of preparation. Candidates should learn how to identify the subject of a question, determine which book contains the relevant information, locate the applicable provision, table, formula, definition, or standard, and apply that information correctly.

The National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023 is a central reference. Candidates should practice navigating Article 100 definitions, the index, chapter organization, articles, tables, exceptions, notes, and cross-references. Residential preparation should include services, feeders, branch circuits, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, equipment, appliances, motors, and special systems.

Electrical theory should be reviewed alongside NEC navigation. Understanding the electrical principle involved in a question can make it easier to determine which code provision or formula applies.

OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 supports construction-industry safety preparation, while NFPA 70E addresses electrical workplace safety. NFPA 72 supports study involving fire alarm and signaling systems. The International Residential Code provides broader residential construction context.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination does not automatically issue a Florida Residential Electrical Contractor certification. Florida uses the accepted NASCLA examination as part of an endorsement pathway administered through the Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board.

  4. Apply for the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination. Submit the NASCLA examination application through the National Examination Database.

The Florida Electrical Contractors' Licensing Board regulates certified and registered electrical contractors and specialty electrical contractors. Residential electrical contracting is one of the specialty classifications recognized by Florida.

The Florida Residential Electrical Contractor specialty authorizes qualifying electrical work involving wiring, fixtures, appliances, apparatus, raceways, conduit, and related electrical components in one-, two-, three-, or four-family residences not exceeding two stories in height. A registered contractor works based on local competency requirements and is limited to the jurisdictions for which the registration is issued.

The Residential Electrical Contractor classification is a specialty electrical credential. It does not provide the same scope as Florida's unlimited Certified Electrical Contractor classification, which covers broader electrical and alarm work.

Electrical licensing in Nebraska is regulated by the Nebraska State Electrical Division. Nebraska licenses several categories of electrical professionals, including Electrical Contractors, Journeyman Electricians, Residential Journeyman Electricians, Special Installers, Fire Alarm Installers, and Apprentice Electricians.

The residential journeyman license is identified as Type RW. A Residential Journeyman Electrician is licensed to wire for or install electrical wiring, apparatus, and equipment for residential installations and to supervise apprentice electricians within the authorized residential scope.

Nebraska currently requires a Type RW applicant to have at least three years of verifiable experience acceptable to the Board in the electrical trade. Registration as an apprentice electrician during those years may serve as evidence of experience when approved by the Board.

Nebraska also provides an education-based qualification pathway. A candidate may qualify with two years of verifiable experience plus successful completion of a post-high-school electrical wiring program resulting in a Degree in Electrical Technology. Nebraska Board rules allow one year of experience credit for successful completion of an approved two-year post-high-school electrical course.

The Type RW credential is valid only for residential installations. Nebraska defines a residential installation as an installation intended for a single-family or two-family residential dwelling or a multifamily residential dwelling not larger than three stories in height.

Examination applicants are instructed to submit the required attestation so that license issuance is not delayed after a successful examination result.

Work-experience verification must be properly documented. Nebraska requires complete employer information, and verification letters from employers must be provided on company letterhead when required as part of the application process.

Electrical contractor licensing in North Carolina is regulated by the North Carolina State Board of Examiners of Electrical Contractors. Primary experience generally involves direct work installing electrical wiring and equipment governed by the National Electrical Code or work directly related to those installations.

Secondary experience can include electrical work or training related to electrical installations that does not receive the same level of credit as primary experience. Examples can include apprentice electrician experience, approved apprenticeship training, qualifying electrical education, electrical construction design, and certain other related activities.

A key New Mexico requirement applies to NASCLA candidates: the applicant must provide a letter of good standing from another state licensing agency confirming at least one year of licensure. This requirement applies in addition to the passing NASCLA examination result.

The EE-98 Residential and Commercial Electrical Wiring contractor classification requires four years of experience. Its scope covers electrical wiring operating at 5,000 volts nominal or less and includes residential electrical wiring within the ER-1 classification along with specified electrical specialty work.

New Mexico also maintains the ER-1 Residential Electrical Wiring classification. ER-1 requires two years of experience and covers qualifying one- and two-family dwelling units and certain qualifying multifamily residential installations. It does not authorize wiring for commercial uses such as hotels or motels.

The contractor classification being sought determines the applicant's authorized scope. An EE-98 contractor has a broader residential and commercial electrical scope, while ER-1 is limited to residential electrical wiring within the boundaries established by New Mexico rules.

New Mexico contractor licenses and journeyman certificates are separate credentials. A contractor license authorizes the licensed business to contract within an approved classification, while journeyman certification establishes an individual's trade qualification for work performed under the applicable licensing structure.

New Mexico also has a reciprocal journeyman pathway for EE-98J Residential and Commercial Electrical. The state currently identifies EE-98J as the only reciprocated journeyman classification and requires 8,000 hours of experience. Reciprocity is currently recognized from Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Dakota, Texas, and Wyoming.

Reciprocity is separate from the NASCLA pathway. A candidate using reciprocity follows the reciprocal journeyman process, while a candidate relying on NASCLA must satisfy the NASCLA acceptance requirements and all applicable New Mexico application rules.

Open-book testing makes reference navigation an important part of preparation. Candidates should know how to identify a question's subject, determine which reference contains the relevant material, locate the applicable code section, definition, table, formula, or safety requirement, and apply that information correctly.

All rental books included in this Ultimate package are highlighted and permanently tabbed. Highlighting can help draw attention to important material during review, while permanent tabs provide visible navigation points throughout larger codes, standards, manuals, and reference books.

The National Electrical Code, NEC, 2023 should receive substantial study attention. Candidates should practice using Article 100 definitions, the NEC index, chapter organization, individual articles, tables, exceptions, and cross-references. Residential study should include services, feeders, branch circuits, load calculations, conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, equipment, appliances, motors, and other residential electrical systems.

Electrical theory should be reviewed alongside NEC navigation. Important areas include voltage, current, resistance, power, Ohm's law, series and parallel circuits, alternating-current principles, motors, transformers, and practical electrical calculations. Understanding the electrical principle behind a problem can help candidates determine which formula or code provision applies.

OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926 supports construction-industry safety preparation, while NFPA 70E addresses electrical workplace safety. NFPA 72 supports fire alarm and signaling-system preparation. The International Residential Code provides broader residential construction context, and ANSI Z535.4-2023 addresses product safety signs and labels.

The NASCLA Contractors Guide and NASCLA South Carolina Residential Builders, 8th Edition support business-focused preparation. South Carolina candidates should devote dedicated study time to business management and law because that examination requirement remains applicable when the NASCLA residential trade examination is used for the technical waiver.

Licensing Steps

Passing the NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractor examination does not automatically issue a South Carolina Residential Electrician license. Applicants must complete the licensing process through the South Carolina Residential Builders Commission.

  1. Confirm the Residential Electrician classification. Make sure the South Carolina Residential Electrician license matches the work you intend to perform.
  2. Complete the Residential Electrician application. Submit the required application, documentation, and applicable fees to the South Carolina Residential Builders Commission.
  3. Document qualifying work experience. Work experience must be verified and approved by the Commission before examination eligibility or waiver processing is completed.
  4. Use the NASCLA technical-exam waiver when eligible. The NASCLA Residential Electrical Contractors examination must have been passed within the previous three years.
  5. Provide the NASCLA examination transcript. Include a copy of the applicable exam transcript with the South Carolina application.
  6. Prepare for Business Management and Law. The South Carolina Business Management and Law examination remains applicable even when the technical examination is waived.
  7. Use the Ultimate preparation materials. Study with the highlighted and permanently tabbed rental books and the included 1 year of course access.

South Carolina currently requires a license for residential electrical work exceeding $500. Commercial electrical work exceeding the applicable commercial licensing threshold is handled separately through the South Carolina Contractors' Licensing Board.

Applicants seeking licensure through the NASCLA exam-waiver pathway must first submit the appropriate application and required documentation to the Residential Builders Commission. The Commission reviews the application and determines whether the applicant qualifies for the waiver.

Nebraska participates in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program and administers the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination through the Nebraska State Electrical Division. NASCLA defines a Journeyman Electrician as an individual who has demonstrated competency in the knowledge and skills needed to properly perform the installation, maintenance, and repair of electrical work in accordance with applicable standards and codes.

The Nebraska NASCLA Journeyman Electrician - Online Exam Prep course is structured to help candidates organize their preparation around the technical subjects and reference materials associated with journeyman electrical work. Nebraska currently bases electrical examinations on the 2023 National Electrical Code, making familiarity with the current NEC especially important for candidates preparing for licensure.

The reference set includes NFPA 70 - National Electrical Code 2023, Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA), Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1910, NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024, Ugly's Electrical References, 2023, NFPA 72 - National Fire Alarm Code, 2022, and Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications.

Journeyman electrician preparation should go beyond memorizing individual NEC rules. Candidates should understand how electrical systems function, how to apply code requirements to installations, how to perform common electrical calculations, how to identify safety hazards, and how to navigate technical references efficiently during an open-book exam.

The online course is designed to support a structured study routine that combines electrical theory, code application, calculation practice, safety review, and reference navigation. Candidates can use the course to reinforce field knowledge while developing stronger familiarity with the books and standards associated with the examination.

Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program includes a dedicated examination for Journeyman Electricians. Nebraska is a participating administering jurisdiction, and the exam must be taken through the Nebraska State Electrical Division for Nebraska administration.

Nebraska's electrical examination program covers subjects including the 2023 National Electrical Code, basic electricity and theory, the Nebraska State Electrical Act, blueprint reading, emergency circuits, and fire alarm circuits.

Nebraska State Electrical Board rules provide that state electrical examinations contain a minimum of 50 questions and require a minimum passing grade of 75%. Candidates approved for testing receive scheduling information through the state's current testing process.

The Nebraska State Electrical Division transitioned journeyman electrician examinations to PSI. After the State Electrical Division approves a candidate to test, eligibility is submitted to PSI and the candidate receives scheduling information and access to the applicable candidate bulletin.

The NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination is intended to evaluate broad electrical competency rather than residential work alone. Preparation should therefore include code requirements and electrical practices applicable to a wider range of journeyman-level installations, maintenance, troubleshooting, safety, and repair.

Open Book Test

The NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination is an open book test. NASCLA identifies its Journeyman Electrician examination as one of the open-book examinations within the Accredited Electrical Examination Program.

Open-book testing makes familiarity with the references essential. Candidates should know how to locate information through the NEC index, article structure, tables, definitions, exceptions, informational notes, and cross-references rather than attempting to read the code from beginning to end during the exam.

The 2023 National Electrical Code should be at the center of exam preparation. Candidates should develop familiarity with branch circuits, feeders, services, conductor sizing, ampacity, overcurrent protection, grounding and bonding, wiring methods, motors, equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, and other commonly tested NEC subjects.

Safety-related questions may require knowledge from 29 CFR Part 1926, 29 CFR 1910, and NFPA 70E. Candidates should understand both construction-related safety and electrical workplace safety, including shock hazards, arc-flash hazards, personal protective equipment, safe work practices, and energized electrical work considerations.

Fire alarm and emergency-circuit preparation may involve NFPA 72 together with applicable NEC requirements. Electrical theory questions may require direct application of formulas and principles rather than simple reference lookup.

A practical strategy is to classify each question first. Determine whether it involves NEC code application, theory, safety, fire alarm systems, grounding and bonding, motors, conductors, overcurrent protection, calculations, or another topic. Then move directly to the reference most likely to contain the answer.

Licensing Steps

Journeyman electrician licensing in Nebraska is administered by the Nebraska State Electrical Division. Candidates must satisfy the state's experience, application, examination, and licensing requirements.

  1. Obtain qualifying electrical experience. Nebraska requires journeyman electrician applicants to document qualifying experience acceptable to the State Electrical Board.
  2. Maintain appropriate apprentice registration. Apprentices working toward licensure should comply with Nebraska's registration and supervision requirements.
  3. Complete the Nebraska electrical license application. Applicants submit the required application and supporting employment information to the Nebraska State Electrical Division.
  4. Document experience. Current and previous employers must be properly identified, and Nebraska requires complete employment verification information.
  5. Receive examination approval. The State Electrical Division reviews the application before submitting examination eligibility.
  6. Prepare for the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician exam. Study NEC requirements, electrical theory, safety, fire alarm systems, emergency circuits, tools, calculations, and other journeyman-level subjects.
  7. Practice open-book reference navigation. Work regularly with the NEC and supporting references so that important articles, tables, formulas, and safety standards become easier to locate.
  8. Schedule the examination through the approved testing process. Once approved, candidates receive scheduling instructions through PSI.
  9. Pass the required examination. Candidates must earn the passing score required by the applicable Nebraska examination rules.
  10. Complete the licensing process. After successful examination, candidates must satisfy the remaining Nebraska State Electrical Division requirements before the license is issued.

State Requirements

Nebraska requires an applicant for a Journeyman Electrician license to have at least four years of verifiable electrical trade experience, equivalent to 8,000 hours, acceptable to the Nebraska State Electrical Board.

Nebraska recognizes registered apprenticeship experience as evidence of qualifying experience when approved by the Board. The state may also grant one year of work-experience credit for completion of a qualifying two-year post-high-school electrical program resulting in an Associate's degree in electrical technology.

Qualified electrical experience gained through military service may also be considered for work-experience credit under Nebraska's licensing requirements.

If a journeyman applicant has fewer than 4,000 hours of verifiable experience in Nebraska, the resulting Nebraska license may be restricted and may not qualify for reciprocity with another state.

Nebraska currently uses the 2023 National Electrical Code. The state adopted the 2023 NEC for covered installations and switched electrical examinations to the 2023 code beginning August 1, 2024.

Nebraska participates in the NASCLA Accredited Electrical Examination Program for the Journeyman Electrician examination. For Nebraska recognition, the examination must be taken through the Nebraska State Electrical Division, and NASCLA identifies exams taken after August 1, 2025 as accepted under the participating-state arrangement.

Passing the NASCLA Journeyman Electrician examination does not by itself issue a Nebraska electrical license. Applicants must still meet Nebraska's experience, application, lawful-presence attestation, licensing, and other applicable State Electrical Division requirements.

Nebraska also maintains reciprocal licensing agreements for the Journeyman Electrician license with several states, subject to the state's reciprocity requirements and the applicant's licensing history.

Reference Books

  • NFPA 70 - National Electrical Code 2023
    The primary electrical code reference for journeyman exam preparation. Review branch circuits, feeders, services, conductor ampacity, grounding and bonding, overcurrent protection, wiring methods, motors, equipment, special occupancies, special equipment, and other NEC requirements.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR Part 1926 (OSHA)
    Covers federal construction-industry safety requirements involving electrical hazards, tools, personal protective equipment, ladders, scaffolds, excavation, material handling, and other construction jobsite conditions.
  • Code of Federal Regulations - 29 CFR 1910
    Provides OSHA general-industry safety standards covering workplace hazards, electrical safety requirements, equipment, safe work practices, and other occupational safety topics.
  • NFPA 70E - Standard for Electrical Safety in the Workplace, 2024
    Addresses electrical workplace safety including shock hazards, arc-flash hazards, risk assessment, approach boundaries, personal protective equipment, energized work, and electrically safe work conditions.
  • Ugly's Electrical References, 2023
    A practical electrical reference containing commonly used formulas, conductor information, motor data, calculations, conversions, electrical tables, and other field-oriented information useful for exam preparation.
  • NFPA 72 - National Fire Alarm Code, 2022
    Provides technical requirements involving fire alarm and signaling systems, circuits, initiating devices, notification appliances, installation requirements, and related system concepts.
  • Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications
    Supports review of voltage, current, resistance, power, circuits, electrical calculations, and other electrical fundamentals while connecting theory with NEC applications.

Test Information and Study Materials

A strong Nebraska NASCLA Journeyman Electrician study plan should begin with the 2023 National Electrical Code. Nebraska specifically identifies thorough knowledge of the NEC as an important part of successful examination preparation.

Rather than reading the NEC passively, candidates should practice answering questions that require them to locate specific requirements. Use the index, article numbers, tables, definitions, exceptions, and cross-references repeatedly until navigation becomes familiar.

Branch circuits and feeders should receive regular study. Review conductor sizing, ampacity, required circuits, continuous loads, overcurrent protection, voltage considerations, and the relationship between conductors and protective devices.

Services are another important journeyman-level subject. Candidates should understand service conductors, service equipment, disconnecting means, grounding, bonding, and related installation requirements.

Grounding and bonding frequently requires both code knowledge and careful terminology. Review grounding electrode systems, grounding electrode conductors, equipment grounding conductors, bonding jumpers, service bonding, separately derived systems, and sizing requirements.

Wiring methods should include raceways, cables, conductors, boxes, enclosures, fittings, support requirements, physical protection, conductor fill, box fill, and installation requirements for common wiring systems.

Motors and equipment require familiarity with conductor sizing, overcurrent protection, overload protection, disconnecting means, motor calculations, and related NEC tables. Candidates should practice recognizing when different motor calculations apply.

Electrical theory is another core preparation area. Review Ohm's law, power formulas, series circuits, parallel circuits, alternating current concepts, voltage, current, resistance, and other basic electrical relationships.

Use Understanding Electrical Theory for NEC Applications and Ugly's Electrical References to reinforce calculations and practical electrical formulas. Work through calculations repeatedly rather than relying only on memorization.

Construction safety should be reviewed using OSHA 29 CFR Part 1926. Journeyman electricians may encounter ladders, scaffolds, tools, temporary wiring, excavation, energized systems, material-handling hazards, and other construction-site conditions.

General-industry safety preparation should include applicable subjects from 29 CFR 1910. Candidates should understand how workplace electrical-safety requirements differ from construction-specific OSHA rules.

NFPA 70E should be used to reinforce electrical workplace safety concepts. Review shock risk, arc-flash risk, approach boundaries, protective equipment, work practices, and establishing electrically safe work conditions.

For fire alarm systems and emergency circuits, study relevant NEC requirements together with NFPA 72. Nebraska specifically identifies emergency circuits, including fire alarm circuits, among the subjects covered by its electrical examination program.

Blueprint reading is also identified as a Nebraska electrical examination subject. Candidates should be comfortable interpreting symbols, circuits, electrical layouts, equipment locations, and other information found on construction drawings.

When practicing, separate knowledge errors from navigation errors. If a question is missed because you selected the wrong NEC article, the solution is more code-navigation practice. If the problem is a calculation error, additional theory and math practice may be needed.

Timed practice is useful even for an open-book examination. Candidates should become comfortable determining when an answer is known immediately and when reference lookup is necessary. Efficient use of the books can preserve time for calculations and more difficult code questions.

1 Exam Prep supports Nebraska NASCLA Journeyman Electrician candidates with organized study guidance, electrician-focused technical review, practice-oriented preparation, electrical theory reinforcement, and code-navigation training.

Preparation can focus on NEC requirements, electrical theory, grounding and bonding, conductors, branch circuits, feeders, services, motors, wiring methods, safety, fire alarm systems, emergency circuits, calculations, and blueprint reading.

Open-book reference navigation is incorporated into the preparation approach. Candidates can practice finding NEC articles, tables, OSHA requirements, NFPA 70E safety provisions, NFPA 72 fire alarm information, and electrical formulas in the applicable references.

Practice-oriented study also helps candidates identify their weaker areas. An experienced electrician may be comfortable with field installation but need more work on theory, calculations, code lookup, NFPA 70E, or fire alarm requirements. Another candidate may understand calculations well but need additional practice with grounding and bonding or NEC navigation.

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors covers a broad range of construction knowledge. Exam Details

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is a standardized commercial building trade examination used by participating contractor licensing jurisdictions. South Carolina recognizes the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor exam as the technical examination equivalent for its Unlimited Building classification.

  • Exam: NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors
  • Number of Questions: 115
  • Time Allowed: 330 minutes
  • Minimum Passing Score: 70%, requiring 81 correct answers
  • South Carolina Classification: Unlimited Building
  • Additional South Carolina Requirement: South Carolina Business Management and Law for Commercial Contractors Exam
  • South Carolina Testing Provider: PSI

The current NASCLA examination content outline includes 25 questions on General Requirements, 15 on Site Construction, 6 on Concrete, 4 on Masonry, 6 on Metals, 5 on Wood, 5 on Thermal and Moisture Protection, 4 on Doors, Windows and Glazing, 5 on Finishes, 6 on Mechanical and Plumbing Systems, 3 on Electrical Systems, and 31 on Procurement and Contracting Requirements.

This distribution makes it important to prepare across the entire commercial construction scope. Procurement, contracting, and general requirements account for a substantial share of the examination, while technical trade subjects remain important throughout the test.

With 115 questions and 330 minutes available, time management should be part of your preparation. Open Book Test

The NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors is an Open Book Test. Approved reference materials may be used during the examination according to the applicable examination and testing-center requirements.

The open-book format makes reference familiarity especially important. Candidates should not approach the examination with the expectation that every answer can simply be searched from scratch. The reference library is extensive, and inefficient searching can consume valuable testing time.

A stronger strategy begins with understanding the construction topic. Read the question carefully, identify what subject is being tested, select the most relevant reference, locate the needed information, confirm the answer, and continue. This find-and-confirm process is more efficient than moving randomly between several books.

During preparation, become familiar with each reference's table of contents, index, chapter organization, technical tables, definitions, and terminology. Build direct associations between subjects and books. Accessibility questions should direct you toward ICC A117.1-2017. OSHA questions should point toward 29 CFR Part 1926. Structural concrete questions may require ACI 318-19, while broader commercial building-code questions may require the International Building Code.

Practice is especially useful because reference-navigation speed improves with repetition. The more frequently you work with the same books while studying, the easier it becomes to determine where to begin when a lookup is required.

Licensing Steps

  1. Determine the South Carolina contractor classification you need. Commercial contractor licenses are organized by classifications and subclassifications. The NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination is recognized as the technical exam equivalent for Unlimited Building.
  2. Identify the Primary Qualifying Party. South Carolina applicants must designate a Primary Qualifying Party for each classification or subclassification requested.
  3. Meet the applicable experience requirement. Applicants seeking qualifying-party certification by examination generally must document at least two years of applicable work experience performed within the previous five years.
  4. Complete the technical examination requirement. Candidates pursuing Unlimited Building may use the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors toward this requirement.
  5. Pass the South Carolina Business Management and Law examination. All individuals must pass the South Carolina Business Management and Law for Commercial Contractors Exam before requesting qualifying-party certification.
  6. Complete the qualifying-party certification process. Submit the applicable qualifying-party information and supporting documentation.
  7. Complete the contractor license application. The contractor business must submit the required licensing application to the South Carolina Contractor's Licensing Board.
  8. Meet applicable financial requirements. South Carolina uses license groups and project limitations supported by required financial documentation or qualifying surety bonds.
  9. Complete remaining business and licensing requirements. Submit the documentation applicable to the business entity and requested license group.

State Requirements

Commercial contractor licensing in South Carolina is administered by the South Carolina Contractor's Licensing Board. The Board regulates commercial general and mechanical contractor classifications and establishes the licensing requirements that apply to each classification and subclassification.

For the Unlimited Building classification, South Carolina recognizes the NASCLA Commercial General Building Contractor examination as an accepted technical examination equivalent. This allows candidates to use their NASCLA examination result toward the applicable technical exam requirement rather than completing a separate South Carolina Unlimited Building technical exam.

South Carolina still requires the Business Management and Law for Commercial Contractors Exam. The Board states that all individuals must pass this examination before requesting qualifying-party certification, regardless of how they are applying for licensure.

The contractor business must designate a Primary Qualifying Party for each applicable classification. Candidates qualifying by examination generally must also demonstrate at least two years of relevant work experience performed during the previous five years.

South Carolina commercial contractor licenses use financial group limitations. These groups determine the project-value range available to the license holder. Applicants must satisfy the financial requirements associated with the group they request through applicable financial documentation or an approved surety bond.

Passing the NASCLA examination does not automatically issue a South Carolina contractor license. The examination satisfies an accepted technical testing component. Applicants must still complete the qualifying-party, Business Management and Law, experience, financial, application, and other requirements established for South Carolina licensure.

This Georgia CILB NASCLA 5th Edition title appears on Georgia Secretary of State (Professional Licensing Boards Division) suggested reference lists for multiple Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board divisions, including:

  • Conditioned Air Contractors (listed as a reference that may be used during the examination)

Open Book Test

For several Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board exams, the official reference lists state that only the listed references may be used during the examination. Those same lists include a candidate notice that references may be highlighted, underlined, or tabbed with permanent tabs, and warn candidates not to bring photocopied materials or handwritten notes (even if pasted into the book).

Plumbing exception (important): Georgia’s plumbing reference list specifically states the Journeyman Plumber exam is open-book format, and that for all other plumbing exams the listed references may not be used during the examination. Always follow the current reference list for your exact exam and license class.

Licensing Steps

  1. Select your division and license class: Plumbing, Conditioned Air, Low Voltage, Electrical, or Utility (each has its own application and exam pathway).

  3. Receive exam eligibility/authorization: Follow your division’s instructions for scheduling with the testing provider.
  4. Use the current exam reference list: Confirm the exact references and editions required for your exam (and whether references are allowed in the testing room).
  5. Bring approved materials only: If your exam permits references, bring only what the list allows and keep the book compliant with the candidate notice.

Georgia Construction Industry Licensing Board requirements vary by division and license class. Test with Confidence!

  • The exam is OPEN BOOK

  • The exam has 115 questions, with a minimum passing score of 81
